This is because the influence of natures, spheres, stars, the sun and the moon is one and the same with respect to all things. Then we see that when a grape is produced, its skin has one nature, its seed another nature, its flesh a third nature, and its water a fourth nature. Indeed, we see in the rose that one face of a single leaf is in extreme yellowness, while the other face of that same leaf is in extreme redness, and that leaf is in extreme thinness and delicacy. We know by necessity that the relation of the stars and spheres to the two faces of that thin leaf is one and the same relation. And one nature in one matter produces only one effect. Do you not see that they said: the shape of the simple body is the sphere, because the influence of one nature on one matter must be uniform, and the shape whose all sides are alike is the sphere. Also, if we place wax, and five cubits of that wax are lit on one side, then a similar effect must occur on all sides, because the influencing nature must have a uniform relation to all sides.

Given this, we say: it is clear that the relation of the sun, moon, stars, spheres and natures to the two faces of that fine, thin leaf is one and the same relation. And it is established that when the influencing nature has one relation, the effect is uniform. And it is established that the effect is not uniform, because one face of that leaf is in extreme yellowness while the other face is in extreme redness. This indicates with certainty that the influencer in producing these attributes, colours and states is not nature, but the free, wise agent, who is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth of various colours﴾.

Know that since the basis of this argument is that an influencer that is essentially and naturally causative must have one and the same relation to all things, then when the senses show in these plant bodies the difference of their attributes and the variance of their states, it becomes clear that the influencer in them is not essentially necessary but a free agent. This is the complete statement of these proofs. It is established that the concluding of the first verse with His saying: ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, the second verse with His saying: ﴿for a people who use reason﴾, and the third verse with His saying: ﴿for a people who take heed﴾, is what draws attention to these precious benefits and clear proofs. Praise be to Allah for His kindnesses in religion and in this world.

The second issue: Ibn ʿAmir recited (wal-shamsu wal-qamaru wal-nujumu), all of them in the nominative case, as inceptive (mubtada'), with the predicate being His saying (musakhkharatun). Hafs from ʿAsim recited ﴿wal-nujumu﴾ in the nominative, so that His saying ﴿wal-nujumu﴾ is an inceptive. He was led to this only so that the word for subjection would not be repeated, since the Arabs do not say "I subjected this thing, subjected." Its answer is that the meaning is that He, exalted is He, subjected these things for us while they are subjected under His power and will. This is the sound statement, and the sense: He, exalted is He, subjected these things for mankind and made them suited to their interests while they are subjected under the power, command and permission of Allah, exalted is He. On this interpretation, the repetition devoid of benefit is not necessary. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Taskhir (subjection) is an expression for compulsion and forcing, and this is fitting only for one who is capable and can compel. How then is this valid regarding night and day, and regarding inanimate things, the sun and the moon?

The answer is in two ways:

The first: When He arranged these things in one manner conforming to the interests of the servants, they became like an obedient, submissive servant. For this reason, this kind of arrangement was termed subjection.

As for the second answer: it holds only according to the doctrine of the astronomers. They say: the natural motion of the sun and the moon is the motion from west to east, and Allah moves these stars by means of the motion of the greatest sphere from east to west. So this motion is forced, and for this reason the word "taskhir" was used regarding it.

The second question: If the occurrence of night and day comes about only through the motions of the sun, then mentioning night and day would suffice without mentioning the sun.

The answer: the occurrence of day and night is not due to the motion of the sun; rather, their occurrence is due to the motion of the greatest sphere, whose motion we have shown is nothing but by the motion of Allah, glorified is He. As for the motion of the sun, it is the cause of the occurrence of the year, not of the day.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿subjected by His command﴾, when the one who effects subjection is power, not command?

The answer: this verse is based on whether the spheres and stars are inanimate or not. Most Muslims hold that they are inanimate, and therefore they interpreted the command in this verse as creation and decree. The word "amr" with the meaning of affair and act occurs frequently; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. Some people say that they are not inanimate, and in that case the command is interpreted as permission and obligation. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 14:**

[The Qur'anic verse:] ﴿It is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it tender meat and extract from it ornaments which you wear. And you see the ships plowing through it, and that you may seek of His bounty and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, argued for the existence of God, first through the bodies of the heavens, second through the human body and soul, third through the wonders of the creation of animals, and fourth through the wonders of the natures of plants, He mentioned, as the fifth level, the proof of the existence of the Creator through the wonders of the states of the elements. He began with the element of water.

[p. 6]

Know that the astronomers (ʿulamaʾ al-hayʾa, the scholars of cosmology) said: three-quarters of the sphere of the earth is submerged in water. That is the Surrounding Ocean (al-bahr al-muhit), and it is the totality of the element of water. In this inhabited quarter there are seven seas, as He said after this: ﴿And the sea, which is extended by seven seas after it﴾ [Luqman: 27]. The sea which God, exalted is He, subjected for people is these seas. The meaning of God subjecting them to creation is making them such that people are able to benefit from them, either by riding or by diving.

Know that the benefits of the seas are many, and God, exalted is He, mentioned three types of them in this verse.

* * *

The first benefit: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may eat from it tender meat﴾. Concerning this there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "laḥm ṭariyy" (tender meat) is without hamza. It is said: ṭaruwa, yaṭruwu, ṭarāwa (ṭarāwa being the verbal noun). Al-Farraʾ said: ṭaraʾa, yaṭraʾu, ṭarāʾan (with a hamza, lengthened) and ṭarāwa, just as it is said: shaqiya, yashqā, shaqāʾan and shaqāwa.

Know that in mentioning the tender there is additional benefit, because if all fish were salty, one would not know through it of the power of God, exalted is He, what is known through the tender. For when from the salty, brackish sea there came out an animal whose flesh is extremely sweet, it is known that this came about not according to nature, but by the power and wisdom of God, in that He manifested the opposite from the opposite.

The second issue: Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: if someone swears not to eat meat and then eats fish meat, he does not break his oath. They said: because fish flesh is not meat. Others said: he does break it, because God, exalted is He, explicitly stated in this verse that it is meat, and there is no clarification beyond God's clarification. It is narrated that when Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said this statement, Sufyan al-Thawri heard it and denounced him for it, and argued against him with this verse. [Abu Hanifa] sent a man to him and asked him about a man who swore not to pray on a carpet, and then prayed on the ground: does he break the oath or not? Sufyan said: he does not break it. The questioner said: Did not God, exalted is He, say: ﴿And God has made the earth for you a carpet﴾ [Nuh: 19]? He said: Sufyan then realized that this had been by the prompting of Abu Hanifa.

It may be said: this statement is not strong, because at most in this matter we have abandoned acting on the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in the word "carpet" due to the evidence that has established that. So how is it binding on us to abandon acting on the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in another verse? The difference between the two cases is in two respects:

The first: If he swore not to pray on a carpet, then if we were to include the earth under the word "carpet," we would have to prevent him from praying, because if he prays on earth spread with a carpet, he will inevitably break his oath, and if he prays on earth that is not spread, he will also break it, on the assumption that the earth is included under the word "carpet." So this would require preventing him from praying, and that is something with no way to it. This is unlike when we include fish meat under the word "meat," because there is no prohibited consequence in forbidding him from eating meat in general. So the difference is clear.

The second: We know necessarily from the usage of the people of language that the application of the name "carpet" to bare earth is metaphorical. As for the application of the name "meat" to fish meat, it is not known to be metaphorical. So the difference is clear, and God knows best.

The argument of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him: oaths are based on custom, and the custom of people, when "meat" is mentioned without qualification, is that fish meat is not understood from it. The evidence: if a man says to his servant, "Buy meat with these dirhams," and he brings fish, he deserves to be denounced.

The answer: We have seen you in the book of oaths sometimes considering the wording and sometimes considering custom, and we have not seen you mention a fixed rule distinguishing the two categories.

[p. 7]

The evidence for this: if he says to his servant, "Buy meat with these dirhams," and he brings sparrow meat, he deserves to be denounced for it, even though you say that he breaks the oath by eating sparrow meat. So it is established that custom is inconsistent, and returning to the text of the Qur'an is required. And God knows best.

The second benefit from the benefits of the sea is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾. By "ornaments" is meant pearls and coral, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22]. And by "their wearing" is meant the wearing of their women, because the women are part of them, and because their undertaking to adorn themselves with these is for their sake. So they are their adornment and their clothing. I saw some of our companions (scholars of our school) relying, on the question that zakat is not obligatory on permissible jewelry, on the hadith of ʿUrwa from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There is no zakat on jewelry." I said: this hadith is weak in its transmission. Even if it is authentic, it can be said about it: the word "al-ḥulī" (the jewelry) is a singular noun with the definite article, and we have explained in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣul al-fiqh, legal theory) that this kind of wording must be understood as referring to what is previously known. What is previously known as jewelry is what God, exalted is He, mentioned in His Book in this verse, which is His saying: ﴿and that you extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾. So, granting the soundness of that report, there is no zakat on pearls, and in that case the argument from it falls away. And God knows best.

The third benefit: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see the ships plowing through it, and that you may seek of His bounty﴾. The people of language said: the "makhr" of a ship is its cutting of the water with its prow. And it is narrated from al-Farraʾ that it is the sound of the ship's running with the winds.

Knowing this, the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas: "mawākhir" meaning "jawārī" (running), the explanation with it is fitting only because they do not cut the water except when they are running. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ means: that you may ride it for trade, so you seek profit from God's bounty. And when you find God's bounty and His beneficence, perhaps you will proceed to thank Him. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb, "The Keys to the Unseen") on Surah 16, verses 15–16:**

The Almighty says: ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided﴾ ﴿and landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾.

Know that the purpose of this verse is to mention some of the blessings that God, exalted is He, has created upon the earth.

The first blessing is His saying: ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you.﴾ On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ means "so that it does not shake with you," according to the Kufans, and "for fear that it might shake with you," according to the Basrans. We discussed this at His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176]. *Al-maid* (the sway) is movement and agitation to the right and left. It is said: *mada yameedu maydan* (it swayed).

**The second issue:** The well-known view of the majority (al-Jumhur) regarding the interpretation of this verse is that they said: when a ship is set upon the surface of the water, it sways from side to side and is agitated. When heavy loads are placed in that ship, it settles upon the surface of the water and becomes stable. They said: likewise, when God, exalted is He, created the earth upon the surface of the water, it was agitated and swayed, so God created upon it these heavy mountains, and it settled upon the surface of the water by virtue of the weight of these mountains.

[p. 8]

One may object: this raises difficulties in several respects.

**The first:** This causal explanation either is stated while accepting that the earth and water are heavy by nature, or while denying this principle and holding that the movements of these bodies are either by their natures or not by their natures but are brought about by the creation of the free Agent (al-Fa'il al-Mukhtar). As for the first assumption, this explanation is problematic, because on this principle there is no doubt that the earth is heavier than the water, and what is heavier than water sinks into the water and does not remain floating upon it. And if it does not remain floating upon it, it is impossible to say that it sways, inclines, and is agitated. This is unlike the ship, because it is made of wood, and within the wood there are cavities filled with air; for this reason the piece of wood remains floating upon the water, and then it is agitated, sways, and inclines upon the surface of the water. When it is anchored with heavy bodies, it settles and becomes calm, and the difference becomes apparent. As for the second assumption, which is that neither the earth nor the water has natures that necessitate heaviness and sinking, and that the earth only descends because God, exalted is He, has made His custom to be so, and that the water came to surround the earth merely through the enactment of custom, and there is no nature in the earth or in the water that necessitates a specific state, then we say: on this assumption, the cause of the earth's stillness is that God creates stillness in it, and the cause of its being swaying and agitated is that God creates movement in it. And on this assumption, the claim that the earth was inclining, so God created the mountains and anchored them upon it so that it would remain still, is also invalid; because this would only be sound if the nature of the earth necessitated swaying and the nature of the mountains necessitated anchoring and firmness. And we are now speaking on the assumption of the negation of the natures that necessitate these states. Thus it is established that this explanation is problematic on every assumption.

**The second question:** The anchoring of the earth by the mountains is only intelligible for the purpose of the earth remaining upon the surface of the water without swaying and inclining from side to side. This is only intelligible if the water upon whose surface the earth rests is stationary. So we say: what requires the stillness of that water and its standing in its specific place? If you say: what requires its stillness in that specific place is that its particular nature necessitates its standing in that specific location, then why do you not say the same of the earth, namely that the particular nature of the earth necessitates its standing in that specific place, and this would imply that the earth only stood because God anchored it with the mountains? If you say: what requires the stillness of the water in its specific place is that God, by His power, made the water still in that specific place, then why do you not say the same regarding the stillness of the earth? And then this explanation is also invalid.

**The third question:** The totality of the earth is a great body. Even if its whole were to sway and be agitated upon the surface of the encompassing sea, that state would not appear to people.

If it is said: Do not the vapors trapped within the earth move it during earthquakes, and those movements appear to people? Why then do you deny the claim of the one who says: "Were it not for the mountains, the earth would move; but since God anchored it with heavy mountains, the winds were unable to move it"?

We say: those vapors are only trapped within a small piece of the earth, so when movement occurs in that small piece, that movement appears. Those who hold this view say: the appearance of movement in that particular piece of the earth is like a twitching occurring in a specific limb of the human body. But if the whole earth were moved, that movement would not appear. Do you not see that the one who is inside a ship does not sense the movement of the whole ship, even though it is moving at the swiftest and strongest pace? So it is likewise here. This is what is in this place of subtle and profound discussions.

What I hold concerning this problematic point is this: it is established by certain proofs that the earth is a sphere, and it is established that these mountains upon the surface of this sphere function as roughnesses occurring on the face of this sphere.

Having established this, we say: if we suppose that these roughnesses did not exist, and the earth were a true sphere, free of roughnesses and elevations, it would become such that it would rotate by circular motion with the slightest cause. For a simple round body either necessarily has to be moving in circular motion upon its own axis, or, even if this is not necessitated by reason, it moves in this manner with the slightest cause. Now, since these mountains exist upon the outer surface of the sphere of the earth, and they are like the roughnesses on the face of the sphere, each one of these mountains by its nature inclines toward the center of the world, and the inclination of that mountain toward the center of the world, with its great weight and its strong force, functions as a stake that prevents the sphere of the earth from rotating circularly. Thus the creation of these mountains upon the face of the earth is like stakes driven into the sphere, preventing it from circular motion. So they prevent the earth from swaying, inclining, and agitation; in other words, they prevent the earth from circular motion. This is the conclusion that my inquiry has reached in this matter. And God knows best His intent.

\* \* \*

**The second blessing:** Among the blessings that God, exalted is He, has made manifest upon the face of the earth is that He caused the rivers to flow upon the face of the earth. Know that two investigations arise here.

**The first investigation:** His saying ﴿and rivers﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "He cast firm mountains and rivers." The creation of rivers may well be called "casting," so it is said: "He cast rivers into the earth," just as He said: ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾ [Qaf: 7]. Casting means placing or making. Do you not see that in another verse He said: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it and blessed it﴾ [Fussilat: 10]? And casting is close to sending down, because casting indicates throwing something from above to below; however, what is meant by this casting is placing and creating, as He said: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39].

**The second investigation:** It is established in the rational sciences that most rivers have their springs gushing forth in the mountains. For this reason, when God mentioned the mountains, He followed their mention with the gushing forth of springs and rivers.

\* \* \*

**The third blessing:** His saying ﴿and roads, that you may be guided﴾, which is also coordinated with His saying ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "And He cast into the earth roads." Its meaning is that He made them manifest and clear so that you might be guided by them in your journeys. A parallel to this is His saying in another verse: ﴿and He threaded for you therein roads﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53]. And His saying ﴿that you may be guided﴾ means: so that you may be guided.

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned that He had made manifest in the earth specific roads, He also mentioned that He had made manifest in it specific landmarks, so that the responsible person (al-mukallaf) could be enabled to reason by them and thereby reach his destination through them. So He said: ﴿and landmarks﴾. This is also coordinated with His saying ﴿in the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "And He cast into the earth firm mountains, and He cast into it rivers and roads, and He cast into it landmarks." By "landmarks" is meant the markers of the paths, which are the things by which one is guided. These landmarks are the mountains and the winds. I have seen a group of people who smell the earth, and through that smelling they recognize the roads.

Al-Akhfash said: the speech is complete at His saying ﴿and landmarks﴾, and His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is a separate statement from the first. The intended meaning of "the star" is the category (al-jins), as when you say: "the dirham has become abundant in the hands of the people."

[p. 10]

According to al-Suddi, it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Guards (al-Farqadan), the Bear's daughters (Banat Na'sh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi). Al-Hasan recited (*wa-bin-nujum*) with two dammas and a damma followed by a sukun, which is the plural of *najm*, like *rahn* and *rUhun*, and the sukun is for lightening. It is also said that the waw was dropped from *al-najm* for lightening.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ is addressed to those present, while His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is addressed to those absent; what is the reason for this?

We say: The Quraysh used to undertake many journeys in search of wealth, and whoever travels much has greater and more complete knowledge of the benefits gained from being guided by the stars. So His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is a reference to the Quraysh, for the reason we have mentioned. And God knows best.

The exegetes differed. Some of them said: His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is specific to the sea, because when God mentioned the nature of the sea and the benefits within it, He clarified that those who travel upon it are guided by the star. Others said: rather, it is general, encompassing travel by land and by sea, and this view is preferable, because it is more comprehensive as a blessing, and because being guided by the star may occur at both times together. Some jurists take this as evidence that a traveler who is confused about the direction of the qiblah (the direction of prayer) must seek guidance by the stars and by the landmarks upon the earth, which are the mountains and the winds. This is correct, because just as it is possible to be guided by these landmarks in knowing the paths and routes, it is likewise possible to reason by them in seeking the qiblah.

Know that confusion about the qiblah either occurs with clear indications or it does not. If the indications are clear, it is obligatory to exert effort (al-ijtihad, i.e., independent reasoned effort) and to face the direction in which one's strong assumption (ghalabat al-zann) is that it is the qiblah. If the error becomes clear, repetition of the prayer is obligatory, because he was negligent in what was required of him. If the indications do not appear, then there are two ways:

The first way: he has the choice to pray toward whatever direction he wishes, because since the directions are equal and preference is impossible, only choice remains.

The second way: he prays toward all the directions, and then he knows with certainty that he has discharged his obligation. This is like what the jurists say concerning one who forgot a prayer and does not know which one it was specifically: the obligation upon him in making up the missed prayer is to perform the five prayers, so that he may be certain of having fulfilled what was incumbent upon him. Some say that only one of them is obligatory, but this is an error, because since he is required to perform them all, all of them become obligatory, even though the cause of the obligation of each of these prayers is the missing of one prayer. And God knows best.

What I hold concerning this problematic point is this: it is established by certain proofs that the earth is a sphere, and it is established that these mountains upon the surface of this sphere function as roughnesses occurring on the face of this sphere.

Having established this, we say: if we suppose that these roughnesses did not exist, and the earth were a true sphere, free of roughnesses and elevations, it would become such that it would rotate by circular motion with the slightest cause. For a simple round body either necessarily has to be moving in circular motion upon its own axis, or, even if this is not necessitated by reason, it moves in this manner with the slightest cause. Now, since these mountains exist upon the outer surface of the sphere of the earth, and they are like the roughnesses on the face of the sphere, each one of these mountains by its nature inclines toward the center of the world, and the inclination of that mountain toward the center of the world, with its great weight and its strong force, functions as a stake that prevents the sphere of the earth from rotating circularly. Thus the creation of these mountains upon the face of the earth is like stakes driven into the sphere, preventing it from circular motion. So they prevent the earth from swaying, inclining, and agitation; in other words, they prevent the earth from circular motion. This is the conclusion that my inquiry has reached in this matter. And God knows best His intent.

\* \* \*

**The second blessing:** Among the blessings that God, exalted is He, has made manifest upon the face of the earth is that He caused the rivers to flow upon the face of the earth. Know that two investigations arise here.

**The first investigation:** His saying ﴿and rivers﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "He cast firm mountains and rivers." The creation of rivers may well be called "casting," so it is said: "He cast rivers into the earth," just as He said: ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾ [Qaf: 7]. Casting means placing or making. Do you not see that in another verse He said: ﴿And He placed in it firm mountains above it and blessed it﴾ [Fussilat: 10]? And casting is close to sending down, because casting indicates throwing something from above to below; however, what is meant by this casting is placing and creating, as He said: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39].

**The second investigation:** It is established in the rational sciences that most rivers have their springs gushing forth in the mountains. For this reason, when God mentioned the mountains, He followed their mention with the gushing forth of springs and rivers.

\* \* \*

**The third blessing:** His saying ﴿and roads, that you may be guided﴾, which is also coordinated with His saying ﴿And He has cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "And He cast into the earth roads." Its meaning is that He made them manifest and clear so that you might be guided by them in your journeys. A parallel to this is His saying in another verse: ﴿and He threaded for you therein roads﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53]. And His saying ﴿that you may be guided﴾ means: so that you may be guided.

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned that He had made manifest in the earth specific roads, He also mentioned that He had made manifest in it specific landmarks, so that the responsible person (al-mukallaf) could be enabled to reason by them and thereby reach his destination through them. So He said: ﴿and landmarks﴾. This is also coordinated with His saying ﴿in the earth firm mountains﴾, and the implied meaning is: "And He cast into the earth firm mountains, and He cast into it rivers and roads, and He cast into it landmarks." By "landmarks" is meant the markers of the paths, which are the things by which one is guided. These landmarks are the mountains and the winds. I have seen a group of people who smell the earth, and through that smelling they recognize the roads.

Al-Akhfash said: the speech is complete at His saying ﴿and landmarks﴾, and His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is a separate statement from the first. The intended meaning of "the star" is the category (al-jins), as when you say: "the dirham has become abundant in the hands of the people."

[p. 10]

According to al-Suddi, it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Guards (al-Farqadan), the Bear's daughters (Banat Na'sh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi). Al-Hasan recited (*wa-bin-nujum*) with two dammas and a damma followed by a sukun, which is the plural of *najm*, like *rahn* and *rUhun*, and the sukun is for lightening. It is also said that the waw was dropped from *al-najm* for lightening.

If it is asked: His saying ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ is addressed to those present, while His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is addressed to those absent; what is the reason for this?

We say: The Quraysh used to undertake many journeys in search of wealth, and whoever travels much has greater and more complete knowledge of the benefits gained from being guided by the stars. So His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is a reference to the Quraysh, for the reason we have mentioned. And God knows best.

The exegetes differed. Some of them said: His saying ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ is specific to the sea, because when God mentioned the nature of the sea and the benefits within it, He clarified that those who travel upon it are guided by the star. Others said: rather, it is general, encompassing travel by land and by sea, and this view is preferable, because it is more comprehensive as a blessing, and because being guided by the star may occur at both times together. Some jurists take this as evidence that a traveler who is confused about the direction of the qiblah (the direction of prayer) must seek guidance by the stars and by the landmarks upon the earth, which are the mountains and the winds. This is correct, because just as it is possible to be guided by these landmarks in knowing the paths and routes, it is likewise possible to reason by them in seeking the qiblah.

Know that confusion about the qiblah either occurs with clear indications or it does not. If the indications are clear, it is obligatory to exert effort (al-ijtihad, i.e., independent reasoned effort) and to face the direction in which one's strong assumption (ghalabat al-zann) is that it is the qiblah. If the error becomes clear, repetition of the prayer is obligatory, because he was negligent in what was required of him. If the indications do not appear, then there are two ways:

The first way: he has the choice to pray toward whatever direction he wishes, because since the directions are equal and preference is impossible, only choice remains.

The second way: he prays toward all the directions, and then he knows with certainty that he has discharged his obligation. This is like what the jurists say concerning one who forgot a prayer and does not know which one it was specifically: the obligation upon him in making up the missed prayer is to perform the five prayers, so that he may be certain of having fulfilled what was incumbent upon him. Some say that only one of them is obligatory, but this is an error, because since he is required to perform them all, all of them become obligatory, even though the cause of the obligation of each of these prayers is the missing of one prayer. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 16, verses 17–21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾ ﴿They are dead, not living; and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾

On the verse, there are several issues.

The first issue: Allah, having mentioned the proofs that point to the existence of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, in the best arrangement and most perfect order, and since those proofs were both proofs and an explanation and detailing of the kinds of Allah's blessings and the varieties of His beneficence, He followed them with the refutation of worship of other than Allah, Exalted is He. The purpose is this: since these dazzling proofs and manifest, overpowering evidences point to the existence of a powerful, wise God, and it has been established that He is the Master of all these blessings and the Giver of all these good things, how is it reasonable for minds to occupy themselves with worshipping another existent, especially when that existent is an inanimate object that neither understands nor has power? For this reason, after those verses, He said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ The meaning is: Is He who creates these things we have mentioned like one who creates nothing, rather who is absolutely incapable of anything? Will you not then remember? For this matter does not require reflection, contemplation, or deliberation. It suffices that you take heed of what is in your intellects, namely that worship is fitting only for the Greatest Benefactor. You see in the visible world a rational, understanding human who bestows a great blessing, yet you know that worshipping him is ugly. These idols are pure inanimate objects, having no understanding, no power, and no will. How, then, do you venture to worship them? And how do you consider it permissible to occupy yourselves with serving and obeying them?

The second issue: The intended meaning of His words ﴿like one who creates not﴾ is the idols, and that they are inanimate, so the word "man" (*man*) does not fittingly apply to them, since it is used for those of knowledge. This has been answered in several ways.

The first way: Since the unbelievers named them gods and worshipped them, they were consequently treated as those of knowledge. Do you not see that He then said: ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾

The second answer: the reason for it is the parallelism between it and "He who creates" (*man yakhluqu*).

The third answer: the meaning is that He who creates is not like those of knowledge who create not, so how much less one who has no knowledge at all? This is like His words: ﴿Do they have feet with which to walk?﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:195). That is, the gods you invoke are of a status lower than those who have feet, hands, ears, and hearts, because those are living and these are dead. So how could worship of them be valid for them? The point is not that if these limbs were valid for them, worship of them would be valid.

If it is said: The purpose of His words ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ is to put the idol-worshippers under obligation, since they made what does not create equal to the Creator in being named a god and in being occupied in worshipping it. Therefore, the proper form of the rebuke should have been: "Is one who creates not like one who creates?"

The answer: The meaning is that He who creates these great things and gives these noble benefits—how can He be made equal to these base inanimate objects in being named by the name of God, and in being occupied with worshipping them and proceeding to the utmost exaltation of them? So this meaning was expressed by His words: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾

* * *

The third issue: Some of our companions (i.e., the Ash'arite school) argued by this verse that the servant is not a creator of his own acts. They said: He, Exalted is He, distinguished Himself from all the other things that they used to worship by the attribute of creating, because His words ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ are intended to show that He is distinguished from the rivals by the attribute of creating, and that He deserved divinity and being worshipped only by virtue of being the Creator. This indicates that if the servant were a creator of some things, it would necessarily follow that he is a god worthy of worship. Since that is false, we know that the servant has no power to create and originate. The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) said: The answer to this is in several ways.

The first way: The meaning is: Is He who creates what has been mentioned before, of the heavens and the earth, the human being, the animals, the plants, the seas, the stars, and the mountains, like one who has no power to create anything at all? This indicates that whoever is a creator of these things is a god, but it does not follow from this that whoever has power over his own acts should be a god.

The second way: The meaning of the verse is that whoever is a creator is more excellent than one who is not a creator, so it is necessary to forbid equating the two in divinity and being worshipped. This degree alone does not indicate that every creator must be a god. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿Do they have feet with which to walk?﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:195). Its meaning is that the one who has a foot with which he walks is more excellent than the one who has a foot with which he cannot walk. This requires that the human being is more excellent than the idol, and the more excellent is not fitting to worship the lowlier. This is the intended point of this verse. Then, it does not indicate that whoever has a foot with which he walks must be a god. Likewise, here the purpose of this verse is to show that the Creator is more excellent than the non-creator, so the equating of the two in divinity and being worshipped is impossible. It does not follow from this that the mere possession of the attribute of creating makes one a god.

The third answer: Many of the Mu'tazila do not apply the term "creator" to the servant. Al-Ka'bi said in his *Tafsir*: We do not say that we create our acts. He said: Whoever applies that has erred, except in places that Allah mentioned, such as His words: ﴿And when you were creating from clay like the form of a bird﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:110) and His words: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:14).

Know that the followers of Abu Hashim apply the term "creator" to the servant. Indeed, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Basri went so far as to say: The application of the word "creator" to the servant is literal, and to Allah it is figurative, because "creating" means "estimating" (*taqdir*), and that means "supposing and reckoning," which exists in the case of the servant but is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He.

Know that these answers are strong, but using this verse as evidence for the soundness of our school is not strong. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His words ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, Exalted is He, showed in the previous verse that occupying oneself with worship of other than Allah is false and mistaken, He showed in this verse that the servant cannot perform the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, nor thank Him for His blessings, nor fulfil the rights of His generosity, in a perfect and complete manner. Rather, even if the servant exhausts himself in performing acts of obedience and worship, and exaggerates in thanking Allah for His blessing, he will still be deficient. This is because occupying oneself with thanking blessings is conditional upon knowing those blessings in detail and comprehensively. For whatever is not conceived, understood, or known, it is impossible to occupy oneself with thanking it. However, knowledge of the blessings of Allah in detail is not attained by the servant, because the blessings of Allah are many, their kinds and branches are vast and great, and the intellects of creatures are too short to encompass their origins, let alone their ends, and they are not known in detail. What is like this makes it impossible to occupy oneself with thanking Him in the manner that would be fitting for those blessings. This is the understanding of His words: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾, meaning: you do not know them in complete and perfect fashion, and if you do not know them, it is impossible for you to fulfil thanking them in complete and perfect fashion. This indicates that the thanks of the creature falls short of the blessings of the Real (al-Haqq), that the acts of obedience of creatures fall short of the lordship of the Real, and that the knowledge of creatures falls short of the reality of the majesty of the Real. Among what decisively indicates that the intellects of creatures fall short of knowing the kinds of Allah's blessings is that if any slight defect appeared in any part of the human body, life would become miserable for the human being, and he would wish to spend the whole world in order that this defect might be removed from him. Then, Allah, Exalted is He, manages the states of the human body in the most perfect and most beneficial manner, although the human being has no knowledge of the existence of that part, nor of how its benefits operate, nor of how to repel its harms. So let this example be present in your mind. Then reflect on all that Allah created in this world of minerals, plants, and animals, and made ready for your benefit, until you know that the intellects of creatures perish in understanding the wisdom of the All-Merciful in creating the human being, let alone the other aspects of grace and kindness.

If it is said: Since you established that occupying oneself with thanks depends upon attaining knowledge of the kinds of blessings, and you demonstrated that attaining knowledge of the kinds of blessings is impossible or does not occur, how then did Allah command creatures to perform the thanking of blessings?

We say: The way to it is that one thanks Allah, Exalted is He, for all His blessings, both detailed and summarized. This is the way by which it is possible to discharge the obligation of thanks. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Some have said: Allah has no blessing upon unbelievers. Most have said: Allah has many blessings upon both the unbeliever and the believer. The evidence for this is that the bestowal through creating the heavens and the earth, the bestowal through creating the human being from a drop of semen, the bestowal through creating livestock, horses, mules, and donkeys, and through creating kinds of blessings such as grain, olives, date palms, and grapes, and through subjecting the sea so that the human being may eat fresh meat from it and extract ornaments from it to wear—all of these are shared between believer and unbeliever. Then He, Exalted is He, emphasized this by His words: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾, and this indicates that all these things are blessings from Allah, Exalted is He, with respect to everyone. This indicates that Allah's blessings reach the unbelievers. And Allah knows best.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: know that He, Exalted is He, said in the surah of Ibrahim: ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is a wrongdoer and ungrateful﴾ (Ibrahim 14:34), and here He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The meaning is: since He showed that the human being cannot perform the thanking in detail, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful,﴾ that is, Forgiving of the shortcoming that proceeds from you in thanking His blessings, Merciful to you in that He did not cut off His blessings upon you because of your shortcoming.

As for His words: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾, there are two explanations:

The first: The unbelievers, while occupied with worshipping other than Allah, Exalted is He, were secretly devising various forms of disbelief in plots against the Messenger, peace be upon him. So this was a deterrent to them from those things.

The second: In the first verse He, Exalted is He, rejected the worship of idols on the ground that they have no power to create or to bestow blessings. In this verse He also rejected their worship, on the ground that the God must necessarily know the secret and the open, while these idols are inanimate objects with no knowledge of anything at all. So how could their worship be fitting?

As for His words: ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created﴾, know that He, Exalted is He, described these idols with many attributes.

The first attribute: They create nothing, and they are themselves created. Hafs, from 'Asim, read "yusirruna" (they conceal), "yu'linuna" (they declare), and "yud'awna" (they are invoked) all with the *ya'* (third person, the report about an absent party). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "yad'una" (they invoke) with the *ya'* alone, in the third person, while "tusirruna" and "tu'linuna" with the *ta'* (second person, addressing the audience). The rest read all of them with the *ta'*, in the second person, as a conjunction with what precedes it.

Then if it is said: Did not His saying at the beginning of the verse, ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾, indicate that these idols create nothing, and His saying here, ﴿They create nothing﴾, indicate the very same meaning, so that this would be pure repetition?

Its answer: What is mentioned at the beginning of the verse is that they create nothing, while what is mentioned here is that they create nothing and that they are themselves created for others. This is therefore an addition in meaning. It is as if the Exalted began by explaining their deficiency in their own essences and attributes: first He clarified that they create nothing, then secondly that just as they do not create others, they are themselves created for others.

The second attribute is His saying: ﴿They are dead, not living﴾. The meaning is that if they were gods in reality, they would be living, not dead; that is, death would not be permissible for them, like the Living who does not die, glory be to Him and exalted. The matter of these idols is the opposite of that.

Then if it is said: When He said ﴿dead﴾, it was known that they are not living, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿not living﴾?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: The god is the Living who does not, after His life, undergo death, whereas these idols are dead, and after their death there is no life for them.

The second: This speech is addressed to the disbelievers who worship idols, who are in the extreme of ignorance and misguidance. Whoever speaks with an ignorant, dull, stupid person may well express one meaning with many expressions, its purpose being to inform that addressee of his extreme stupidity, and that the speaker repeats those words only because that listener is in the extreme of ignorance and does not understand the intended meaning from a single expression.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised up﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿they do not perceive﴾ refers to the idols. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿they will be raised up﴾, there are two views:

One of them: It refers to the worshippers of the idols. That is, the idols do not perceive when their worshippers will be raised up. In this there is a mockery of the polytheists, and that their gods do not know the time of their resurrection, so how could there be for them a time of recompense from them for their worship?

The second: It refers to the idols. That is, these idols do not know when God the Exalted will raise them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: God will raise the idols, and they will have spirits, and with them their devils, and they will be commanded to the Fire.

Then if it is said: The idols are inanimate objects, and inanimate objects are not described as dead, nor is it said of them that "they do not perceive" such-and-such.

The answer to this is in several respects:

The first: An inanimate thing may be described as dead. God the Exalted said: ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ [al-Rum: 19].

The second: When the people ascribed to those idols divinity and worship, it was said to them: The matter is not so; rather they are dead and know nothing, so these expressions came in accordance with their own belief.

The third: That what is meant by His saying ﴿And those whom they call upon besides God﴾ is the angels, and some of the disbelievers worshipped them. God said: They are dead, having inevitably to undergo death, not living, that is, their life is not lasting. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised up﴾, that is, they have no knowledge of the time of their resurrection. And God knows best.

The third: That what is meant by His saying ﴿And those whom they call upon besides God﴾ is the angels, and some of the disbelievers worshipped them. And God knows best.

The first issue: Allah, having mentioned the proofs that point to the existence of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, in the best arrangement and most perfect order, and since those proofs were both proofs and an explanation and detailing of the kinds of Allah's blessings and the varieties of His beneficence, He followed them with the refutation of worship of other than Allah, Exalted is He. Will you not then remember?﴾ The meaning is: Is He who creates these things we have mentioned like one who creates nothing, rather who is absolutely incapable of anything? Will you not then remember? For this matter does not require reflection, contemplation, or deliberation. It suffices that you take heed of what is in your intellects, namely that worship is fitting only for the Greatest Benefactor. You see in the visible world a rational, understanding human who bestows a great blessing, yet you know that worshipping him is ugly. These idols are pure inanimate objects, having no understanding, no power, and no will. How, then, do you venture to worship them? The first way: Since the unbelievers named them gods and worshipped them, they were consequently treated as those of knowledge. Do you not see that He then said: ﴿And those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are themselves created.﴾

The second answer: the reason for it is the parallelism between it and "He who creates" (*man yakhluqu*).

This is like His words: ﴿Do they have feet with which to walk?﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:195). That is, the gods you invoke are of a status lower than those who have feet, hands, ears, and hearts, because those are living and these are dead. So how could worship of them be valid for them? The answer: The meaning is that He who creates these great things and gives these noble benefits—how can He be made equal to these base inanimate objects in being named by the name of God, and in being occupied with worshipping them and proceeding to the utmost exaltation of them? So this meaning was expressed by His words: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 22–23:

Page 15

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had refuted in what preceded the way of the worshippers of idols and statues, and had demonstrated the corruption of their doctrine by overwhelming proofs, He said: ﴿Your God is one God.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what it was that made the disbelievers persist in saying there is partnership (shirk) and in denying monotheism (tawhid), so He said: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ The meaning is: those who believe in the Hereafter, who desire to win the lasting reward and fear falling into the lasting punishment, when they hear the proofs and the encouragement and the warning, they fear the punishment, so they reflect and contemplate what they hear. Therefore, they benefit from hearing the proofs and return from falsehood to truth. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter and deny it, they do not desire to obtain the reward, nor do they fear falling into the punishment. So they remain denying every speech that contradicts their own view, and they are arrogant about returning to the words of others. Therefore they remain persisting in the ignorance and misguidance in which they were.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ The meaning is: He, exalted is He, knows that their persistence in these corrupt doctrines is not due to a doubt they have conceived or a problem they have imagined, but rather it is due to blind imitation (taqlid), aversion to returning to the truth, zealous devotion to supporting the doctrines of their forefathers, and pride and haughtiness. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ And this threat encompasses all the arrogant.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 24–25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had thoroughly established the proofs of monotheism and presented the overpowering evidences refuting the doctrines of the idol-worshippers, He then mentioned the doubts of those who deny prophethood, together with the answers to them.

The first doubt: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) argued for the truth of his own prophethood by the Qur'an being a miracle, they attacked the Qur'an and said, "It is tales of the ancients," and it is not of the kind of miracles. In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: They differed about who that questioner was. It was said: it is the speech of some of them to others. It was said: it is the statement of the Muslims to them. It was said: it is the statement of the "al-Muqtasimin" (those who divided the entrances of Mecca), who would divide the approaches to Mecca to turn people away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the delegations of pilgrims came to them asking about what had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Second issue: One may say: how can their Lord's revelation be "tales of the ancients"?

Its answer is in several respects:

The first: it is mentioned in the manner of mockery, like His saying, exalted is He, about them: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 27], and His saying: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman﴾ [al-Hijr 6], and His saying: ﴿O sorcerer, invoke your Lord for us﴾ [al-Zukhruf 49].

The second: the meaning is: "This which you mention, that it is sent down from your Lord, is tales of the ancients."

The third: It is possible that the intended meaning is that this Qur'an, supposing it is from what Allah has sent down, is nevertheless "tales of the ancients," containing nothing of knowledge, eloquence, subtleties, or realities.

Know that when He, exalted is He, related their doubt, He said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam in ﴿li-yahmilu﴾ is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), because they did not describe the Qur'an as tales of the ancients in order that they might bear burdens; but since their outcome was that, the mention of this lam was fitting, like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. And His saying ﴿kamilatan﴾ ("in full") means: He, exalted is He, does not lighten any of their punishment at all, but delivers that punishment to them in its entirety. I say: this indicates that He, exalted is He, may remove some punishment from the believers, for if this meaning were achieved for all, there would be no point in specifying these disbelievers with this completeness. And His saying ﴿and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾ means: the leaders will receive the like of the burdens of the followers. The reason for this is what is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever calls to guidance and is followed, he will have a reward like the reward of those who follow him, without any of their rewards being diminished; and whoever calls to misguidance and is followed, he will bear a burden like the burden of those who follow him, without any of their sins being diminished."

Know that what is meant is not that He, exalted is He, transfers the punishment that the followers deserve onto the leaders, because this does not befit the justice of Allah, exalted is He. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And that man has nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm 39], and His saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Isra' 15]. Rather, the meaning is: when a leader establishes an evil practice, his punishment becomes great, to the extent that this punishment equals all that each one of the followers deserves. Al-Wahidi said: the word "min" in His saying ﴿and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾ is not partitive, because if it were partitive, some of the burdens would be lightened from the followers, and that is not permissible, due to his saying, upon him be peace: "without any of their burdens being diminished." Rather, it is for genus, i.e., that they bear burdens of the same kind as the burdens of the followers. His saying ﴿without knowledge﴾ means: these leaders only undertake this misguidance out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for it. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the speech with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾, and the purpose is intensifying the warning.

If it is said: When He, exalted is He, related this doubt from the people, He did not answer it, but limited Himself to pure warning; what is the reason for this?

We say: the reason is that He, exalted is He, clarified that the Qur'an is a miracle by two ways.

The first: that He (ﷺ) challenged them with the entire Qur'an, and at other times with ten surahs, and at other times with a single surah, and at other times with a single hadith, and they were unable to produce a counterpart, and this indicates that it is a miracle.

The second: that He, exalted is He, related this very doubt in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿He has written it down, and it is dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan 5], and refuted it with His saying: ﴿Say: It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Furqan 6]. Its meaning is that the Qur'an contains reports of the unseen, and that is not possible except from one who knows the secrets of the heavens and the earth. So when it was established that the Qur'an is a miracle by these two ways, and the explanation of these two ways was repeated many times, it follows that in this verse he restricted himself to mere warning and did not mention what would serve as an answer to this doubt. And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 26–28:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Those before them did indeed scheme, so God came at their structure from its foundations, and the roof fell down upon them from above, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say: "Where are My partners, concerning whom you used to dispute?" Those who were given knowledge will say: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers,"﴾ ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission: "We did not used to do any evil." Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾

Know that the purpose of the verse is to emphasise the severity of the threat against those disbelievers. Regarding the meaning of "those before them," there are two opinions.

The first opinion, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes, is that it refers to Nimrod ibn Kan'an, who built a great tower (ṣarḥ) in Babylon whose height was five thousand cubits, and some said two farsakhs. He intended to ascend to the heaven in order to fight its inhabitants. Thus the "scheming" here means the building of the tower to fight the people of the heavens.

The second opinion, which is the more correct one, is that this is general to all the falsifiers who attempt to inflict harm and deceit upon the righteous.

As for His saying: ﴿God came at their structure from its foundations﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: coming and movement are impossible for God, so the meaning is that when they disbelieved, God struck them with earthquakes by which He uprooted their structures from their foundations and bases.

The second issue: concerning His saying ﴿God came at their structure from its foundations﴾, there are two opinions.

The first opinion: this is purely an illustration (tamthīl). The meaning is that they arranged erected structures in order to scheme with them against the prophets of God, so God made their condition in those structures like the condition of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars; the building collapsed and those pillars weakened, so the roof fell upon them. A parallel to this is their saying: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother, God makes him fall into it."

The second opinion: the meaning is what the apparent sense indicates, namely that God brought the roof down upon them and caused them to die beneath it. The first opinion is closer to the meaning.

As for His saying ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above﴾, there is a question: a roof does not fall except from above them, so what is the meaning of this statement?

Its answer is in two respects:

The first: the purpose is emphasis.

The second: a roof may fall while no one is beneath it. So when He said ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above﴾, this statement indicates that they were beneath it, and in that case this statement conveys that the buildings had collapsed while they died beneath them.

As for His saying ﴿and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾: if we take this statement as purely illustrative, the matter is clear. The meaning is that they relied upon their erected structures, then the affliction arose from those very structures. If we take it according to its apparent sense, the meaning is that the roof came down upon them suddenly, because when it is so, it is more effective in deterring whoever follows a path like theirs.

Then God explained that their punishment is not confined to this degree alone; rather, God will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection. Disgrace (khizy) is punishment together with humiliation. God explained that humiliation by saying to them: ﴿Where are My partners concerning whom you used to dispute?﴾ Concerning this there are several discussions.

First discussion: al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ means: where are My partners according to your assumption and belief? A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ [al-An'am: 22], and He also said: ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not used to worship us."﴾ [Yunus: 28]. This idafah (attributive construction linking "partners" to "Me") is good because a minimal connection suffices for the goodness of an idafah. This is like one who says to someone carrying a piece of wood: "Take your end, and I will take my end," so the "end" is attributed to him.

Second discussion: His saying ﴿concerning whom you used to dispute﴾ means: you used to oppose and contend with the believers concerning their affair. It has been said that mushāqqah (dispute) is an expression for one of the two adversaries being on one side and the other being on the other side.

Third discussion: Nafi' recited (tushāqqūnī) with a kasrah on the nūn, as an idafah, while the rest recited with a fatḥah on the nūn, as the plural.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers."﴾ Concerning this there are two discussions.

First discussion: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the angels. Others said: they are the believers who say, when they see the disgrace of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers." The benefit of this is that the disbelievers used to deny the believers in the world; so when the believer utters this statement on the Day of Resurrection in the context of humiliating the disbeliever, the effect of this statement upon the disbeliever and its impact in hurting him is more complete, and the achievement of gloating over him is stronger.

Second discussion: The Murji'ah (the postponers) argued with this verse that punishment is specific to the disbeliever. They said: because His saying ﴿Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers﴾ indicates that the reality of disgrace and misfortune on the Day of Resurrection is specific to the disbeliever, and that negates the realisation of this reality in regard to others. This is reinforced by the saying of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]. Then God described the punishment of these disbelievers from another aspect, saying: ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves.﴾ Hamzah recited (yatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikatu) with the ya', because the angels are masculine, while the rest recited with the ta' in accordance with the wording.

Then He said: ﴿Then they will offer submission: "We did not used to do any evil."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first opinion: God related of them the offering of submission at the approach of death. Ibn 'Abbas said: they submitted and acknowledged to God servitude at the time of death.

His saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil"﴾ means: they said, "We did not used to do any evil," and the evil here is polytheism. So the angels responded to them in refutation and denial: ﴿Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do of denial and polytheism.﴾ The meaning of "Yes" (balā) is a rebuttal of their saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first opinion: God related of them the offering of submission at the approach of death.

The second opinion: the statement was complete at His saying ﴿while they are wronging themselves﴾, then the discourse returned to relating the speech of the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection they will offer submission and say: "We did not used to do any evil in the world." Then here they differed. Those who permitted lying on the people of the Resurrection said: this statement from them is in the manner of a lie, and they only resorted to this lie out of extreme fear. Those who said that lying is not permissible for them said: the meaning of the verse is "We did not used to do any evil" in our own selves or in our belief. As for the clarification of whether lying toward the people of the Resurrection is permissible or not, we have mentioned it in surah al-An'am in the exegesis of His saying: ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they say: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

Know that when He related of them that they said, "We did not used to do any evil," He said: ﴿Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾ It is not far-fetched that the speaker of this statement is God, exalted is He, or some of the angels, in response to them and refutation of them. The meaning of "Yes" (balā) is a rebuttal of their saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil."﴾ His saying ﴿"Indeed, God is Knowing of what you used to do"﴾ means: He knows what you were upon in the world, so this lie will not benefit you, for He will requite you for the disbelief which He knew from you.
