The first opinion, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes, is that it refers to Nimrod ibn Kan'an, who built a great tower (ṣarḥ) in Babylon whose height was five thousand cubits, and some said two farsakhs. He intended to ascend to the heaven in order to fight its inhabitants. Thus the "scheming" here means the building of the tower to fight the people of the heavens.

The second opinion, which is the more correct one, is that this is general to all the falsifiers who attempt to inflict harm and deceit upon the righteous.

As for His saying: ﴿God came at their structure from its foundations﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: coming and movement are impossible for God, so the meaning is that when they disbelieved, God struck them with earthquakes by which He uprooted their structures from their foundations and bases.

The second issue: concerning His saying ﴿God came at their structure from its foundations﴾, there are two opinions.

The first opinion: this is purely an illustration (tamthīl). The meaning is that they arranged erected structures in order to scheme with them against the prophets of God, so God made their condition in those structures like the condition of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars; the building collapsed and those pillars weakened, so the roof fell upon them. A parallel to this is their saying: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother, God makes him fall into it."

The second opinion: the meaning is what the apparent sense indicates, namely that God brought the roof down upon them and caused them to die beneath it. The first opinion is closer to the meaning.

As for His saying ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above﴾, there is a question: a roof does not fall except from above them, so what is the meaning of this statement?

Its answer is in two respects:

The first: the purpose is emphasis.

The second: a roof may fall while no one is beneath it. So when He said ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above﴾, this statement indicates that they were beneath it, and in that case this statement conveys that the buildings had collapsed while they died beneath them.

As for His saying ﴿and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾: if we take this statement as purely illustrative, the matter is clear. The meaning is that they relied upon their erected structures, then the affliction arose from those very structures. If we take it according to its apparent sense, the meaning is that the roof came down upon them suddenly, because when it is so, it is more effective in deterring whoever follows a path like theirs.

Then God explained that their punishment is not confined to this degree alone; rather, God will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection. Disgrace (khizy) is punishment together with humiliation. God explained that humiliation by saying to them: ﴿Where are My partners concerning whom you used to dispute?﴾ Concerning this there are several discussions.

First discussion: al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ means: where are My partners according to your assumption and belief? A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ [al-An'am: 22], and He also said: ﴿And their partners will say: "You did not used to worship us."﴾ [Yunus: 28]. This idafah (attributive construction linking "partners" to "Me") is good because a minimal connection suffices for the goodness of an idafah. This is like one who says to someone carrying a piece of wood: "Take your end, and I will take my end," so the "end" is attributed to him.

Second discussion: His saying ﴿concerning whom you used to dispute﴾ means: you used to oppose and contend with the believers concerning their affair. It has been said that mushāqqah (dispute) is an expression for one of the two adversaries being on one side and the other being on the other side.

Third discussion: Nafi' recited (tushāqqūnī) with a kasrah on the nūn, as an idafah, while the rest recited with a fatḥah on the nūn, as the plural.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers."﴾ Concerning this there are two discussions.

First discussion: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the angels. Others said: they are the believers who say, when they see the disgrace of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers." The benefit of this is that the disbelievers used to deny the believers in the world; so when the believer utters this statement on the Day of Resurrection in the context of humiliating the disbeliever, the effect of this statement upon the disbeliever and its impact in hurting him is more complete, and the achievement of gloating over him is stronger.

Second discussion: The Murji'ah (the postponers) argued with this verse that punishment is specific to the disbeliever. They said: because His saying ﴿Indeed, disgrace and misfortune this Day are upon the disbelievers﴾ indicates that the reality of disgrace and misfortune on the Day of Resurrection is specific to the disbeliever, and that negates the realisation of this reality in regard to others. This is reinforced by the saying of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]. Then God described the punishment of these disbelievers from another aspect, saying: ﴿those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves.﴾ Hamzah recited (yatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikatu) with the ya', because the angels are masculine, while the rest recited with the ta' in accordance with the wording.

Then He said: ﴿Then they will offer submission: "We did not used to do any evil."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first opinion: God related of them the offering of submission at the approach of death. Ibn 'Abbas said: they submitted and acknowledged to God servitude at the time of death.

His saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil"﴾ means: they said, "We did not used to do any evil," and the evil here is polytheism. So the angels responded to them in refutation and denial: ﴿Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do of denial and polytheism.﴾ The meaning of "Yes" (balā) is a rebuttal of their saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions:

[Page 19]

The first opinion: God related of them the offering of submission at the approach of death.

The second opinion: the statement was complete at His saying ﴿while they are wronging themselves﴾, then the discourse returned to relating the speech of the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection they will offer submission and say: "We did not used to do any evil in the world." Then here they differed. Those who permitted lying on the people of the Resurrection said: this statement from them is in the manner of a lie, and they only resorted to this lie out of extreme fear. Those who said that lying is not permissible for them said: the meaning of the verse is "We did not used to do any evil" in our own selves or in our belief. As for the clarification of whether lying toward the people of the Resurrection is permissible or not, we have mentioned it in surah al-An'am in the exegesis of His saying: ﴿Then their temptation will be only that they say: "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

Know that when He related of them that they said, "We did not used to do any evil," He said: ﴿Yes, indeed God is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾ It is not far-fetched that the speaker of this statement is God, exalted is He, or some of the angels, in response to them and refutation of them. The meaning of "Yes" (balā) is a rebuttal of their saying ﴿"We did not used to do any evil."﴾ His saying ﴿"Indeed, God is Knowing of what you used to do"﴾ means: He knows what you were upon in the world, so this lie will not benefit you, for He will requite you for the disbelief which He knew from you.

Then he explicitly mentioned the punishment, saying: ﴿So enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein forever.﴾

This indicates that their ranks differ in punishment, so the punishment of some of them is greater than the punishment of others. God, exalted is He, explicitly mentioned abiding forever so that the grief and sorrow would be greater.

Then He said: ﴿And wretched is the abode of the arrogant,﴾ those who were arrogant toward accepting monotheism and all that the prophets brought. The explanation of arrogance has already been given in this book more than once. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 30–32:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good." For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow. For them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the conditions of the peoples who, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?", said, "The fables of the ancients," and mentioned that they bear their own burdens and some of the burdens of those who follow them, and mentioned that the angels take them in death while they are wronging themselves, and mentioned that they will offer submission in the Hereafter, and mentioned that He will say to them, "Enter the gates of Hell," He followed this with a description of the believers, who, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?", said, "Good," and with a mention of what He has prepared for them in this world and the Hereafter of abodes of good and degrees of felicity,

[p. 20]

so that the promise to these might be mentioned alongside the threat to those. In the verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: Included in God-consciousness (taqwa) is that one abstains from all prohibited things and performs all obligatory duties, and whoever combines these two matters is a believer of complete faith. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: It means those who guarded against shirk and were certain that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. I say: This is more preferable than what the judge said, because we have explained that for the truth of the statement "So-and-so is a killer or a striker" it suffices that he has committed one killing and one striking, and the truth of this statement does not depend on his having committed all kinds of killing and all kinds of striking. Accordingly, His saying, ﴿to those who were mindful of God﴾, encompasses everyone who has performed one kind of God-consciousness. However, we agree that God-consciousness from disbelief and shirk is necessary, so it is obligatory not to add beyond this restriction. Because restricting the absolute is contrary to the original principle, restricting the restricted is even more contrary to it. Also, He mentioned these people in contrast to those who disbelieved and associated partners, so it is necessary that the intended meaning be whoever guarded against that disbelief and shirk. And God knows best.

**Second issue:** One may ask: In the first verse He said, "They say, 'The fables of the ancients,'" and in this verse He said, "They say, 'Good.'" Why was the first put in the nominative and this in the accusative?

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) answered this by saying: The purpose of it is to distinguish between the answer of the one who acknowledges and the answer of the one who denies. That is, when these were asked, they did not hesitate, but matched their answer to the question clearly and plainly, making it the object of "sent down," so they said, "Good," meaning: He sent down good. As for those others, they evaded the question in their answer and said, "It is the fables of the ancients," which has nothing to do with sending down.

**Third issue:** The exegetes said: This happened during the season of pilgrimage. A man would come to Mecca and ask the polytheists about Muhammad and his affair, and they would say, "He is a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and a liar." Then he would come to the believers and ask them about Muhammad and what God had sent down to him, and they would say, "Good," meaning: He sent down good. It is also possible that the intended answer they gave is described as being good, and their saying "good" comprises the fact that it is truth and correctness, and their acknowledgment of its soundness and binding force. This is the opposite of the saying of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, that it is "the fables of the ancients," in the manner of denial.

**Fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿for those who did good﴾, and what follows it, is an appositive (badal) of His saying, ﴿good﴾, and it is a quotation of the saying of those who were mindful of God, meaning: they said this statement. It is also permissible that His saying, ﴿for those who did good﴾, be an informing about God, and the implied sense is: when the God-fearing were told, ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" they said, "Good,"﴾ then He, exalted is He, confirmed their statement and said, ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good.﴾ Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿those who did good﴾ there are two opinions. As for those who say that the people of "There is no god but God" will come out of the Fire, they understand it as referring to saying "There is no god but God" together with correct belief. As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), who say that the sinners among the people of prayer will not come out of the Fire, they understand His saying, ﴿did good﴾, as referring to one who brought faith and all obligatory duties and abstained from all prohibited things. As for His saying, ﴿in this world﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is connected to His saying, ﴿did good﴾, and the implied sense is: to those who were mindful of God by doing good in this world, there is good in the Hereafter for them, and that good is the great reward. It has also been said that this good is that its reward is multiplied tenfold, and seven hundredfold, and without limit.

The second opinion: His saying, ﴿in this world﴾, is connected to His saying, ﴿good﴾, and the implied sense is: for those who did good, there is that good will be attained for them in this world. This opinion is preferable, because He said after it, ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better.﴾ On this interpretation, there are several explanations of this good attained in this world:

First: It is possible that what is meant is the praise, honor, commendation, and elevated standing they deserve, and all of that is a reward for what they did.

Second: It is possible that what is meant is victory over the enemies of the religion through proof and dominance over them, the seizing of their wealth and the conquest of their lands, as occurred at Badr and at the conquest of Mecca, when they (the believers) drove them out and forced them to migrate, to leave their homeland and to part from family and children. All of this is of great consequence.

Third: It is possible that what is meant is that when they did good, meaning that they performed acts of obedience, God opened to them the doors of unveiling, witnessing, and subtle favors, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

As for His saying, ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, we have explained in surah al-An'am, in His saying, ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful﴾ [al-An'am: 32], by means of rational, decisive proofs, that this good is attained. Then He said, ﴿and excellent is the abode of the God-fearing﴾, meaning: excellent is the abode of the God-fearing, the abode of the Hereafter, and it has been omitted because it was previously mentioned. This is when this verse is not connected to what follows it. But if you connect it to what follows, you say: "And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing: Gardens of perpetual residence," so you put "Gardens" in the nominative as the subject of "excellent (ni'ma)," just as you say, "Excellent is the abode: an abode where Zayd dwells."

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Know that if it is connected to what precedes it, we have already mentioned the reason for its nominative case. As for if it is disconnected, al-Zajjaj said: "Gardens of perpetual residence" is in the nominative by an implied "hiya" (it is), as though when you said, "Excellent is the abode of the God-fearing," it was asked, "What abode is this praised one?" and you answered, "It is Gardens of perpetual residence." And if you wish, you may say: "Gardens of perpetual residence" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "they will enter it" is its predicate; or if you wish, you may say: "Excellent is the abode of the God-fearing" is its predicate, and the implied sense is: Gardens of perpetual residence, excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.

**Second issue:** His saying, ﴿Gardens﴾, indicates palaces and orchards; His saying, ﴿perpetual residence (adn)﴾, indicates permanence; and His saying, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, indicates that there are structures there upon which they stand, with rivers flowing beneath them. Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ and in this there are two discussions:

First: This expression indicates the attainment of all goods and felicities, and this is more eloquent than His saying, ﴿Therein is whatever the souls desire and whatever the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71], because these two categories are included in His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ along with other categories.

Second: His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ means that this condition is not attained except in Paradise, because His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ conveys restriction (hasr), and that indicates that a person does not find everything he wants in this world.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Thus does God reward the God-fearing,﴾ meaning: such is the reward of God-consciousness. Then He, exalted is He, returned to describing the God-fearing and said, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure,﴾ and this is mentioned in contrast to His saying, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. Whoever is in this condition does not suffer pain at death. Most exegetes hold that this "taking" (tawaffi) is the seizing of souls, although al-Hasan says it is the taking (tawaffi) of the Resurrection. Then

God, exalted is He, explained that it will be said to them in this state, ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ Al-Hasan used this as proof that the intended meaning of that taking is the taking of the Resurrection, because it is not said at the seizing of souls in this world, "Enter the Garden for what you used to do." Those who hold the first opinion, and they are the majority, say: When the angels gave them the glad tidings of Paradise, Paradise became as though it were their home and as though they were in it. Thus the intended meaning of their saying, "Enter the Garden," is: it is especially for you, as though you were in it.

Most exegetes hold that this "taking" (tawaffi) is the seizing of souls, although al-Hasan says it is the taking (tawaffi) of the Resurrection. Then

[p. 22]

God, exalted is He, explained that it will be said to them in this state, ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ Al-Hasan used this as proof that the intended meaning of that taking is the taking of the Resurrection, because it is not said at the seizing of souls in this world, "Enter the Garden for what you used to do." Those who hold the first opinion, and they are the majority, say: When the angels gave them the glad tidings of Paradise, Paradise became as though it were their home and as though they were in it. Thus the intended meaning of their saying, "Enter the Garden," is: it is especially for you, as though you were in it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 30–32:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good." For those who did good in this world there is good, and the abode of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow. For them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure, saying, "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the conditions of the peoples who, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?", said, "The fables of the ancients," and mentioned that they bear their own burdens and some of the burdens of those who follow them, and mentioned that the angels take them in death while they are wronging themselves, and mentioned that they will offer submission in the Hereafter, and mentioned that He will say to them, "Enter the gates of Hell," He followed this with a description of the believers, who, when it was said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?", said, "Good," and with a mention of what He has prepared for them in this world and the Hereafter of abodes of good and degrees of felicity,

[p. 20]

so that the promise to these might be mentioned alongside the threat to those. In the verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: Included in God-consciousness (taqwa) is that one abstains from all prohibited things and performs all obligatory duties, and whoever combines these two matters is a believer of complete faith. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: It means those who guarded against shirk and were certain that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. I say: This is more preferable than what the judge said, because we have explained that for the truth of the statement "So-and-so is a killer or a striker" it suffices that he has committed one killing and one striking, and the truth of this statement does not depend on his having committed all kinds of killing and all kinds of striking. Accordingly, His saying, ﴿to those who were mindful of God﴾, encompasses everyone who has performed one kind of God-consciousness. However, we agree that God-consciousness from disbelief and shirk is necessary, so it is obligatory not to add beyond this restriction. Because restricting the absolute is contrary to the original principle, restricting the restricted is even more contrary to it. Also, He mentioned these people in contrast to those who disbelieved and associated partners, so it is necessary that the intended meaning be whoever guarded against that disbelief and shirk. And God knows best.

**Second issue:** One may ask: In the first verse He said, "They say, 'The fables of the ancients,'" and in this verse He said, "They say, 'Good.'" Why was the first put in the nominative and this in the accusative?

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) answered this by saying: The purpose of it is to distinguish between the answer of the one who acknowledges and the answer of the one who denies. That is, when these were asked, they did not hesitate, but matched their answer to the question clearly and plainly, making it the object of "sent down," so they said, "Good," meaning: He sent down good. As for those others, they evaded the question in their answer and said, "It is the fables of the ancients," which has nothing to do with sending down.

**Third issue:** The exegetes said: This happened during the season of pilgrimage. A man would come to Mecca and ask the polytheists about Muhammad and his affair, and they would say, "He is a sorcerer, a soothsayer, and a liar." Then he would come to the believers and ask them about Muhammad and what God had sent down to him, and they would say, "Good," meaning: He sent down good. It is also possible that the intended answer they gave is described as being good, and their saying "good" comprises the fact that it is truth and correctness, and their acknowledgment of its soundness and binding force. This is the opposite of the saying of those who do not believe in the Hereafter, that it is "the fables of the ancients," in the manner of denial.

**Fourth issue:** His saying, ﴿for those who did good﴾, and what follows it, is an appositive (badal) of His saying, ﴿good﴾, and it is a quotation of the saying of those who were mindful of God, meaning: they said this statement. It is also permissible that His saying, ﴿for those who did good﴾, be an informing about God, and the implied sense is: when the God-fearing were told, ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" they said, "Good,"﴾ then He, exalted is He, confirmed their statement and said, ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good.﴾ Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿those who did good﴾ there are two opinions. As for those who say that the people of "There is no god but God" will come out of the Fire, they understand it as referring to saying "There is no god but God" together with correct belief. As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), who say that the sinners among the people of prayer will not come out of the Fire, they understand His saying, ﴿did good﴾, as referring to one who brought faith and all obligatory duties and abstained from all prohibited things. As for His saying, ﴿in this world﴾, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is connected to His saying, ﴿did good﴾, and the implied sense is: to those who were mindful of God by doing good in this world, there is good in the Hereafter for them, and that good is the great reward. It has also been said that this good is that its reward is multiplied tenfold, and seven hundredfold, and without limit.

The second opinion: His saying, ﴿in this world﴾, is connected to His saying, ﴿good﴾, and the implied sense is: for those who did good, there is that good will be attained for them in this world. This opinion is preferable, because He said after it, ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better.﴾ On this interpretation, there are several explanations of this good attained in this world:

First: It is possible that what is meant is the praise, honor, commendation, and elevated standing they deserve, and all of that is a reward for what they did.

Second: It is possible that what is meant is victory over the enemies of the religion through proof and dominance over them, the seizing of their wealth and the conquest of their lands, as occurred at Badr and at the conquest of Mecca, when they (the believers) drove them out and forced them to migrate, to leave their homeland and to part from family and children. All of this is of great consequence.

Third: It is possible that what is meant is that when they did good, meaning that they performed acts of obedience, God opened to them the doors of unveiling, witnessing, and subtle favors, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

As for His saying, ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, we have explained in surah al-An'am, in His saying, ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful﴾ [al-An'am: 32], by means of rational, decisive proofs, that this good is attained. Then He said, ﴿and excellent is the abode of the God-fearing﴾, meaning: excellent is the abode of the God-fearing, the abode of the Hereafter, and it has been omitted because it was previously mentioned. This is when this verse is not connected to what follows it. But if you connect it to what follows, you say: "And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing: Gardens of perpetual residence," so you put "Gardens" in the nominative as the subject of "excellent (ni'ma)," just as you say, "Excellent is the abode: an abode where Zayd dwells."

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾, there are several issues:

**First issue:** Know that if it is connected to what precedes it, we have already mentioned the reason for its nominative case. As for if it is disconnected, al-Zajjaj said: "Gardens of perpetual residence" is in the nominative by an implied "hiya" (it is), as though when you said, "Excellent is the abode of the God-fearing," it was asked, "What abode is this praised one?" and you answered, "It is Gardens of perpetual residence." And if you wish, you may say: "Gardens of perpetual residence" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "they will enter it" is its predicate; or if you wish, you may say: "Excellent is the abode of the God-fearing" is its predicate, and the implied sense is: Gardens of perpetual residence, excellent is the abode of the God-fearing.

**Second issue:** His saying, ﴿Gardens﴾, indicates palaces and orchards; His saying, ﴿perpetual residence (adn)﴾, indicates permanence; and His saying, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, indicates that there are structures there upon which they stand, with rivers flowing beneath them. Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ and in this there are two discussions:

First: This expression indicates the attainment of all goods and felicities, and this is more eloquent than His saying, ﴿Therein is whatever the souls desire and whatever the eyes delight in﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71], because these two categories are included in His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ along with other categories.

Second: His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ means that this condition is not attained except in Paradise, because His saying, ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish,﴾ conveys restriction (hasr), and that indicates that a person does not find everything he wants in this world.

Then He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Thus does God reward the God-fearing,﴾ meaning: such is the reward of God-consciousness. Then He, exalted is He, returned to describing the God-fearing and said, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure,﴾ and this is mentioned in contrast to His saying, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. His saying, ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾, is a description of the God-fearing in His saying, ﴿Thus does God reward the God-fearing.﴾ His saying, ﴿pure (tayyibin)﴾, is a concise word comprehensive of many meanings, because it includes their doing all that they were commanded, and their avoiding all that they were forbidden; it includes their being described with virtuous character, free from blameworthy character; it includes their being free from bodily attachments, turning toward the presence of holiness and purity; and it includes that the taking of their souls was pleasant to them, and that their souls were not taken except with the glad tidings of Paradise, until they became as though they were witnessing it. Whoever is in this condition does not suffer pain at death. Most exegetes hold that this "taking" (tawaffi) is the seizing of souls, although al-Hasan says it is the taking (tawaffi) of the Resurrection. Then

[p. 22]

God, exalted is He, explained that it will be said to them in this state, ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ Al-Hasan used this as proof that the intended meaning of that taking is the taking of the Resurrection, because it is not said at the seizing of souls in this world, "Enter the Garden for what you used to do." Those who hold the first opinion, and they are the majority, say: When the angels gave them the glad tidings of Paradise, Paradise became as though it were their home and as though they were in it. Thus the intended meaning of their saying, "Enter the Garden," is: it is especially for you, as though you were in it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them act. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock enveloped them.﴾

Know that this is the second objection (shubha) of those who deny prophethood. They asked the Prophet ﷺ that Allah send down an angel from heaven to testify to the truth of his claim to prophethood. So Allah said: ﴿Do they await anything?﴾ regarding belief in your prophethood, ﴿but that the angels should come to them as witnesses to that?﴾ It is also possible to say: when the people attacked the Qur'an by saying, "It is merely the fables of the ancients," and Allah mentioned the various kinds of threat and warning against them, then He followed this with the promise for those who described the Qur'an as good, true and right, He returned to explaining that those disbelievers would not desist from disbelief because of the clear proofs we have mentioned. Rather, they would not desist from those false statements except when the angels came to them with the threat, and the command of your Lord came to them, which is the punishment of annihilation.

Know that under both interpretations, Allah said: ﴿Thus did those before them act,﴾ meaning: the words and deeds of these people resemble the words and deeds of the earlier disbelievers.

Then He said: ﴿Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ The sense is: thus did those before them act, and so the immediate destruction befell them. Allah did not wrong them by this, for He sent down upon them what they deserved because of their disbelief. Rather, they wronged themselves by disbelieving and denying the Messenger, and so they merited what befell them.

Then He said: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them.﴾ What is meant is that the punishment for the evil of what they did befell them. ﴿And what they used to mock enveloped them﴾ meaning it descended upon them in a way that encompassed all their sides. ﴿What they used to mock﴾ means: the punishment for their mockery.

[p. 23]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah say: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything apart from Him." Thus did those before them act. So upon the Messengers is only the clear delivery.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities)." Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray, and for them there are no helpers.﴾

Know that this is the third objection of those who deny prophethood. Its formulation is that they held fast to the validity of the doctrine of compulsion (jabr) in order to attack prophethood. They said: "If Allah willed faith, faith would occur, whether you came or not. If Allah willed disbelief, disbelief would occur, whether you came or not. Since the matter is so, everything is from Allah the Exalted, and there is no benefit in your coming or your being sent. So the doctrine of prophethood is false." There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: know that this objection is the very same thing Allah related of them in Surah al-An'am, in His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners will say, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated anything, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Thus did those before them deny.﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. The Mu'tazila's argument from it is like their argument from that verse, and the discussion of it, both as argument and objection, is exactly what was stated there, so there is no benefit in repeating it. There is no harm, however, in mentioning a little of it, so we say: The answer to this objection is that they said: since everything is from Allah the Exalted, His sending of prophets is pointless. We say: this is an objection against Allah the Exalted. Their statement, "If sending a Messenger offers no extra benefit in producing faith and removing disbelief, then the sending of prophets is not permissible for Allah the Exalted," is a demand for the cause (illah) of Allah's rulings and His actions. That is false. Rather, Allah the Exalted may judge in His dominion and kingdom as He wills, and do what He desires, and it is not permissible to say to Him, "Why did You do this, and why did You not do that?" The evidence that the denial was directed at this very meaning is that He stated this meaning explicitly at the end of this verse, when He said: ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut."﴾ So Allah the Exalted made clear that His practice with His servants is to send Messengers to them, commanding them to worship Allah and forbidding them to worship the Taghut.

Then He said: ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ The meaning is: although He commanded all to believe and forbade all from disbelief, He nonetheless guided some and led others astray. This is an ancient practice of Allah the Exalted with His servants: He commands everyone to believe and forbids them from disbelief, then He creates faith in some and disbelief in others. Since Allah's practice in this regard is an ancient practice with respect to all the prophets and all the communities and religions, and it is proper for Him to do this only by virtue of His being a God exalted above the objections of objectors and the demands of contenders, the raising of this question by these disbelievers was a cause of ignorance, error and distance from Allah. Thus it is established that Allah the Exalted decreed for these people only that they deserve disgrace and curse, not because they lied in their statement, ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him,﴾ but because they believed that the matter being so prevents the permissibility of sending prophets and messengers, and this is false. Therefore they deservedly merited further blame and curse for this belief. This is the correct answer that should be relied upon in this matter. As for those who preceded us among the theologians and exegetes, they mentioned another interpretation of it, saying: the polytheists uttered this statement in mockery, as the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided.﴾ [Hud: 87] And had they said that sincerely, they would have been believers. And Allah knows best.

[p. 24]

The second issue: know that when Allah related this objection, He said: ﴿Thus did those before them act,﴾ meaning: these disbelievers have always held fast to this objection.
Then He said: ﴿So upon the Messengers is only the clear delivery.﴾ As for the Mu'tazila, they said: its meaning is that Allah did not prevent anyone from faith nor drive anyone into disbelief, and the Messengers have no obligation except conveyance. Since they conveyed the obligations, and it is established that He did not prevent anyone from the truth, this objection falls away. As for our companions (the Ash'aris), they said: its meaning is that Allah commanded the Messengers to convey. This conveyance is obligatory upon them. As for whether faith occurs or does not occur, the Messenger has no connection to it; rather, Allah guides whom He wills by His favor and leads astray whom He wills by His abandonment.

The third issue: our companions argued for the proof that guidance and misguidance are from Allah from His saying: ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut."﴾ This indicates that Allah the Exalted was always, in all religions and communities, commanding faith and forbidding disbelief.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ That is: among them were those whom Allah guided to faith, truthfulness and truth, and among them were those whom He led astray from the truth, blinded from truthfulness, and drove into disbelief and error. This indicates that the command of Allah the Exalted does not coincide with His will; rather He may command a thing without willing it, and forbid a thing while willing it, as is our doctrine. The summary is that the Mu'tazila say: command and will are coextensive, while knowledge and will may differ. The wording of this verse is explicit in our position, namely that the command to faith is general with respect to all, while the will for faith is particular to some and not others.

Al-Jubba'i answered that what is meant by: ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided﴾ is to attain His reward and Paradise, and by: ﴿Among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ is punishment. He said: the description, "decreed upon him," indicates that it refers to the punishment and not to the word of disbelief, because disbelief and disobedience cannot be described as "true" (haqq). He also said: Allah the Exalted said after it: ﴿Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers,﴾ and this end is the traces of destruction for those earlier communities whom Allah uprooted with punishment. This indicates that what is meant by the error mentioned is the punishment of annihilation.

Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying: His statement, ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided,﴾ means: whoever was guided, and so he was guided in Allah's judgment. ﴿Among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ means: whose error became manifest, just as one says to a wrongdoer, "your wrong has been established and made clear." It is also possible that what is meant is: it was decreed upon them by Allah that He would lead them astray if they went astray, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah leads the wrongdoers astray.﴾

Know that we have shown, in many verses, by decisive rational proofs, that guidance and leading astray can only come from Allah the Exalted, so there is no benefit in repeating it. These strained interpretations and forced explanations we have shown to be weak and invalid many times, so there is no need to repeat them. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: concerning the Taghut there are two opinions.
One of them: what is meant by it is: avoid worshipping what you worship apart from Allah, so He called all of them Taghut. It is not impossible that what is meant is: avoid obeying the Satan in his calling you (to it).

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿Among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ indicates our doctrine, because when He informed that error was decreed upon him, it became impossible that error should not proceed from him, for otherwise the true report of Allah would turn into a lie, and that is impossible. And what entails an impossibility is impossible. So the absence of error from them became impossible, and the presence of error from them became rationally necessary. Thus this verse indicates the soundness of our doctrine in these many respects. And Allah knows best. Similar verses are numerous, among them His saying: ﴿A group He guided, and a group upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ [al-A'raf: 30] And His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been decreed will not believe.﴾ [Yunus: 96] And His saying: ﴿The word has certainly been justified against most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7]

[p. 25]
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers.﴾ The meaning: travel through the earth taking heed, so that you may know that the punishment will descend upon you as it descended upon them. Then He affirmed that whoever has error decreed upon him will not be guided, and said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance,﴾ that is: if you seek that with your utmost effort, ﴿indeed Allah does not guide whom He leads astray.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿yahdī﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl, while the rest read (lā yuhdā) with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the dāl.

As for the first reading, there are two possibilities:
The first: Allah does not guide anyone whom He has led astray. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it in this way.

The second: that "yahdī" means "yahtadī" (is guided). Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs say, "the man has guided (hadā)," meaning "he has been guided (ihtadā)." The meaning is that when Allah leads someone astray, that person does not become one who is guided.

As for the well-known reading, the approach to it is: "Allah does not guide whom He leads astray," meaning: whom He leads astray. So the returning pronoun to the relative "man" is omitted and implied. This is like His saying: ﴿Whom Allah leads astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] And like His saying: ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], meaning: after Allah's leading him astray.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for them there are no helpers,﴾ meaning: there is no one for them who will help them, that is, assist them in attaining their goals in this world and the Hereafter. I say: the first of these verses gives the impression of the Mu'tazila position, while the last of them contains many aspects that indicate our position, and most verses are similar, containing two aspects. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them act. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock enveloped them.﴾

Know that this is the second objection (shubha) of those who deny prophethood. They asked the Prophet ﷺ that Allah send down an angel from heaven to testify to the truth of his claim to prophethood. So Allah said: ﴿Do they await anything?﴾ regarding belief in your prophethood, ﴿but that the angels should come to them as witnesses to that?﴾ It is also possible to say: when the people attacked the Qur'an by saying, "It is merely the fables of the ancients," and Allah mentioned the various kinds of threat and warning against them, then He followed this with the promise for those who described the Qur'an as good, true and right, He returned to explaining that those disbelievers would not desist from disbelief because of the clear proofs we have mentioned. Rather, they would not desist from those false statements except when the angels came to them with the threat, and the command of your Lord came to them, which is the punishment of annihilation.

Know that under both interpretations, Allah said: ﴿Thus did those before them act,﴾ meaning: the words and deeds of these people resemble the words and deeds of the earlier disbelievers.

Then He said: ﴿Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ The sense is: thus did those before them act, and so the immediate destruction befell them. Allah did not wrong them by this, for He sent down upon them what they deserved because of their disbelief. Rather, they wronged themselves by disbelieving and denying the Messenger, and so they merited what befell them.

Then He said: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them.﴾ What is meant is that the punishment for the evil of what they did befell them. ﴿And what they used to mock enveloped them﴾ meaning it descended upon them in a way that encompassed all their sides. ﴿What they used to mock﴾ means: the punishment for their mockery.

[p. 23]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah say: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything apart from Him." Thus did those before them act. So upon the Messengers is only the clear delivery.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities)." Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray, and for them there are no helpers.﴾

Know that this is the third objection of those who deny prophethood. Its formulation is that they held fast to the validity of the doctrine of compulsion (jabr) in order to attack prophethood. They said: "If Allah willed faith, faith would occur, whether you came or not. If Allah willed disbelief, disbelief would occur, whether you came or not. Since the matter is so, everything is from Allah the Exalted, and there is no benefit in your coming or your being sent. So the doctrine of prophethood is false." There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: know that this objection is the very same thing Allah related of them in Surah al-An'am, in His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners will say, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated anything, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Thus did those before them deny.﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. The Mu'tazila's argument from it is like their argument from that verse, and the discussion of it, both as argument and objection, is exactly what was stated there, so there is no benefit in repeating it. There is no harm, however, in mentioning a little of it, so we say: The answer to this objection is that they said: since everything is from Allah the Exalted, His sending of prophets is pointless. We say: this is an objection against Allah the Exalted. Their statement, "If sending a Messenger offers no extra benefit in producing faith and removing disbelief, then the sending of prophets is not permissible for Allah the Exalted," is a demand for the cause (illah) of Allah's rulings and His actions. That is false. Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying: His statement, ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided,﴾ means: whoever was guided, and so he was guided in Allah's judgment. ﴿Among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ means: whose error became manifest, just as one says to a wrongdoer, "your wrong has been established and made clear." It is also possible that what is meant is: it was decreed upon them by Allah that He would lead them astray if they went astray, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah leads the wrongdoers astray.﴾

Know that we have shown, in many verses, by decisive rational proofs, that guidance and leading astray can only come from Allah the Exalted, so there is no benefit in repeating it. These strained interpretations and forced explanations we have shown to be weak and invalid many times, so there is no need to repeat them. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: concerning the Taghut there are two opinions.
One of them: what is meant by it is: avoid worshipping what you worship apart from Allah, so He called all of them Taghut. It is not impossible that what is meant is: avoid obeying the Satan in his calling you (to it).

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿Among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed﴾ indicates our doctrine, because when He informed that error was decreed upon him, it became impossible that error should not proceed from him, for otherwise the true report of Allah would turn into a lie, and that is impossible. And what entails an impossibility is impossible. So the absence of error from them became impossible, and the presence of error from them became rationally necessary. Thus this verse indicates the soundness of our doctrine in these many respects. And Allah knows best. Similar verses are numerous, among them His saying: ﴿A group He guided, and a group upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ [al-A'raf: 30] And His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been decreed will not believe.﴾ [Yunus: 96] And His saying: ﴿The word has certainly been justified against most of them, so they do not believe.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7]

[p. 25]
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers.﴾ The meaning: travel through the earth taking heed, so that you may know that the punishment will descend upon you as it descended upon them. Then He affirmed that whoever has error decreed upon him will not be guided, and said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance,﴾ that is: if you seek that with your utmost effort, ﴿indeed Allah does not guide whom He leads astray.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿yahdī﴾ with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl, while the rest read (lā yuhdā) with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the dāl.

As for the first reading, there are two possibilities:
The first: Allah does not guide anyone whom He has led astray. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it in this way.

The second: that "yahdī" means "yahtadī" (is guided). Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs say, "the man has guided (hadā)," meaning "he has been guided (ihtadā)." The meaning is that when Allah leads someone astray, that person does not become one who is guided.

As for the well-known reading, the approach to it is: "Allah does not guide whom He leads astray," meaning: whom He leads astray. So the returning pronoun to the relative "man" is omitted and implied. This is like His saying: ﴿Whom Allah leads astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ [al-A'raf: 186] And like His saying: ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], meaning: after Allah's leading him astray.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for them there are no helpers,﴾ meaning: there is no one for them who will help them, that is, assist them in attaining their goals in this world and the Hereafter. I say: the first of these verses gives the impression of the Mu'tazila position, while the last of them contains many aspects that indicate our position, and most verses are similar, containing two aspects. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come? Thus did those before them act. Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them, and what they used to mock enveloped them.﴾

Know that this is the second objection (shubha) of those who deny prophethood. They asked the Prophet ﷺ that Allah send down an angel from heaven to testify to the truth of his claim to prophethood. So Allah said: ﴿Do they await anything?﴾ regarding belief in your prophethood, ﴿but that the angels should come to them as witnesses to that?﴾ It is also possible to say: when the people attacked the Qur'an by saying, "It is merely the fables of the ancients," and Allah mentioned the various kinds of threat and warning against them, then He followed this with the promise for those who described the Qur'an as good, true and right, He returned to explaining that those disbelievers would not desist from disbelief because of the clear proofs we have mentioned. Rather, they would not desist from those false statements except when the angels came to them with the threat, and the command of your Lord came to them, which is the punishment of annihilation.

Know that under both interpretations, Allah said: ﴿Thus did those before them act,﴾ meaning: the words and deeds of these people resemble the words and deeds of the earlier disbelievers.

Then He said: ﴿Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ The sense is: thus did those before them act, and so the immediate destruction befell them. Allah did not wrong them by this, for He sent down upon them what they deserved because of their disbelief. Rather, they wronged themselves by disbelieving and denying the Messenger, and so they merited what befell them.

Then He said: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them.﴾ What is meant is that the punishment for the evil of what they did befell them. ﴿And what they used to mock enveloped them﴾ meaning it descended upon them in a way that encompassed all their sides. ﴿What they used to mock﴾ means: the punishment for their mockery.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah say: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything apart from Him." Thus did those before them act. So upon the Messengers is only the clear delivery.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut (false deities)." Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and see what was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those whom He leads astray, and for them there are no helpers.﴾

Know that this is the third objection of those who deny prophethood. Its formulation is that they held fast to the validity of the doctrine of compulsion (jabr) in order to attack prophethood. They said: "If Allah willed faith, faith would occur, whether you came or not. If Allah willed disbelief, disbelief would occur, whether you came or not. Since the matter is so, everything is from Allah the Exalted, and there is no benefit in your coming or your being sent. So the doctrine of prophethood is false." There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: know that this objection is the very same thing Allah related of them in Surah al-An'am, in His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners will say, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated anything, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Thus did those before them deny.﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. The Mu'tazila's argument from it is like their argument from that verse, and the discussion of it, both as argument and objection, is exactly what was stated there, so there is no benefit in repeating it. There is no harm, however, in mentioning a little of it, so we say: The answer to this objection is that they said: since everything is from Allah the Exalted, His sending of prophets is pointless. We say: this is an objection against Allah the Exalted. Their statement, "If sending a Messenger offers no extra benefit in producing faith and removing disbelief, then the sending of prophets is not permissible for Allah the Exalted," is a demand for the cause (illah) of Allah's rulings and His actions. That is false. Rather, Allah the Exalted may judge in His dominion and kingdom as He wills, and do what He desires, and it is not permissible to say to Him, "Why did You do this, and why did You not do that?" The evidence that the denial was directed at this very meaning is that He stated this meaning explicitly at the end of this verse, when He said: ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut."﴾ So Allah the Exalted made clear that His practice with His servants is to send Messengers to them, commanding them to worship Allah and forbidding them to worship the Taghut.

Then He said: ﴿Among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some upon whom error was justly decreed.﴾ The meaning is: although He commanded all to believe and forbade all from disbelief, He nonetheless guided some and led others astray. This is an ancient practice of Allah the Exalted with His servants: He commands everyone to believe and forbids them from disbelief, then He creates faith in some and disbelief in others. Since Allah's practice in this regard is an ancient practice with respect to all the prophets and all the communities and religions, and it is proper for Him to do this only by virtue of His being a God exalted above the objections of objectors and the demands of contenders, the raising of this question by these disbelievers was a cause of ignorance, error and distance from Allah. Thus it is established that Allah the Exalted decreed for these people only that they deserve disgrace and curse, not because they lied in their statement, ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him,﴾ but because they believed that the matter being so prevents the permissibility of sending prophets and messengers, and this is false. Therefore they deservedly merited further blame and curse for this belief. This is the correct answer that should be relied upon in this matter. As for those who preceded us among the theologians and exegetes, they mentioned another interpretation of it, saying: the polytheists uttered this statement in mockery, as the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided.﴾ [Hud: 87] And had they said that sincerely, they would have been believers. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: know that when Allah related this objection, He said: ﴿Thus did those before them act,﴾ meaning: these disbelievers have always held fast to this objection.
Then He said: ﴿So upon the Messengers is only the clear delivery.﴾ As for the Mu'tazila, they said: its meaning is that Allah did not prevent anyone from faith nor drive anyone into disbelief, and the Messengers have no obligation except conveyance. Since they conveyed the obligations, and it is established that He did not prevent anyone from the truth, this objection falls away. As for our companions (the Ash'aris), they said: its meaning is that Allah commanded the Messengers to convey. This conveyance is obligatory upon them. As for whether faith occurs or does not occur, the Messenger has no connection to it; rather, Allah guides whom He wills by His favor and leads astray whom He wills by His abandonment.

The third issue: our companions argued for the proof that guidance and misguidance are from Allah from His saying: ﴿We certainly sent into every community a Messenger, saying: "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut."﴾ This indicates that Allah the Exalted was always, in all religions and communities, commanding faith and forbidding disbelief.

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 38–39:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by God with their most solemn oaths that God would not raise up those who die. Yes indeed! It is a promise binding upon Him, true, but most people do not know﴾ ﴿So that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾ ﴿Indeed, when We intend a thing, Our word to it is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾.

In it are two issues:

The first issue: Know that this is the fourth doubt (shubha) of those who deny prophethood. They said: the affirmation of resurrection, gathering and dispersal is false, and therefore the affirmation of prophethood is false.

As for the first stage: its statement is that a human being is nothing but this particular composition. When he dies and his parts are scattered and that temperament and balance are destroyed, it is impossible for him to return in his very self, because when a thing ceases to exist it has perished, and after its perishing and non-existence it has no essence and no reality remaining. So what returns must be something other than the first, and therefore it cannot be its very self.

As for the second stage: since the affirmation of resurrection is false, the affirmation of prophethood is false. Its statement is in two respects.

The first: Muhammad was calling to the affirmation of the return (ma'ad). If that is false, it is established that he was calling to a false doctrine, and whoever is like that is not a truthful messenger.

The second: he affirms his own prophethood and the obligation of obeying him on the basis of encouraging reward and warning against punishment. If that is false, his prophethood is false.

Having understood this, we say: His saying ﴿And they swore by God with their most solemn oaths that God would not raise up those who die﴾ means that they claimed to have necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-darurI) that when a thing perishes and becomes pure non-existence and sheer negation, after this pure non-existence it does not return in its very self, but the one that returns is something else other than it. This oath and swearing is an indication that they claimed necessary knowledge that its return in its very self after its non-existence is impossible by the immediate judgment of reason: ﴿And they swore by God with their most solemn oaths﴾, while in their hearts and minds they deny this necessary knowledge. As for the demonstration that when the affirmation of resurrection is false the affirmation of prophethood is false, He did not mention it explicitly, because it is a clear statement that comes immediately to minds, so they left it for this reason. Then He, Exalted, showed that the affirmation of resurrection is possible, and two proofs point to it:

The first proof: it is a true promise upon God, Exalted, so its fulfilment is obligatory. Then He explained the cause for which it was a true promise upon God, Exalted, namely the distinguishing between the obedient and the disobedient, between the one in the right and the one in the wrong, and between the wrongdoer and the wronged. This is His saying: ﴿So that He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars﴾. We have exceeded in explaining and establishing this method in surah Yunus.

The second proof, in demonstrating the possibility of gathering and dispersal: God's being the one who brings things into existence and originates them does not depend on a prior matter, nor on a period of time, nor on an instrument. He, Exalted, brings them into being only by the sheer power and will of His. There is no repeller of His power and no preventer of His will. So He, Exalted, expressed this unobstructed execution free of opposition by His saying: ﴿Indeed, when We intend a thing, Our word to it is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾. Since that is so, just as He, Exalted, was able to originate in the beginning, it must be that He is able to restore it. Thus by these two conclusive proofs it is established that the affirmation of resurrection, gathering, dispersal, raising and the Last Hour is true and right. What they said was that they attacked the soundness of prophethood on the basis of attacking this principle, so when this attack is refuted, their attack on prophethood is refuted too. And God knows best.

The second issue: His saying ﴿And they swore by God with their most solemn oaths﴾ is a report about those who associated partners (with God). His saying ﴿Yes indeed (bala)﴾ is an affirmation of what follows a negation, i.e. "Yes indeed, He will raise them up." His saying ﴿a promise binding upon Him, true﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), i.e. He promised the resurrection with a true promise, with no failing in it; because His saying "He will raise them" indicates His saying "He promised the resurrection." His saying ﴿So that He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾ concerns matters of the resurrection, i.e. "Yes indeed, He will raise them so that He may make clear to them" and so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars in what they swore to.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, when We intend a thing, Our word to it is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾. In it are issues:

The first issue: One may say: His saying "Be" (kun), if it is an address to the non-existent, then it is impossible; and if it is an address to the existent, then this is a command to obtain what is already obtained, which is impossible.

The answer: This is an illustration of the negation of speech and of effort, and an address to creatures in terms they can understand. It is not an address to the non-existent, because what God, Exalted, intends is existent in every state and in whatever speed He intends. Had He intended to create this world and the Hereafter with what is in them of heavens and earth in the span of a glance, He would have been able to do so. But the servants were addressed in this way according to the measure of their minds.

The second issue: His saying, Exalted: ﴿Our word﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿that We say to Him﴾ (an an naqula) is its predicate, and ﴿"Be," and it is﴾ (kun fa-yakun) is from kana, the complete verb, meaning "to come into being and existence." That is, when We intend the coming into being of a thing, there is nothing but that We say to it: "Come into being," and it comes into being immediately after that without any delay.

The third issue: Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ (with the subjunctive) with a fatha on the nun, while the rest read it with a damma (indicative). Al-Farra' said: the reading with the damma has the following basis: that His saying ﴿that We say to Him﴾ is made a complete utterance, and then one reports about it that "it will be," just as one says: "Indeed Zayd, it suffices him if he is commanded, and he does it," so you raise your saying "he does it" by making it an independent utterance. As for the reading with the fatha, its basis is that you make it a coordination (atf) upon "an naqula," and the meaning is: that We say "Be" and it is. This is the view of all the grammarians. Al-Zajjaj said: it may also be in the subjunctive as an answer to "Be" (kun). Abu 'Ali said: the word "Be," though in the form of a command, is not intended here as a command; rather, it is, and God knows best, a report about the existence and coming into being of a thing. Since the matter is so, then the claim that it is in the subjunctive as an answer to "Be" is invalidated. And God knows best.
