The second issue: His saying, Exalted: ﴿Our word﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿that We say to Him﴾ (an an naqula) is its predicate, and ﴿"Be," and it is﴾ (kun fa-yakun) is from kana, the complete verb, meaning "to come into being and existence." That is, when We intend the coming into being of a thing, there is nothing but that We say to it: "Come into being," and it comes into being immediately after that without any delay.

The third issue: Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ (with the subjunctive) with a fatha on the nun, while the rest read it with a damma (indicative). Al-Farra' said: the reading with the damma has the following basis: that His saying ﴿that We say to Him﴾ is made a complete utterance, and then one reports about it that "it will be," just as one says: "Indeed Zayd, it suffices him if he is commanded, and he does it," so you raise your saying "he does it" by making it an independent utterance. As for the reading with the fatha, its basis is that you make it a coordination (atf) upon "an naqula," and the meaning is: that We say "Be" and it is. This is the view of all the grammarians. Al-Zajjaj said: it may also be in the subjunctive as an answer to "Be" (kun). Abu 'Ali said: the word "Be," though in the form of a command, is not intended here as a command; rather, it is, and God knows best, a report about the existence and coming into being of a thing. Since the matter is so, then the claim that it is in the subjunctive as an answer to "Be" is invalidated. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: Some of our companions argued from this verse for the eternity (qidam) of the Qur'an. They said: God's words ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ show that when God intends to bring something into existence, He says to it "Be" and it is. So if His word "Be" were originated, its bringing into existence would require that He say to it "Be," and that would entail an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Therefore God's speech is eternal.

Know that this argument, in my view, is not very strong, and its weakness can be shown in several ways:

The first way: the word ﴿idha﴾ (when) does not indicate repetition. The evidence is that if a man says to his wife, "If you enter the house, you are divorced," and she enters the house once, she is divorced with one pronouncement. If she enters a second time, she is not divorced a second time. So we know that the word "idha" does not indicate repetition. Given this, it follows that it is not required for everything God originates that He say to it "Be," and so no infinite regress arises.

The second way: if this argument were sound, it would require the claim that the word "Be" is eternal, and this is known to be false by necessity. The word "kun" is composed of the letter kaf and the letter nun. When the kaf is present, the nun is not yet present, and when the nun comes, the kaf has passed. This shows that the word "kun" cannot be eternal. What our companions claim to be eternal is an attribute distinct from the word "kun." So what the verse indicates is not what our companions maintain, and what they maintain is not indicated by the verse. Thus reliance on it falls away.

The third way: if a man says, "So-and-so does not undertake any speech or act except that he seeks help in it from God Most High," no rational person would say that his seeking help from God is itself one of his acts, which would require that every seeking of help be preceded by another seeking of help, without end. This is because such a statement is invalid by convention. Likewise, what they have claimed is invalid.

The fourth way: this verse indicates that the speech is originated in several respects:

The first aspect: God's words ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing, when We intend it﴾ imply that the saying takes place through the will, and whatever is so is originated.

[p. 28]

The second aspect: He made the saying dependent on the word ﴿idha﴾ (when), and there is no doubt that the word "idha" applies to the future.

The third aspect: His words ﴿that We say to it﴾ — there is no disagreement that this points to the future.

The fourth aspect: His words ﴿"Be," and it is﴾ indicate that the coming into being of existence occurs immediately after His word "Be." So the word "Be" precedes the coming into being of existence by a single moment of time, and whatever precedes an originated thing by a single moment of time must itself be originated.

The fifth aspect: this is contradicted by God's words: ﴿And the command of God is ever an accomplished matter﴾ (An-Nisa 4:47); ﴿And the command of God is a decree determined﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:38); ﴿God has sent down the best statement﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:23); ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it﴾ (At-Tur 52:34); and ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and mercy﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:12).

If it is said: Suppose this verse does not indicate the eternity of speech, but you have mentioned that it indicates the origination of speech; what is your answer to that?

We say: We direct these proofs to the audible speech, which is composed of letters and sounds, and we affirm that it is originated and created. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 41–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers that they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths denying resurrection and the Last Day, this indicates that they persisted in error, ignorance and misguidance. In such a state it is not unlikely that they would proceed to harm the Muslims and afflict them, and to inflict punishments upon them. At that point it becomes incumbent upon the believers to emigrate from those lands and dwellings. So in this verse He, exalted is He, mentioned the ruling on that emigration and explained what these emigrants possess of good in this world and reward in the Hereafter, because they emigrated, were patient and relied upon Allah. This is an encouragement for others to obey Allah, exalted is He.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: This verse was revealed concerning six of the Companions: Suhayb, Bilal, 'Ammar, Khabbab, 'Abis and Jubayr, the two freedmen of Quraysh. They began to torture them in order to turn them back from Islam. As for Suhayb, he said to them: "I am an old man; if I am with you, I shall not benefit you, and if I am against you, I shall not harm you." So he ransomed himself from them with his wealth. When Abu Bakr saw him he said: "Suhayb has made a profitable sale." 'Umar said: "What an excellent man Suhayb is! If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." This is a great praise; he means: If Allah had not created the Fire, he would have obeyed Him; so how do you think of him, when He has created it? As for the rest of them, they uttered some of what the people of Mecca wanted of the words of disbelief and of returning from Islam, so they left off their torment; then they emigrated, and this verse was revealed. Through this verse Allah, exalted is He, made clear the great station of emigration and the station of the emigrants. The reasoning behind it is evident, for through their emigration the strength of Islam became manifest, just as through the support of the Helpers their power grew. By His saying: ﴿those who emigrated for the sake of Allah﴾ He indicated that emigration, if it is not for Allah, has no value, and is merely like moving from one land to another.

His saying: ﴿after they had been wronged﴾ means that they were oppressed in the hands of the disbelievers, for they were tormenting them.

Then He said: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, and concerning this there are several views:

The first: His saying ﴿a good place﴾ is an adjective of the verbal noun in His saying ﴿We will surely settle them in this world﴾, and the implied meaning is: We will surely settle them in a good settlement. In the reading of 'Ali, peace be upon him: (لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهم إبْواءَةً حَسَنَةً) [We will surely settle them with a good settling].

The second: We will surely lodge them in this world in a good station, namely dominance over the people of Mecca who wronged them, and over all the Arabs, and over the people of East and West. It is reported from 'Umar that whenever he gave a man among the emigrants a gift he would say: "Take it; may Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah has promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater."

The third view: We will surely settle them in a good abode, which is Medina, where its people sheltered them and supported them. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah, and the implied meaning is: We will surely settle them in this world in a good house or a good town, meaning Medina.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾ and more magnificent and more noble; ﴿if they only knew﴾. As for the pronoun, to what does it refer? There are two views concerning it:

The first: It refers to the disbelievers, meaning: if they knew that Allah, exalted is He, gathers for these weak ones in their hands both this world and the Hereafter, they would have desired their religion.

The second: It refers back to the emigrants, meaning: if they knew that, they would have increased their striving and their patience.

Then He said: ﴿Those who were patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ Concerning the grammatical position of ﴿those who﴾ there are several views:

The first: It is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿And those who emigrated﴾.

The second: The implied meaning is: "They are those who were patient."

The third: The implied meaning is: "I mean: those who were patient." Both of these two aspects are praise, and the meaning is that they were patient under torment and upon separation from the homeland which is the sanctuary of Allah, and in striving and in spending wealth and lives in the way of Allah. In sum, He mentioned patience and reliance. As for patience, it is for striving to subdue the self; as for reliance, it is for complete detachment from creation and complete turning toward the Truth. So the first is the beginning of the path to Allah, exalted is He.

The second is the end of this path and its final stage. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 43–44:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed, so ask the people of the reminder if you do not know﴾ ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them, and perhaps they will reflect﴾ ﴿Do those who devised evil deeds feel secure that Allah will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth, and they will not escape?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them with gradual decline? Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾.

In the verse there are issues:

[p. 30]

The first issue: Know that this is the fifth doubt of those who deny prophethood. They used to say: "Allah is too exalted and too great that His messenger should be one of the human beings. Rather, if He wanted to send a messenger to us, He would send an angel." We have already mentioned the statement of this doubt in Surat al-An'am, so we will not repeat it here. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿And they said: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. And they said: ﴿Shall we believe two men like ourselves?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47]. And they said: ﴿This is only a human being like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾, ﴿and if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33–34]. And He said: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man among them?﴾ [Yunus: 2]. And they said: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7].

Allah, exalted is He, answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾. The meaning is: the custom of Allah, exalted is He, from the beginning of creation and the imposition of obligations, is that He has never sent a messenger except from among humans. This custom is constant for Allah, glorified and exalted is He. And the attack of these ignorant people with this feeble question is also an old attack, so it should not be paid attention to.

The second issue: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, did not send any woman. It also indicates that He did not send an angel. However, the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir: 1] indicates that the angels are the messengers of Allah to the rest of the angels. So the apparent meaning of this verse is evidence that He did not send a messenger from among the angels to the people. The judge (al-Qadi) said: Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i claimed that He did not send to the prophets, peace be upon them, except one who is in the form of men from among the angels. Then the judge said: Perhaps he meant that the angel who is sent to the prophets, peace be upon them, in the presence of their nations, must also be in the form of men, as it is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi and in the form of Suraqa. We only said this because what is known of the state of the angels is that when conveying the message from Allah, exalted is He, to the Messenger, they may remain in their original angelic form. It has been narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril, peace be upon him, in his own form twice," and on this basis they interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13].

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this statement, He followed it with His saying: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: Regarding the meaning of "the people of the reminder" there are several views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: It means the people of the Torah, and the "reminder" is the Torah. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly wrote in the Psalms after the reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], meaning: the Torah.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: "Ask the people of the Books who know the meanings of the books of Allah, exalted is He, for they know that all the prophets were human."

The third: "The people of the reminder" are the people of knowledge of the news of the past, since one who knows a thing is one who remembers it.

The fourth: Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: ask everyone who is mentioned for knowledge and verification. And I say: It is apparent that this doubt, namely their saying: "Allah is too exalted and too great that His messenger should be one of the human beings," was only held by the disbelievers of Makkah. Then they used to acknowledge that the Jews and the Christians were the people of knowledge and the Books. So Allah commanded them to return in this matter to the Jews and the Christians, so that they might show them the weakness and the collapse of this doubt, for a Jew or a Christian must refute this doubt and explain its falsity.

The second issue: People differed on whether it is permissible for a mujtahid (a qualified jurist who derives rulings independently) to follow (taqlid) another mujtahid. Some ruled that it is permissible and argued with this verse, saying: Since one of the two mujtahids is not a knower, it is obligatory for him to return to the other mujtahid who is a knower, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know﴾. If it is not obligatory, then at least it is permissible.

The third issue: Those who deny analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy from a known ruling to a new case) argued with this verse, saying: When an accountable person faces an incident, if he knows its ruling, it is not permissible for him to use analogy; and if he does not know its ruling, it is obligatory for him to ask one who knows it, by the apparent meaning of this verse. If analogy were a valid proof, it would not be obligatory for him to ask the knower, because he could derive that ruling through analogy. Thus it is established that permitting action by analogy necessitates abandoning the apparent meaning of this verse, so it must not be permitted. And Allah knows best.

Its answer: The permissibility of acting on analogy has been established by the consensus (ijma') of the Companions, and consensus is stronger than this proof. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several views regarding what governs this particle "bi" (with):

The first: The estimated sense is: "And We did not send before you with the clear proofs and the scriptures except men to whom We revealed." Al-Farra' rejected this and said: The complement of "ma qabla" (what is before) does not come after "illa" (except). The evidence for this is that what is excepted from is the whole of "ma qabla illa" together with its complement, so as long as this whole has not been mentioned completely, it is impossible to place the exception upon it.

The second: The estimated sense is: "And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed with the clear proofs and the scriptures." On this estimate, His saying ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ is connected to the excepted term.

The third: The governing word of this "bi" is omitted, and the estimate is: "We sent them with the clear proofs." This is the view of al-Farra'. He said: Its parallel is: "Only your brother passed by Zayd," then he says: "passed by Zayd" (with the governing verb restored).

The fourth: It may be said: "The reminder" means knowledge, and the estimate is: "So ask the people of the reminder with the clear proofs and the scriptures if you do not know."

The fifth: The estimate may be: "If you do not know with the clear proofs and the scriptures, then ask the people of the reminder."

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ is an expression comprising everything through which the message is completed, because the basis of its affair rests upon the miracles that indicate the truthfulness of the one who claims to be a messenger, which are the "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat), and upon the obligations which the Messenger conveys from Allah, exalted is He, to the servants, which are the "scriptures" (al-zubur).

The third issue: Those who deny analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy from a known ruling to a new case) argued with this verse, saying: When an accountable person faces an incident, if he knows its ruling, it is not permissible for him to use analogy; and if he does not know its ruling, it is obligatory for him to ask one who knows it, by the apparent meaning of this verse. If analogy were a valid proof, it would not be obligatory for him to ask the knower, because he could derive that ruling through analogy. Thus it is established that permitting action by analogy necessitates abandoning the apparent meaning of this verse, so it must not be permitted. And Allah knows best.

Its answer: The permissibility of acting on analogy has been established by the consensus (ijma') of the Companions, and consensus is stronger than this proof. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several views regarding what governs this particle "bi" (with):

The first: The estimated sense is: "And We did not send before you with the clear proofs and the scriptures except men to whom We revealed." Al-Farra' rejected this and said: The complement of "ma qabla" (what is before) does not come after "illa" (except). The evidence for this is that what is excepted from is the whole of "ma qabla illa" together with its complement, so as long as this whole has not been mentioned completely, it is impossible to place the exception upon it.

The second: The estimated sense is: "And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed with the clear proofs and the scriptures." On this estimate, His saying ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ is connected to the excepted term.

The third: The governing word of this "bi" is omitted, and the estimate is: "We sent them with the clear proofs." This is the view of al-Farra'. He said: Its parallel is: "Only your brother passed by Zayd," then he says: "passed by Zayd" (with the governing verb restored).

The fourth: It may be said: "The reminder" means knowledge, and the estimate is: "So ask the people of the reminder with the clear proofs and the scriptures if you do not know."

The fifth: The estimate may be: "If you do not know with the clear proofs and the scriptures, then ask the people of the reminder."

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ is an expression comprising everything through which the message is completed, because the basis of its affair rests upon the miracles that indicate the truthfulness of the one who claims to be a messenger, which are the "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat), and upon the obligations which the Messenger conveys from Allah, exalted is He, to the servants, which are the "scriptures" (al-zubur).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 45–47:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The apparent meaning of this statement requires that this Reminder (dhikr) is in need of clarification by the Messenger of Allah, and what is in need of clarification is unclear (mujmal). The apparent meaning of this text therefore requires that the entire Qur'an is unclear. For this reason some scholars said: Whenever a contradiction occurs between the Qur'an and a khabar (report), it is obligatory to give precedence to the khabar, because the Qur'an is unclear, and the evidence for this is this verse, and the khabar clarifies it by the indication of this verse, and what clarifies takes precedence over what is unclear.

The answer: The Qur'an contains the muhkam (clear, definitive) and the mutashabih (ambiguous), and the muhkam must be clarifying. Thus it is established that the Qur'an is not entirely unclear; rather, there is in it what is unclear. So His saying ﴿that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ is to be understood as referring to the unclear matters.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of this verse requires that the Messenger ﷺ be the one who clarifies everything that Allah has sent down to the responsible persons (mukallafin). At this point, those who reject analogy (qiyas) said: If qiyas were a proof, it would not have been obligatory upon the Messenger to clarify every ruling that Allah sent down to the responsible persons, since the responsible person might clarify that ruling by way of analogy. And since this verse indicates that the one who clarifies all the obligations and rulings is the Messenger ﷺ, we know that qiyas is not a proof.

It is answered: When the Messenger ﷺ clarified that qiyas is a proof, then whoever refers to qiyas in clarifying rulings and obligations, that is in reality a return to the clarification of the Messenger ﷺ.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do those who devise evil deeds feel secure﴾. Makr (plotting) in the language is an expression for striving toward corruption in a concealed manner, and an implied term must be supplied here; the estimate is "the evil plots (al-makarat al-sayyi'at)". The intended people are the people of Makkah and those around Madinah. Al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning of this makr is their occupation with worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted. The closer view is that what is intended is their striving to harm the Messenger ﷺ and his companions in a covert manner. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned in their warning four matters:

The first: that Allah causes the earth to swallow them, as He caused it to swallow Qarun.

The second: that the punishment comes upon them from where they do not perceive, and what is intended is that the punishment comes to them from the sky, from where it surprises them, so that He destroys them suddenly, as He did to the people of Lut.

The third: that He seizes them in their movements (taqallub), so they cannot escape. In explaining this taqallub there are several aspects:

The first: that He seizes them with punishment during their journeys, for He is capable of destroying them while traveling just as He is capable of destroying them at home, and they cannot overcome Allah by means of their wandering in distant lands; rather Allah overtakes them wherever they are. Understanding the word taqallub in this sense is taken from His saying: ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the lands deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196].

The second: interpreting this word as that He seizes them by night and day in their states of advancing and retreating, going and coming; and its true sense is in their conduct regarding the affairs in which people like them conduct themselves.

The third: that the meaning is "or He seizes them while they are turning over the matters of their plans," so that Allah prevents them by force from completing those schemes, as He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, so they would race to the path, but how would they see?﴾ [Ya Sin: 66]. Understanding the word taqallub in this sense is taken from His saying: ﴿And they turned over the affairs for you﴾ [At-Tawbah: 48], for when they turn them over, they have indeed turned about in them.

The fourth of the matters that Allah mentioned in this verse by way of threat is His saying: ﴿Or He seizes them with gradual loss (takhawwuf)﴾. Concerning the explanation of takhawwuf there are two views:

The first view: takhawwuf is a form of tafa''ul from fear (khawf); it is said: "I feared the thing and takhawwaftuhu (I was apprehensive of it)." The meaning is that He, exalted is He, does not seize them with punishment first, but first instills fear in them, and then punishes them after that. That instilling of fear is that He destroys one group and the next group becomes afraid, so this is a seizing and a return against them after they have passed a long time before that in fear and desolation.

The second view: that takhawwuf means tanaqqus (diminishing). Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said "takhawwaftu al-shay'" and "takhayyaftuhu" when you diminish it. It is related from Umar that he said from the pulpit: "What do you say about this verse?" They were silent, and a shaykh from Hudhayl stood and said: "This is our dialect: takhawwuf is tanaqqus (diminishing)." Umar said: "Do the Arabs know that in their poetry?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Our poet said," and recited:

"The saddle-bag was apprehensive of her, hardened and fat-humped, as the arrow-shafts of the nab'a wood are diminished by wear."

Umar said: "O people, keep to your diwan, lest you go astray." They said: "And what is our diwan?" He said: "The poetry of the Jahiliyya, in which is the explanation of your Book."

Having understood this, we say: this diminishing may mean that which occurs in the outskirts of their lands, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts?﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 44]. The meaning is that He does not hasten the punishment upon them, but diminishes from the outskirts of their lands, toward the villages neighboring them, until the matter reaches them, and then He destroys them. It may also mean that He gradually diminishes their wealth and their persons, little by little, until annihilation comes upon all of them. This is the explanation of these four matters. The summary is that He, exalted is He, threatened them with a sinking that occurs in the earth, or a punishment that descends from the sky, or calamities that arise all at once while they are unaware of its signs and indications, or calamities that arise little by little until destruction comes upon the last of them. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾. The meaning is that He gives respite in most matters, because He is Kind and Merciful, so He does not hasten punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 48–50 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not considered the things God has created, whose shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating themselves to God while they are humbled?﴾ ﴿To God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted be He, warned the polytheists with the four kinds of punishment mentioned, He followed this with a mention of what indicates the perfection of His power in governing the affairs of the higher and lower worlds, and the governing of the affairs of spirits and bodies, to show them that with the perfection of this overpowering power and His limitless strength, He is not unable to bring punishment upon them in any of those four ways.

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا, "have you not seen?") with the letter ta' (tā'), as an address (khitab), and likewise in Surat al-'Ankabut: (أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ يَبْدَأُ اللَّهُ الخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ, "Have they not seen how God originates creation, then repeats it?") [al-'Ankabut: 19] with ta' as an address. The rest read it with ya' in both places, as a reference (kinayah) to those who devised evil schemes. Also, what precedes it is in the third person, namely His saying: ﴿Are they secure that God will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them﴾ [al-Nahl: 45–46], so likewise His saying: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. Abu 'Amr alone read (تَتَفَيَّأُ, "turn about") with ta', and the rest with ya', and both are permissible because the verb precedes the plural noun.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿Have they not considered what God has created﴾. Since seeing here means consideration (nazar), it is connected with (ila, "to"), because what is meant is reflection (i'tibar), and reflection does not occur through mere sight, unless it is accompanied by a look at the thing and contemplation of its conditions. His saying: ﴿what God has created of anything﴾, the people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He meant of anything that has a shadow, from a mountain, a tree, a building, or an upright body, and the wording of the verse suggests this restriction, because His saying: ﴿of anything whose shadows incline from the right and the left﴾ indicates that this thing is dense, so that a shadow falls upon the ground from it.

His saying: ﴿whose shadows incline﴾ is an information about the word ﴿anything﴾, not a description of it. (Yatafayya'u, "incline"), is yatafa'alu from al-fay'. It is said: the shadow (fa'a al-zill, yafi'u, fay'an) when it returns and comes back after the sun's light has abolished it. The root meaning of al-fay' is return, and from it comes (fay' al-mawla, the return of a master) (the return to the wife after an oath). We mentioned this in His saying: ﴿And if they return, then God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]. Likewise the fay' of the Muslims, for what returns to the Muslims from the property of those who oppose their religion, and from it His saying: ﴿And what God gave as fay' to His Messenger from them﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. The origin of all this is return.

Having understood this, we say: when fa'a is made transitive, it is made transitive either by adding a hamzah or by doubling the 'ayn. As for transitivity by the hamzah, like His saying: ﴿what God gave as fay'﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. As for doubling the 'ayn, like the saying: fayya'a Allahu al-zilla fa-tafayya'a (God made the shadow incline, so it inclined), and tafayya'a is the intransitive counterpart of fayya'a. Al-Azhari said: the inclining of shadows is their return after midday, so the tafayyu' occurs only in the evening after the sun has departed from it, and the shadow (zill) is what occurs in the morning, which is what the sun has not reached, as the poet said:

صفحة ٣٤
Neither does the shade bear the cold of the forenoon, nor does the fay' taste the cold of the evening.

Tha'lab said: I was informed from Abu 'Ubaydah that Ru'bah said: whatever the sun has been upon and then left, it is fay', and whatever the sun has not been upon is shade (zill). Some denied this, for Abu Zayd recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

So the greeting of God comes to them each morning, and the fuyuc of the plantations, full of shades.

This verse uses the word fay' for what the sun has not abolished, because what is in Paradise of shade is what came about after having been removed by the light of the sun. The Arabs say, in the plural of fay': afya', which is for small numbers, and fuyuc for large numbers, like nufus and 'uyun. His saying: ﴿shadows﴾ (zilal) is the plural attributed to a singular, and its meaning is an attribution to possessors of shadows. This is good because the pronoun refers back to what is in wording singular, namely His saying: "what God created," though in meaning it is plural. A parallel is His saying: ﴿that you may sit firmly upon its back﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13], where He attributes (zuhur, "backs"), which is plural, to a singular pronoun, because it refers to a singular that is meant as plurality, namely His saying: ﴿what you ride﴾. All this is the words of al-Wahidi, and it is a fine investigation.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿on the right and the left﴾, there are two investigations:

The first investigation: concerning what is meant by the right and the left, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: the right of the celestial sphere (falak) is the east, and its left is the west. The reason for specifying these two names for these two sides is that the strongest side of a human being is his right, and from it strong movement appears. Since the daily celestial motion takes its course from east to west, it is necessarily the case that the east is the right of the sphere and the west its left.

Having understood this, we say: when the sun rises until the time it reaches the middle of the sphere, the shadows fall toward the western side. When the sun descends from the middle of the sphere toward the western side, the shadows fall on the eastern side. This is what is meant by the inclining of shadows from right to left and the reverse. On this reckoning, at the beginning of the day, the shadows begin from the right of the sphere, falling on the western quarter of the earth, and from the time the sun descends from the middle of the sphere, the shadows begin from the left of the sphere, falling on the eastern quarter of the earth.

The second opinion: the land whose latitude is less than the measure of a mile. In summer the sun is on their left, and then the shadows fall on their right. This is what is meant by the shifting of shadows from the right to the left and the reverse. This is what I have gathered on this topic, and the statements of the exegetes on it are not summarized.

The second investigation: someone may ask: what is the reason that He mentioned "the right" in the singular and "the left" in the plural form?

It has been answered in several ways:

One: He used the singular for the right while meaning the plural, but He limited the wording to the singular, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45].

Second: al-Farra' said: it is as if, when He uses the singular, He refers to one of the possessors of shadows, and when He uses the plural, He refers to all of them. This is because His saying: ﴿what God created of anything﴾ is singular in wording and plural in meaning, as we have explained, so both matters are admissible.

Third: when the Arabs mention two plural forms, they express one of them with the singular wording, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and His saying: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].

Fourth: when we interpret the right as the east, the point which is the sunrise is one and the same, so the right is singular. As for the left, it is an expression for the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many, so God, exalted be He, expressed them in the plural form. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: As for His saying: ﴿prostrating to God﴾, there are possibilities:

The first: that prostration here means submission and compliance. It is said: the camel prostrated when it lowered its head to be ridden, and the palm tree prostrated when it bent because of the abundance of its load. It is also said: "prostrate to the monkey of evil in its time," meaning: submit to it. The poet said:

You see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves,

meaning: humbled. Having understood this, we say: He, exalted be He, arranged the luminous celestial bodies and the stellar figures in such a way that their lights fall upon this lower world in specific ways. Then we observe that those lights and those shadows fall in this world only according to the arrangement and decree of God, exalted be He. We observe that when the sun rises, there fall for dense bodies extended shadows on the western side of the earth. Then as the sun rises higher, those shadows contract and diminish toward the eastern side, until the sun reaches the middle of the sphere. When it descends toward the western side, the shadows begin to fall on the eastern side, and as the sun descends more, the shadows expand and increase on the eastern side. Just as we observe this condition within a single day, so too we observe the shadows differing in rightward and leftward inclination across the length of the year, due to the differing movements of the sun from south to north and the reverse. When we witness these shadows differing because of the daily variations occurring in the east and west of the earth, and according to the variations occurring over the length of the year on the right and left of the sphere, and we see that they fall in a specific manner and a fixed order, we know that they are subject to the power of God and submissive to His decree and arrangement. Thus prostration is an expression for this condition.

If it is said: why would it not be permissible to say that the variation in the state of these shadows is caused by the difference in the course of the greatest luminary, which is the sun, and not for the sake of God's decree and arrangement?

We say: We have already shown that a body is not moving by its own essence. For if its essence were the cause of this specific portion of motion, this portion of motion would remain as long as its essence remained, and if that portion of motion remained, the occurrence of another portion of motion would be impossible. If that were the case, it would be rest, not motion. So the claim that a body that moves by its essence necessitates that it is at rest by its essence, and that is impossible, and whatever its affirmation leads to its negation is false. So we know that it is impossible for a body to be moving by its own essence. Furthermore, we have shown that bodies are alike in their complete quiddity, so the particular specific power and particular property belonging to the body of the sun must necessarily be by the arrangement of the Creator, the Chooser, the Wise.

Having established this, we say: suppose the variation in the states of the shadows was indeed due to the movements of the sun. Nevertheless, since we have shown that the mover of the sun in its specific motion is none other than God, glorified be He, this is a proof that the variation in the states of the shadows occurred only by the arrangement and creation of God, exalted be He. Thus it is established that the meaning of this prostration is submission and humility. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6], and His saying: ﴿and their shadows at morning and evening﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15], whose explanation and commentary has already passed.

The second opinion concerning the interpretation of this prostration is that these shadows fall upon the earth, clinging to it in the form of one who prostrates. Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri said, describing a valley:

With a crack in which the ravine prolongs its prostration, and the earth has the appearance of a worshipping monk.

Since the shadows resemble, in their shape, the shape of those who prostrate, God applied this term to them. Al-Hasan used to say: as for your shadow, it prostrates to your Lord, but as for you, you do not prostrate to Him; how evil is what you have done. Mujahid said: the shadow of the unbeliever prays while he himself does not pray. It is also said: the shadow of everything prostrates to God, whether it is a prostrating thing or not.

Know that the first aspect is closer to rational realities, and the second is closer to apparent doubts.

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿prostrating﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the shadows, and His saying: ﴿while they are humbled﴾, that is: abased (saghirun). It is said: dakhara yadkharu dukhuran, meaning: sagura yasghuru saghaaran, and it refers to one who does what he is commanded, whether he wishes or not. This is because these things are subject to the power and arrangement of God, exalted be He. His saying: ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is also a circumstantial state of the shadows.

If it is said: shadows are not among the rational beings, so how is it permissible to pluralize them with the masculine sound plural ending (waw and nun)?

We say: because when He, exalted be He, described them as obedient and abased, they became like rational beings.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**Issue 1:** There are two kinds of prostration. One is worship, like the prostration of the Muslims to God, Exalted. The other is an expression of submission and humility before God, Exalted. The outcome of this second kind of prostration comes down to this: a thing is in itself capable of existing or not existing, and it is equally open to both. Neither of the two possibilities is preferred over the other except by a preponderant cause.

Having understood this, we say: Some people said that the prostration mentioned in this verse means the second sense, which is humility and submission. The evidence for this is that the only prostration fitting for a creature that crawls (dābba) is this one. Others said that the prostration here means the first sense, because the prostration that befits the angels is prostration in this sense. The prostration in the second sense exists in all animals, plants and inanimate things. Others said that prostration (sujūd) is a homonym (lafẓ mushtarak) covering both meanings, and that it is permissible to use a homonym to convey all of its meanings together. So the word "prostration" in this verse is applied to both at once: with regard to the creature that crawls it means humility, and with regard to the angels it means the prostration of the Muslims to God, Exalted. This view is weak, because it has been established that using a homonym to convey all its meanings simultaneously is not permissible.

**Issue 2:** As for His words, ﴿from a creature that crawls﴾, al-Akhfash said: it means "from among the creatures that crawl," and he used the singular as one says, "No one came to me from a man like him," and "No one came to me from among the men like him." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means everything that crawls on the earth.

**Issue 3:** Someone may ask: what is the reason for singling out the creatures that crawl and the angels for mention? We say that there are several reasons.

**The first reason:** In the verse of the shadows, God showed that all inanimate things are submissive to God, Exalted. In this verse He showed that all living beings are submissive to God, Exalted, since the lowest of them are the creatures that crawl and the most noble of them are the angels. When He showed that both the lowest and the most noble are submissive to God, Exalted, this is evidence that all of them are submissive and humbled before God, Exalted.

**The second reason:** The philosophers of Islam (ḥukamāʾ al-Islām) said: the word dābba (creature that crawls) is derived from dabīb (crawling), and dabīb means physical movement. So dābba is the name for every physical living being that moves and crawls. When God, Exalted, distinguished the angels from the dābba, we know that they are not among what crawls, but are pure, immaterial spirits. This can be answered: flight by wings is different from crawling, as is evident from His words, ﴿And there is no creature in the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām: 38]. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted: ﴿And they are not arrogant. They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded﴾.

On this there are several issues.

**Issue 1:** The purpose of this verse is to describe the attributes of the angels, and it is a compelling and decisive proof of the angels' infallibility (ʿiṣma) from all sins. His words, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾, indicate that they are submissive to their Maker and Creator, and that they did not disobey Him in any matter. A parallel to this is His words, Exalted: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and His words: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 27]. As for His words, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, this too indicates that they did everything they were commanded to do, and this indicates their infallibility from all sins.

If they say: Grant that this verse indicates that they did everything they were commanded; why do you say that it indicates that they abandoned everything they were forbidden?

We say: Because whoever is forbidden from something has also been commanded to abandon it, and thus it enters into the wording. Once it is established by this verse that the angels are infallible from all sins, and it is established that Iblīs was not infallible from sins but was a disbeliever, it necessarily follows with certainty that Iblīs was not among the angels.

**The second reason** for this aim: God, Exalted, said about the angels, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾, and then He said to Iblīs: ﴿Have you become arrogant, or were you among the haughty?﴾ [Ṣād: 75]. He also said to him: ﴿So descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 13]. Thus it is established that the angels are not arrogant, and it is established that Iblīs was arrogant and acted with pride, so it is necessary that he was not among the angels. Furthermore, since the infallibility of the angels has been established by this verse, it is established that the vile story which they tell about Hārūt and Mārūt is false speech. For God, Exalted, who is the most truthful of speakers, has testified in this verse to the infallibility of the angels and their freedom from every sin, so it is necessary to hold with certainty that that story is untrue and false. And God knows best.

Those who attack the infallibility of the angels have argued from this verse, saying: He, Exalted, described them as fearful, and had they not considered it possible for themselves to commit major sins and transgressions, there would be no fear.

The answer has two parts.

**The first:** He, Exalted, warns them of the punishment, saying: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," then We will recompense him with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 29]. And because of this fear they abandon sin.

**The second**, which is the more correct: that fear is the fear of reverence (khawf al-ijlāl). This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. The evidence for its soundness is His words, Exalted: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fāṭir: 28]. This indicates that the more complete one's knowledge of God, Exalted, is, the greater one's fear of Him, and this fear is only the fear of majesty and greatness. And God knows best.

**Issue 2:** The anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbiha) said: His words, Exalted, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, indicate that God, Exalted, is above them in essence.

Know that we went to great lengths in answering this doubt in the explanation of His words, Exalted: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-Anʿām: 18]. What we add here is this: His words, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, mean: they fear their Lord lest He send down punishment upon them from above them. And if the wording allows this meaning, their claim falls. Furthermore, this "aboveness" must be understood as aboveness by power and dominance, as in His words: ﴿And indeed We are above them, subduing﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 127]. What strengthens this interpretation is that when He, Exalted, said, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, the cause of this fear must be that their Lord is above them, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that a ruling attached to a descriptive attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute.

Having established this, we say: this interpretation would only be valid if the intended aboveness were aboveness by domination and power, because that is what produces fear. As for aboveness in direction and place, it does not produce fear. The evidence is that the guard of a house is "above" the king in place and direction, yet he is the lowliest of his servants. Thus this doubt is refuted.

**Issue 3:** This verse indicates that the angels are obligated by God, Exalted, and that commands and prohibitions apply to them as they apply to all the obligated. And whenever they are like this, it is necessary that they be capable of good and evil.

**Issue 4:** Some people used this verse to show that the angel is superior to the human being, in several respects.

**The first respect:** He, Exalted, said: ﴿And to God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, of creatures that crawl, and the angels﴾. We mentioned that singling out these two kinds for mention is only appropriate if one of the two extremes is the lowest of ranks and the other extreme is the highest of them, so that mention of these two extremes alerts the mind to what lies between them. If that is so, then the angels must be the most noble of God's creation.

**The second respect:** His words, Exalted, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾ indicate that there is no pride or haughtiness in their hearts. His words, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ indicate that their deeds are free of sin and disobedience. The combination of these two statements indicates that their inner and outer selves are free of corrupt characteristics and false deeds. As for human beings, they are not like this. This is shown by the Qur'an and the Hadith. From the Qur'an, His words, Exalted: ﴿Cursed is man; how disbelieving he is!﴾ [ʿAbasa: 17]. This ruling is general to man, and at the very least it means that human nature tends toward these blameworthy states. From the Hadith, His words, peace be upon him: "There is none of us but that he has disobeyed or intended disobedience, except Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā." It is known by necessity that one who is free from disobedience and the intention of it is more excellent than one who has disobeyed or intended it.

**The third respect:** There is no doubt that God, Exalted, created the angels before human beings by long eras and extended periods of time. Then He described them as obedient, submissive and humble throughout this long period. And a long life spent in obedience necessarily brings greater excellence, for two reasons.

**The first:** His words, peace be upon him: "The elder among his people is like the prophet among his community." He preferred the elder over the youth. This is only because his life was longer, so his obedience is apparently greater, and so he is more excellent.

**The second:** He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever establishes a good practice (sunna ḥasana), he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." Since the angels began the acts of obedience before human beings began them, it follows that they are the ones who established this good practice, which is the obedience of the Eternal, Merciful Creator, and human beings came after them and followed their practice. So by the requirement of this report, whatever reward human beings obtain, the angels obtain its like, and they also have the reward of the additional degree of obedience. Therefore they must be more excellent than others.

[Page 39]

**The fourth respect:** The indication of the verse for this meaning is His words, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾. We have shown by proof that this "aboveness" is an expression of superiority in rank, nobility, power and strength. The apparent meaning of the verse therefore indicates that there is nothing above them in nobility and rank except God, Exalted, and this indicates that they are the most excellent of created beings. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 48–50 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not considered the things God has created, whose shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating themselves to God while they are humbled?﴾ ﴿To God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted be He, warned the polytheists with the four kinds of punishment mentioned, He followed this with a mention of what indicates the perfection of His power in governing the affairs of the higher and lower worlds, and the governing of the affairs of spirits and bodies, to show them that with the perfection of this overpowering power and His limitless strength, He is not unable to bring punishment upon them in any of those four ways.

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا, "have you not seen?") with the letter ta' (tā'), as an address (khitab), and likewise in Surat al-'Ankabut: (أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ يَبْدَأُ اللَّهُ الخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ, "Have they not seen how God originates creation, then repeats it?") [al-'Ankabut: 19] with ta' as an address. The rest read it with ya' in both places, as a reference (kinayah) to those who devised evil schemes. Also, what precedes it is in the third person, namely His saying: ﴿Are they secure that God will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them﴾ [al-Nahl: 45–46], so likewise His saying: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. Abu 'Amr alone read (تَتَفَيَّأُ, "turn about") with ta', and the rest with ya', and both are permissible because the verb precedes the plural noun.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿Have they not considered what God has created﴾. Since seeing here means consideration (nazar), it is connected with (ila, "to"), because what is meant is reflection (i'tibar), and reflection does not occur through mere sight, unless it is accompanied by a look at the thing and contemplation of its conditions. His saying: ﴿what God has created of anything﴾, the people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He meant of anything that has a shadow, from a mountain, a tree, a building, or an upright body, and the wording of the verse suggests this restriction, because His saying: ﴿of anything whose shadows incline from the right and the left﴾ indicates that this thing is dense, so that a shadow falls upon the ground from it.

His saying: ﴿whose shadows incline﴾ is an information about the word ﴿anything﴾, not a description of it. (Yatafayya'u, "incline"), is yatafa'alu from al-fay'. It is said: the shadow (fa'a al-zill, yafi'u, fay'an) when it returns and comes back after the sun's light has abolished it. The root meaning of al-fay' is return, and from it comes (fay' al-mawla, the return of a master) (the return to the wife after an oath). We mentioned this in His saying: ﴿And if they return, then God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226]. Likewise the fay' of the Muslims, for what returns to the Muslims from the property of those who oppose their religion, and from it His saying: ﴿And what God gave as fay' to His Messenger from them﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. The origin of all this is return.

Having understood this, we say: when fa'a is made transitive, it is made transitive either by adding a hamzah or by doubling the 'ayn. As for transitivity by the hamzah, like His saying: ﴿what God gave as fay'﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. As for doubling the 'ayn, like the saying: fayya'a Allahu al-zilla fa-tafayya'a (God made the shadow incline, so it inclined), and tafayya'a is the intransitive counterpart of fayya'a. Al-Azhari said: the inclining of shadows is their return after midday, so the tafayyu' occurs only in the evening after the sun has departed from it, and the shadow (zill) is what occurs in the morning, which is what the sun has not reached, as the poet said:

صفحة ٣٤
Neither does the shade bear the cold of the forenoon, nor does the fay' taste the cold of the evening.

Tha'lab said: I was informed from Abu 'Ubaydah that Ru'bah said: whatever the sun has been upon and then left, it is fay', and whatever the sun has not been upon is shade (zill). Some denied this, for Abu Zayd recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di:

So the greeting of God comes to them each morning, and the fuyuc of the plantations, full of shades.

This verse uses the word fay' for what the sun has not abolished, because what is in Paradise of shade is what came about after having been removed by the light of the sun. The Arabs say, in the plural of fay': afya', which is for small numbers, and fuyuc for large numbers, like nufus and 'uyun. His saying: ﴿shadows﴾ (zilal) is the plural attributed to a singular, and its meaning is an attribution to possessors of shadows. This is good because the pronoun refers back to what is in wording singular, namely His saying: "what God created," though in meaning it is plural. A parallel is His saying: ﴿that you may sit firmly upon its back﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13], where He attributes (zuhur, "backs"), which is plural, to a singular pronoun, because it refers to a singular that is meant as plurality, namely His saying: ﴿what you ride﴾. All this is the words of al-Wahidi, and it is a fine investigation.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿on the right and the left﴾, there are two investigations:

The first investigation: concerning what is meant by the right and the left, there are two opinions:

The first opinion: the right of the celestial sphere (falak) is the east, and its left is the west. The reason for specifying these two names for these two sides is that the strongest side of a human being is his right, and from it strong movement appears. Since the daily celestial motion takes its course from east to west, it is necessarily the case that the east is the right of the sphere and the west its left.

Having understood this, we say: when the sun rises until the time it reaches the middle of the sphere, the shadows fall toward the western side. When the sun descends from the middle of the sphere toward the western side, the shadows fall on the eastern side. This is what is meant by the inclining of shadows from right to left and the reverse. On this reckoning, at the beginning of the day, the shadows begin from the right of the sphere, falling on the western quarter of the earth, and from the time the sun descends from the middle of the sphere, the shadows begin from the left of the sphere, falling on the eastern quarter of the earth.

The second opinion: the land whose latitude is less than the measure of a mile. In summer the sun is on their left, and then the shadows fall on their right. This is what is meant by the shifting of shadows from the right to the left and the reverse. This is what I have gathered on this topic, and the statements of the exegetes on it are not summarized.

The second investigation: someone may ask: what is the reason that He mentioned "the right" in the singular and "the left" in the plural form?

It has been answered in several ways:

One: He used the singular for the right while meaning the plural, but He limited the wording to the singular, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45].

Second: al-Farra' said: it is as if, when He uses the singular, He refers to one of the possessors of shadows, and when He uses the plural, He refers to all of them. This is because His saying: ﴿what God created of anything﴾ is singular in wording and plural in meaning, as we have explained, so both matters are admissible.

Third: when the Arabs mention two plural forms, they express one of them with the singular wording, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and His saying: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].

Fourth: when we interpret the right as the east, the point which is the sunrise is one and the same, so the right is singular. As for the left, it is an expression for the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many, so God, exalted be He, expressed them in the plural form. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: As for His saying: ﴿prostrating to God﴾, there are possibilities:

The first: that prostration here means submission and compliance. It is said: the camel prostrated when it lowered its head to be ridden, and the palm tree prostrated when it bent because of the abundance of its load. It is also said: "prostrate to the monkey of evil in its time," meaning: submit to it. The poet said:

You see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves,

meaning: humbled. Having understood this, we say: He, exalted be He, arranged the luminous celestial bodies and the stellar figures in such a way that their lights fall upon this lower world in specific ways. Then we observe that those lights and those shadows fall in this world only according to the arrangement and decree of God, exalted be He. We observe that when the sun rises, there fall for dense bodies extended shadows on the western side of the earth. Then as the sun rises higher, those shadows contract and diminish toward the eastern side, until the sun reaches the middle of the sphere. When it descends toward the western side, the shadows begin to fall on the eastern side, and as the sun descends more, the shadows expand and increase on the eastern side. Just as we observe this condition within a single day, so too we observe the shadows differing in rightward and leftward inclination across the length of the year, due to the differing movements of the sun from south to north and the reverse. When we witness these shadows differing because of the daily variations occurring in the east and west of the earth, and according to the variations occurring over the length of the year on the right and left of the sphere, and we see that they fall in a specific manner and a fixed order, we know that they are subject to the power of God and submissive to His decree and arrangement. Thus prostration is an expression for this condition.

If it is said: why would it not be permissible to say that the variation in the state of these shadows is caused by the difference in the course of the greatest luminary, which is the sun, and not for the sake of God's decree and arrangement?

We say: We have already shown that a body is not moving by its own essence. For if its essence were the cause of this specific portion of motion, this portion of motion would remain as long as its essence remained, and if that portion of motion remained, the occurrence of another portion of motion would be impossible. If that were the case, it would be rest, not motion. So the claim that a body that moves by its essence necessitates that it is at rest by its essence, and that is impossible, and whatever its affirmation leads to its negation is false. So we know that it is impossible for a body to be moving by its own essence. Furthermore, we have shown that bodies are alike in their complete quiddity, so the particular specific power and particular property belonging to the body of the sun must necessarily be by the arrangement of the Creator, the Chooser, the Wise.

Having established this, we say: suppose the variation in the states of the shadows was indeed due to the movements of the sun. Nevertheless, since we have shown that the mover of the sun in its specific motion is none other than God, glorified be He, this is a proof that the variation in the states of the shadows occurred only by the arrangement and creation of God, exalted be He. Thus it is established that the meaning of this prostration is submission and humility. A parallel is His saying: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6], and His saying: ﴿and their shadows at morning and evening﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15], whose explanation and commentary has already passed.

The second opinion concerning the interpretation of this prostration is that these shadows fall upon the earth, clinging to it in the form of one who prostrates. Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri said, describing a valley:

With a crack in which the ravine prolongs its prostration, and the earth has the appearance of a worshipping monk.

Since the shadows resemble, in their shape, the shape of those who prostrate, God applied this term to them. Al-Hasan used to say: as for your shadow, it prostrates to your Lord, but as for you, you do not prostrate to Him; how evil is what you have done. Mujahid said: the shadow of the unbeliever prays while he himself does not pray. It is also said: the shadow of everything prostrates to God, whether it is a prostrating thing or not.

Know that the first aspect is closer to rational realities, and the second is closer to apparent doubts.

The fifth issue: His saying: ﴿prostrating﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the shadows, and His saying: ﴿while they are humbled﴾, that is: abased (saghirun). It is said: dakhara yadkharu dukhuran, meaning: sagura yasghuru saghaaran, and it refers to one who does what he is commanded, whether he wishes or not. This is because these things are subject to the power and arrangement of God, exalted be He. His saying: ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is also a circumstantial state of the shadows.

If it is said: shadows are not among the rational beings, so how is it permissible to pluralize them with the masculine sound plural ending (waw and nun)?

We say: because when He, exalted be He, described them as obedient and abased, they became like rational beings.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**Issue 1:** There are two kinds of prostration. One is worship, like the prostration of the Muslims to God, Exalted. The other is an expression of submission and humility before God, Exalted. The outcome of this second kind of prostration comes down to this: a thing is in itself capable of existing or not existing, and it is equally open to both. Neither of the two possibilities is preferred over the other except by a preponderant cause.

Having understood this, we say: Some people said that the prostration mentioned in this verse means the second sense, which is humility and submission. The evidence for this is that the only prostration fitting for a creature that crawls (dābba) is this one. Others said that the prostration here means the first sense, because the prostration that befits the angels is prostration in this sense. The prostration in the second sense exists in all animals, plants and inanimate things. Others said that prostration (sujūd) is a homonym (lafẓ mushtarak) covering both meanings, and that it is permissible to use a homonym to convey all of its meanings together. So the word "prostration" in this verse is applied to both at once: with regard to the creature that crawls it means humility, and with regard to the angels it means the prostration of the Muslims to God, Exalted. This view is weak, because it has been established that using a homonym to convey all its meanings simultaneously is not permissible.

**Issue 2:** As for His words, ﴿from a creature that crawls﴾, al-Akhfash said: it means "from among the creatures that crawl," and he used the singular as one says, "No one came to me from a man like him," and "No one came to me from among the men like him." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means everything that crawls on the earth.

**Issue 3:** Someone may ask: what is the reason for singling out the creatures that crawl and the angels for mention? We say that there are several reasons.

**The first reason:** In the verse of the shadows, God showed that all inanimate things are submissive to God, Exalted. In this verse He showed that all living beings are submissive to God, Exalted, since the lowest of them are the creatures that crawl and the most noble of them are the angels. When He showed that both the lowest and the most noble are submissive to God, Exalted, this is evidence that all of them are submissive and humbled before God, Exalted.

**The second reason:** The philosophers of Islam (ḥukamāʾ al-Islām) said: the word dābba (creature that crawls) is derived from dabīb (crawling), and dabīb means physical movement. So dābba is the name for every physical living being that moves and crawls. When God, Exalted, distinguished the angels from the dābba, we know that they are not among what crawls, but are pure, immaterial spirits. This can be answered: flight by wings is different from crawling, as is evident from His words, ﴿And there is no creature in the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿām: 38]. And God knows best.

* * *

As for His words, Exalted: ﴿And they are not arrogant. They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded﴾.

On this there are several issues.

**Issue 1:** The purpose of this verse is to describe the attributes of the angels, and it is a compelling and decisive proof of the angels' infallibility (ʿiṣma) from all sins. His words, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾, indicate that they are submissive to their Maker and Creator, and that they did not disobey Him in any matter. A parallel to this is His words, Exalted: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and His words: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 27]. As for His words, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, this too indicates that they did everything they were commanded to do, and this indicates their infallibility from all sins.

If they say: Grant that this verse indicates that they did everything they were commanded; why do you say that it indicates that they abandoned everything they were forbidden?

We say: Because whoever is forbidden from something has also been commanded to abandon it, and thus it enters into the wording. Once it is established by this verse that the angels are infallible from all sins, and it is established that Iblīs was not infallible from sins but was a disbeliever, it necessarily follows with certainty that Iblīs was not among the angels.

**The second reason** for this aim: God, Exalted, said about the angels, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾, and then He said to Iblīs: ﴿Have you become arrogant, or were you among the haughty?﴾ [Ṣād: 75]. He also said to him: ﴿So descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 13]. Thus it is established that the angels are not arrogant, and it is established that Iblīs was arrogant and acted with pride, so it is necessary that he was not among the angels. Furthermore, since the infallibility of the angels has been established by this verse, it is established that the vile story which they tell about Hārūt and Mārūt is false speech. For God, Exalted, who is the most truthful of speakers, has testified in this verse to the infallibility of the angels and their freedom from every sin, so it is necessary to hold with certainty that that story is untrue and false. And God knows best.

Those who attack the infallibility of the angels have argued from this verse, saying: He, Exalted, described them as fearful, and had they not considered it possible for themselves to commit major sins and transgressions, there would be no fear.

The answer has two parts.

**The first:** He, Exalted, warns them of the punishment, saying: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a god besides Him," then We will recompense him with Hell﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 29]. And because of this fear they abandon sin.

**The second**, which is the more correct: that fear is the fear of reverence (khawf al-ijlāl). This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. The evidence for its soundness is His words, Exalted: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fāṭir: 28]. This indicates that the more complete one's knowledge of God, Exalted, is, the greater one's fear of Him, and this fear is only the fear of majesty and greatness. And God knows best.

**Issue 2:** The anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbiha) said: His words, Exalted, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, indicate that God, Exalted, is above them in essence.

Know that we went to great lengths in answering this doubt in the explanation of His words, Exalted: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-Anʿām: 18]. What we add here is this: His words, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, mean: they fear their Lord lest He send down punishment upon them from above them. And if the wording allows this meaning, their claim falls. Furthermore, this "aboveness" must be understood as aboveness by power and dominance, as in His words: ﴿And indeed We are above them, subduing﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 127]. What strengthens this interpretation is that when He, Exalted, said, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, the cause of this fear must be that their Lord is above them, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that a ruling attached to a descriptive attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute.

Having established this, we say: this interpretation would only be valid if the intended aboveness were aboveness by domination and power, because that is what produces fear. As for aboveness in direction and place, it does not produce fear. The evidence is that the guard of a house is "above" the king in place and direction, yet he is the lowliest of his servants. Thus this doubt is refuted.

**Issue 3:** This verse indicates that the angels are obligated by God, Exalted, and that commands and prohibitions apply to them as they apply to all the obligated. And whenever they are like this, it is necessary that they be capable of good and evil.

**Issue 4:** Some people used this verse to show that the angel is superior to the human being, in several respects.

**The first respect:** He, Exalted, said: ﴿And to God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, of creatures that crawl, and the angels﴾. We mentioned that singling out these two kinds for mention is only appropriate if one of the two extremes is the lowest of ranks and the other extreme is the highest of them, so that mention of these two extremes alerts the mind to what lies between them. If that is so, then the angels must be the most noble of God's creation.

**The second respect:** His words, Exalted, ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾ indicate that there is no pride or haughtiness in their hearts. His words, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾ indicate that their deeds are free of sin and disobedience. The combination of these two statements indicates that their inner and outer selves are free of corrupt characteristics and false deeds. As for human beings, they are not like this. This is shown by the Qur'an and the Hadith. From the Qur'an, His words, Exalted: ﴿Cursed is man; how disbelieving he is!﴾ [ʿAbasa: 17]. This ruling is general to man, and at the very least it means that human nature tends toward these blameworthy states. From the Hadith, His words, peace be upon him: "There is none of us but that he has disobeyed or intended disobedience, except Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā." It is known by necessity that one who is free from disobedience and the intention of it is more excellent than one who has disobeyed or intended it.

**The third respect:** There is no doubt that God, Exalted, created the angels before human beings by long eras and extended periods of time. Then He described them as obedient, submissive and humble throughout this long period. And a long life spent in obedience necessarily brings greater excellence, for two reasons.

**The first:** His words, peace be upon him: "The elder among his people is like the prophet among his community." He preferred the elder over the youth. This is only because his life was longer, so his obedience is apparently greater, and so he is more excellent.

**The second:** He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever establishes a good practice (sunna ḥasana), he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." Since the angels began the acts of obedience before human beings began them, it follows that they are the ones who established this good practice, which is the obedience of the Eternal, Merciful Creator, and human beings came after them and followed their practice. So by the requirement of this report, whatever reward human beings obtain, the angels obtain its like, and they also have the reward of the additional degree of obedience. Therefore they must be more excellent than others.

[Page 39]

**The fourth respect:** The indication of the verse for this meaning is His words, ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾. We have shown by proof that this "aboveness" is an expression of superiority in rank, nobility, power and strength. The apparent meaning of the verse therefore indicates that there is nothing above them in nobility and rank except God, Exalted, and this indicates that they are the most excellent of created beings. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 48–50 (part 1 of 2):
