So He made clear that at the removal of harm and the return of safety, they divide: a group of them remains in the same state they were in at the time of harm, in that they seek refuge in none but Allah, exalted is He, while a group of them at that point changes and associates others with Allah. This is ignorance and misguidance, because when their original nature and innate creation bore witness, at the descent of calamity, hardship, afflictions and fears, that there is no refuge except the One, and no one to be appealed to except the One, then when the calamity and hardship are removed, it is necessary that they remain upon that belief. As for one who, when calamity descends, acknowledges that there is no one to be appealed to except Allah, exalted is He, and when the calamity is removed, affirms rivals and partners, this is a great error and complete misguidance. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But when He brings them safely to land, behold, they associate others﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 65].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾. In this lam there are two possibilities:

The first: it is the lam of purpose (kay), and the meaning is that they associated others with Allah in the removal of that harm from them, and their aim in that association is to deny that the blessing came from Allah, exalted is He. Do you not see that when the sick person's pain intensifies, he humbles himself to Allah, exalted is He, to remove that pain, and when it goes away, he attributes its going to such-and-such medicine or such-and-such treatment? This is the case with most of mankind. The author of this book, Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On the day I was writing these pages, which was the first day of Muharram in the year 602, a severe earthquake and a great tremor occurred at the time of dawn, and I saw people crying out in supplication and humility. When it subsided, the air became calm and the time became pleasant, they immediately forgot that earthquake and returned to the same folly and ignorance they had been in. It is as if this state which Allah, exalted is He, described in this verse is like a necessary attribute of the essence of the human soul.

The second opinion: this lam is the lam of consequence, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. That is, the outcome of those supplications was nothing but this disbelief.

Know that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿what We have given them﴾ has two views:

The first: it is an expression for the removal of harm and the lifting of what is disliked.

The second: some have said that it refers to the Qur'an and what Muhammad ﷺ brought of prophethood and laws.

Know that He, exalted is He, then threatened them, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾. This is an imperative form, and what is meant by it is threat, like His saying: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], and His saying: ﴿Say: Believe in it or do not believe﴾ [al-Isra: 107].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But you will soon know﴾, that is, the outcome of your affair and the punishment that will descend upon you. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 56–60 (part 1 of 2):

God says: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. By God, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And they assign to God daughters—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given news of a female child, his face darkens, and he is filled with grief.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil of the news he has been given. Should he keep it despite humiliation, or bury it in the dust? Surely evil is what they judge.﴾ ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the attribute of evil, and for God is the highest attribute. He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Know that when God had demonstrated, by compelling proofs, the corruption of the claims of the people of polytheism and anthropomorphism (tashbih), He then explained in this verse the details of their claims and showed their corruption and feebleness.

The first type of their corrupt statements is that they assign a share to what they do not know. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ refer? There are two views.

The first: It refers to the polytheists mentioned in His words: ﴿then, when a party of you associates others with their Lord﴾. The meaning is that the polytheists do not know.

The second: It refers to the idols, that is, the idols do not know what their worshippers do.

Some said: The first view is preferable, for several reasons.

One: Negating knowledge of a living being is literal (haqiqa), while negating it of an inanimate object is figurative (majaz).

Second: The pronoun in His words ﴿they assign﴾ refers to the polytheists, so likewise in His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ it must refer to them.

Third: His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ are in the plural form with the masculine sound ending (waw and nun), and this is more fitting for rational beings than for idols, which are inanimate.

Others said: Rather, the second view is preferable, for several reasons.

The first: If we say it refers to the polytheists, we need an implied supplement. The implied meaning would be: they assign to what they do not know to be a god, or to what they do not know to be beneficial or harmful. But if we say it refers to the idols, we do not need any supplement, because the implied meaning is: they assign to what has no knowledge or understanding.

The second: If knowledge were attributed to the polytheists, the meaning would be corrupted, because it is absurd that they would assign a share of their provision to what they do not know.

This is what was said in preferring one of these two views over the other.

Know that if we adopt the first view, we need a supplement in it, and that may have several meanings:

One: They assign to what they do not know to have any right (haqq), and they do not know any benefit in obeying it or any harm in turning away from it. Mujahid said: They know that God created them and that He can harm them and benefit them, yet they assign a share to what they do not know can benefit or harm them.

Two: They assign to what they do not know to have divinity.

Three: They assign to what they do not know the cause of its becoming an object of worship.

Four: The purpose is to belittle the idols, as if, because of their insignificance, they do not know anything.

The second issue: On the interpretation of that share, there are several possibilities.

The first: It means that they set aside for God a share of the tilth and livestock, with which they draw near to God, and a share for the idols, with which they draw near to them. We have explained this at the end of Surat al-An'am.

The second: That this share refers to the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: Perhaps they believed that some things came into being only through the help of some of those idols, just as the astrologers distribute the existents of this world among the seven planets. They say that such-and-such minerals, plants, and animals belong to Saturn, and other things belong to Jupiter. So it is here as well.

Know that when God related this doctrine of the polytheists, He said: ﴿By God, you will surely be questioned﴾. For these peoples in particular, this is like His words: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr 15:92]. In either case, God swore by Himself that He will question them, and this is a severe threat from Him, because the meaning is that He will question them with a questioning of rebuke and intimidation.

Regarding the time of this questioning, there are two possibilities.

The first: That this questioning occurs at the approach of death and the witnessing of the angels of punishment. It was also said: at the punishment of the grave.

The second: That it occurs in the Hereafter, and this is preferable, because God has informed us of the kinds of rebuke that take place there during the questioning, so it is closer to the warning.

The second type of their corrupt statements is that they assign daughters to God. Its parallel is His words: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:19]. The Khuza'a and Kinana tribes used to say: the angels are the daughters of God.

I say: I think the Arabs only applied the word "daughters" to the angels because the angels were hidden from sight, and so they resembled women in being concealed, and therefore they applied the word "daughters" to them. Also, the disc of the sun is like something hidden from sight because of its dazzling light and overpowering radiance, so they applied the feminine term to it. This is what is most likely to be the reason for their adopting this corrupt statement and this false doctrine.

When God related this statement of theirs, He said: ﴿glory be to Him﴾, and there are several interpretations of this.

The first: That the purpose is to declare His essence free from being ascribed offspring.

The second: To astonish creation at this shameful ignorance, namely describing the angels as female and then ascribing them to God as offspring.

The third: It was said in tafsir that its meaning is "God forbid," and this is close to the first interpretation.

Then God said: ﴿while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ Al-Farra' permitted two possibilities for "ma" (what):

The first: That it is in the accusative position, meaning: they assign for themselves what they desire.

The second: That it is in the nominative position, as a new beginning, as if the sentence was complete at His words ﴿glory be to Him﴾, and then He began: ﴿for them is what they desire﴾, meaning: sons. This is like His words: ﴿Has He taken daughters for Himself and given you sons?﴾ [al-Tur 52:39]. Then he preferred the second possibility and said: If it were a share, He would have said "and for themselves what they desire," because you say: "You assigned for yourself such-and-such," and you do not say: "You assigned for you."

Al-Zajjaj rejected the first possibility and said: "ma" is only in the nominative position, and the meaning is: for them is the thing they desire. It cannot be accusative, because the Arabs say: "He assigned for himself what he desires," and they do not say: "He assigned for him what he desires," meaning himself.

* * *

Then God mentioned that each one of these polytheists does not accept a daughter for himself. So how can he ascribe to God what he does not accept for himself? Thus He said: ﴿And when one of them is given news of a female child, his face darkens, and he is filled with grief.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: In the customary usage of the language, "tabshir" (giving good news) is specific to news that brings joy. However, according to the original linguistic sense, it is an expression for news that affects the change of complexion of the face. It is known that joy causes a change in the complexion, and likewise grief causes it. Therefore the word "tabshir" must be literal (haqiqa) in both cases. This is reinforced by His words: ﴿So give them news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21]. Some said: The intended meaning of "tabshir" here is simply "informing," but the first view is more precise in verification.

As for His words ﴿his face darkens﴾, the meaning is that it changes in the manner of one who is distressed. It is said of one who has encountered something disagreeable: "His face has blackened from distress and sorrow." I say: The blackening of the face was only made a figure (kinaya) for distress, because when a person's joy is strong, his chest expands and the spirit of his heart spreads from within the heart and reaches the extremities, especially the face, because of the intense connection between them. When the spirit reaches the outer surface of the face, the face shines, glows, and becomes radiant. But when a person's distress is strong, the spirit is confined within the inner heart, and no strong trace of it remains on the outer face. So the face inevitably becomes dull, pale, and black, and the marks of earthliness and density appear in it. Thus it is established that among the necessary consequences of joy is the radiance and brightness of the face, and among the necessary consequences of distress is the dullness, dust-colored tinge, and blackness of the face. For this reason, the whiteness and brightness of the face was made a figure for joy, and its dust-colored tinge, dullness, and blackness a figure for grief, sorrow, and aversion. For this meaning He said: ﴿his face darkens, and he is filled with grief﴾, that is, full of distress and sorrow.

Then God said: ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the evil﴾, that is, he conceals himself and withdraws from the people because of the evil of what he has been given news of. The exegetes said: In the Jahiliyya, when the signs of labor appeared in a man's wife, he would hide himself from the people until he learned what she would bear. If it was a male, he rejoiced in it; if it was a female, he grieved and did not appear to the people for days, during which he deliberated what he should do with her. This is His words: ﴿Should he keep it despite humiliation, or bury it in the dust?﴾ The meaning is: Should he hold it back? Here "keep" (imsak) means "hold," as in His words: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:37]. He said ﴿keep it﴾ with a masculine pronoun because this pronoun refers to "ma" in His words ﴿what he has been given news of﴾. "Hun" means humiliation. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: It is said: "He is more humiliating to him" (ahwanu 'alayhi hunan wa hawanan), and "I humiliated him" (ahantuhu hunan wa hawanan). We discussed this in Surat al-An'am at His words: ﴿the punishment of humiliation﴾. Regarding whom this humiliation is an attribute, there are two views:

The first: It is an attribute of the female child, and its meaning is that he holds her back with humiliation to her.

The second: Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: It is an attribute of the father, and its meaning is that he keeps her while accepting the humiliation of himself and despite his own dislike.

Then He said: ﴿or bury it in the dust﴾. "Dass" means concealing one thing inside another. It is related that the Arabs used to dig a pit and place her in it until she died. It was narrated from Qays ibn 'Asim that he said: "O Messenger of God, I buried eight daughters alive in the Jahiliyya." He (peace be upon him) said: "Free a slave for each one of them." He said: "O Prophet of God, I am a man of camels." He said: "Offer a sacrificial animal for each one of them."

It was narrated that a man said: "O Messenger of God, I have not found the sweetness of Islam since I embraced it. In the Jahiliyya I had a daughter, and I told my wife to adorn her. She brought her out to me, and I took her to a valley with a deep bottom and threw her into it. She said: 'O father, you have killed me!' Whenever I remember her words, nothing benefits me." He (peace be upon him) said: "What was in the Jahiliyya, Islam has erased it, and what is in Islam, seeking forgiveness erases it."

Know that they differed about killing daughters. Some would dig a pit and bury her in it until she died. Others would throw her from the top of a high mountain. Others would drown her, and others would slaughter her. They did this sometimes out of jealousy and zealotry, and sometimes out of fear of poverty and want and the obligation of providing for her.

Then He said: ﴿Surely evil is what they judge﴾, because they reached the utmost extremes in their disdain for daughters:

The first of these is that his face darkens.

The second is that he hides from the people because of his intense aversion to a daughter.

The third is that a child is naturally beloved, yet because of his intense aversion to her, he proceeds to kill her. This indicates that the aversion to daughters and the disdain for them had reached a degree beyond which it cannot increase. Once this is established: how can it be fitting for a sensible person to ascribe to the God of knowledge, the Holy, the Exalted, who is far above resemblance to all created things, something that has been held in such great disdain? A parallel to this verse is His words: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, is an unjust division﴾ [al-Najm 53:21–22].

[Page 44]

Second issue: The judge (al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: This verse proves the falsity of the report, because they attribute to God, exalted is He, injustices and abominations which, if attributed to any one of them, he would exert himself to disown and distance himself from. So their judgment in this matter is similar to the judgment of these polytheists. Then he said: Rather, it is worse, because attributing daughters to Him is attributing one ugliness, whereas attributing all the ugliness and abominations to God, exalted is He, is more severe.

It is said in reply to the judge: When the impossibility of a consort and a child for God, exalted is He, was established by proof, God followed it with mention of this persuasive consideration. Otherwise, not everything that is considered ugly among us by custom is ugly with God, exalted is He. Do you not see a man who adorned his female slaves and male slaves, exaggerated in beautifying their forms, then exaggerated in strengthening desire in them and in them, then gathered them all together and removed the barrier and the obstacle? This is by agreement good from God, exalted is He, and ugly from every creature. So we know that reliance on these considerations, which are based on custom, is what is at issue, and therefore it was good to reinforce them with these persuasive considerations. As for the actions of servants, it has been established by certain, decisive proofs that their Creator is God, exalted is He. How, then, can one of the two categories be attached to the other, were it not for extreme partisanship? And God knows best.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description, and to God belongs the sublime description﴾. The "evil description" is an expression for the bad attribute, namely their need for offspring and their aversion to females out of fear of poverty and shame. ﴿And to God belongs the sublime description﴾, that is, the lofty, sanctified attribute, which is His being exalted above having offspring.

If it is said: How does ﴿And to God belongs the sublime description﴾ come alongside His saying: ﴿So do not strike forth similitudes for God﴾ [al-Nahl: 74]?

We say: The similitude that God mentions is true and sincere, whereas that which others mention is falsehood. And God knows best.

The first of these is that his face darkens.

The second is that he hides from the people because of his intense aversion to a daughter.

The third is that a child is naturally beloved, yet because of his intense aversion to her, he proceeds to kill her. This indicates that the aversion to daughters and the disdain for them had reached a degree beyond which it cannot increase. Once this is established: how can it be fitting for a sensible person to ascribe to the God of knowledge, the Holy, the Exalted, who is far above resemblance to all created things, something that has been held in such great disdain? God says: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. Know that when God had demonstrated, by compelling proofs, the corruption of the claims of the people of polytheism and anthropomorphism (tashbih), He then explained in this verse the details of their claims and showed their corruption and feebleness.

The first type of their corrupt statements is that they assign a share to what they do not know. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ refer? There are two views.

The first: It refers to the polytheists mentioned in His words: ﴿then, when a party of you associates others with their Lord﴾. The meaning is that the polytheists do not know.

The second: It refers to the idols, that is, the idols do not know what their worshippers do.

Some said: The first view is preferable, for several reasons.

One: Negating knowledge of a living being is literal (haqiqa), while negating it of an inanimate object is figurative (majaz).

Second: The pronoun in His words ﴿they assign﴾ refers to the polytheists, so likewise in His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ it must refer to them.

Third: His words ﴿what they do not know﴾ are in the plural form with the masculine sound ending (waw and nun), and this is more fitting for rational beings than for idols, which are inanimate.

Others said: Rather, the second view is preferable, for several reasons.

The first: If we say it refers to the polytheists, we need an implied supplement. The implied meaning would be: they assign to what they do not know to be a god, or to what they do not know to be beneficial or harmful. But if we say it refers to the idols, we do not need any supplement, because the implied meaning is: they assign to what has no knowledge or understanding.

The second: If knowledge were attributed to the polytheists, the meaning would be corrupted, because it is absurd that they would assign a share of their provision to what they do not know.

This is what was said in preferring one of these two views over the other.

Know that if we adopt the first view, we need a supplement in it, and that may have several meanings:

One: They assign to what they do not know to have any right (haqq), and they do not know any benefit in obeying it or any harm in turning away from it. Mujahid said: They know that God created them and that He can harm them and benefit them, yet they assign a share to what they do not know can benefit or harm them.

Two: They assign to what they do not know to have divinity.

Three: They assign to what they do not know the cause of its becoming an object of worship.

Four: The purpose is to belittle the idols, as if, because of their insignificance, they do not know anything.

The second issue: On the interpretation of that share, there are several possibilities.

The second: That this share refers to the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: Perhaps they believed that some things came into being only through the help of some of those idols, just as the astrologers distribute the existents of this world among the seven planets. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 61–64 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. And when their term comes, they will not remain behind it by an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be left neglected.﴾ ﴿By Allah, We had already sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. So he is their ally today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We did not send down upon you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had related the great disbelief of these people and their wretched speech, He explained that He gives these disbelievers respite and does not hasten punishment upon them, as a demonstration of grace, mercy and generosity. There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Those who object to the infallibility (*ʿismah*, the doctrine that prophets are protected from sin) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ in two ways:

The first: He said, ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾, attributing wrongdoing to all of mankind. Without doubt, wrongdoing is among the sins, so this requires that every human being commits sin and disobedience. The prophets, peace be upon them, are among mankind, so it is necessary that they too commit sin and disobedience.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾. This requires that everyone on the surface of the earth is committing wrongdoing and sin, so that the destruction of every wrongdoer would entail the destruction of all mankind.

But if we say that the prophets, peace be upon them, did not commit wrongdoing, then they need not be destroyed, and so the destruction of all the wrongdoers would not entail the destruction of all mankind, nor would no creature remain on the surface of the earth. Since this entailment is invalid, we know that all human beings are wrongdoers, whether they are prophets or not.

The answer: It has been established by evidence that not all people are wrongdoers, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We chose from among Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32]. That is: among the servants there is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost. If the moderate and the foremost were wrongdoers, that division would collapse. So we know that the moderate and the foremost are not wrongdoers. Thus it is established by this evidence that it is not permissible to say that all creation are wrongdoers.

Given this, we say: the people mentioned in His saying ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ are either all the sinners deserving punishment, or those previously mentioned, namely the polytheists and those who attributed daughters to Allah. On this interpretation the argument falls. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** Some people have argued from this verse that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition. They said: If harm were legislated, it would either be legislated in a way that constitutes a recompense for a crime committed by them, or not in this way. Both divisions are invalid, so it must be that harm is not legislated at all.

As for the demonstration of the invalidity of the first division, it is His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾.

The argument from it is in two ways:

The first: The word *law* (لَوْ) is used to indicate the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. So His saying, ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ implies that He did not take them to task for their wrongdoing, and that He left upon its back creatures.

The second: Since the verse indicates that the necessary consequence of Allah taking mankind to task for their wrongdoing is that He would not leave upon its back a single creature, and we observe that He, exalted is He, has left upon its back many creatures, it is certain that He does not take mankind to task for their wrongdoing. Thus it is established by this that harms cannot be legislated in a way that they fall as recompense for crimes.

As for the second division, namely that harm is legislated from the outset and not in a way that falls as recompense for a previous crime, this is invalid by consensus (*ijmaʿ*, the agreement of scholars). Thus it is established that the implication of this verse is the prohibition of harms absolutely. This is further reinforced by other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform﴾ [al-Araf: 56]; His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]; His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]; and His saying, peace be upon him: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm in Islam," and His saying: "Cursed is he who harms a Muslim." Thus it is established from the totality of these verses and reports that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition.

So we say: if an incident occurs that involves harm in every respect, and we find a specific text indicating that it is legislated, we judge by it, giving precedence to the specific over the general. Otherwise we judge that it is prohibited, based on this principle that we have established.

Some have said: This principle indicates that everything a person desires must be legislated for him, because preventing him from it is harm, and harm is not legislated according to this principle. And everything a person dislikes must be prohibited, because its existence is harm, and harm is not legislated. Thus it is established that this principle encompasses all the possible events until the Day of Resurrection.

Then we say: The analogy (*qiyas*, reasoning by extending a ruling from a known case to an unknown one) that is relied upon in establishing rulings is either in accordance with this principle or contrary to it. The first is invalid, because this principle makes it unnecessary. The second is invalid, because the text takes precedence over analogy. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: This verse indicates that wrongdoing and sins are not an act of Allah, the Exalted, but are acts of the servants, because He, exalted is He, attributed the wrongdoing of the servants to them, and not to Himself, saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾. Also, if it were a creation of Allah, the Exalted, then their being taken to task for it would be wrongdoing from Allah, the Exalted. And since Allah, the Exalted, prohibited the servants from wrongdoing in this verse, it is more fitting that He Himself be free from wrongdoing. They said: It also indicates that their deeds have an effect on the necessity of reward and punishment, since His saying, ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ — the *bāʾ* (ب, "for/because of") in it indicates causation, as in His saying: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 13].

Know that the discussion of these issues has been mentioned by us repeatedly, so we will not repeat it. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that people's engaging in wrongdoing necessitates the destruction of all living creatures, and that is not permissible, because the creature has committed no sin. How then is it permissible to destroy it because of the wrongdoing of people?

The answer to this is in two ways:

The first way: We do not concede that His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, encompasses all living creatures. Abu ʿAli al-Jubbaʾi answered this: The meaning is that if Allah took them to task for what they earned of disbelief and disobedience, He would hasten their destruction, and then they would have no offspring. Then it is known that there is no one except that among his forefathers there is someone who deserves punishment. And if they perished, their progeny would be extinguished, so it would follow that no human being would remain in the world. And if they were extinguished, it would necessarily follow that no living creature would remain either, since living creatures were created for the benefit and welfare of the servants. This is a subtle and good answer.

The second way: If the calamity befalls the wrongdoers, it also befalls the rest of mankind and the animals. For the wrongdoers that calamity is a punishment, and for others it is a trial. This event occurred in the time of Noah, peace be upon him.

The third way: If He were to seize them, rain would cease, and with its cessation vegetation would cease, so no creature would remain upon its back. It is reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say: "The wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by Allah! Rather, the bustard (*ḥubārā*) in its nest dies because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." And it is reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The dung beetle nearly perished in its burrow because of the sin of the son of Adam." These three answers are based on the assumption that the word *dābbah* (creature) encompasses all living creatures.

The second answer: The meaning of His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, is: He would not leave upon its back a single disbeliever. So the word *dābbah* refers to the disbeliever. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-Araf: 179]. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fifth issue:** The pronoun in His saying, ﴿upon it [ʿalayhā]﴾ refers to the earth, although it has not been previously mentioned. However, the mention of the creature indicates the earth, since the creature moves only upon it. It is very common to refer to the earth by a pronoun even when it has not been previously mentioned, because they say: "There is no one like so-and-so upon it" and "There is no one more noble than so-and-so upon it," meaning: upon the earth.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But He defers them to a specified term﴾, so that they may reproduce. Regarding the interpretation of this term there are two views:

The first view: This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that it refers to the term of the Resurrection.

The second view: That it means the end of their lifespan.

The reasoning of the first view: most of the punishment reaches them on the Day of Resurrection.

The reasoning of the second view: The polytheists are taken to task with punishment when their lifespans end and they depart from the world.

The third category of the false statements which the disbelievers used to make, and which Allah, the Exalted, related about them, is His saying: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike﴾.

Know that the meaning of His saying ﴿And they attribute [wa-yajʿalūna]﴾ is: the daughters, which they dislike for themselves. And the meaning of His saying ﴿they attribute﴾ is that they describe Allah with this and judge it for Him, like the saying: "I appointed Zayd over the people," meaning: I ruled with this ruling. We have mentioned the meaning of *jaʿl* (appointing/making) at His saying: ﴿Allah did not institute any *baḥīrah* or *sāʾibah*﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 103].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best﴾. Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: The position of *anna* (أنَّ, "that") is in the accusative, because His saying ﴿that for them is the best﴾ is in apposition to *al-kadhib* (the lie), and the sentence is: "And their tongues describe that for them is the best."

Regarding the interpretation of "the best" (*al-ḥusnā*) here there are two views:

The first: What is meant by it is sons, meaning: they said: "For Allah are the daughters, and for us are the sons."

The second: That along with their assertion that daughters belong to Allah, the Exalted, they describe themselves as having gained the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, through this statement, and that they are upon the true religion and the good path.

The third: that they judged for themselves paradise and reward from Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: How can they judge this, when they were deniers of the Resurrection?

We say: Not all of them were deniers of the Resurrection. It has been said that among the Arabs there was a group who affirmed resurrection and the Day of Judgment, and for this reason they used to tie a precious camel at the grave of a dead person and leave it until it died, saying: "Indeed, that dead person, if..."

[Page 50]

...ḥushira fa-innahu yuḥsharu ma'ahu markūbuhu (he is gathered, and his mount is gathered with him). Also, on the assumption that they denied the Resurrection, they may have said: "If Muhammad is truthful in his claim of resurrection and gathering, then we shall obtain Paradise and reward through this true religion that we follow." Some people said: "It is preferable to take *al-ḥusnā* (the best reward) in this sense, as evidence by His saying after it: ﴿Undoubtedly, theirs is the Fire﴾. He thus rejected their claim and affirmed the Fire for them, which indicates that they had judged Paradise for themselves."

Al-Zajjāj said: "*Lā* (no) is a rejection of their statement, meaning: the matter is not as they describe. *Jarama* means: their act, that is, the earning of that statement, has brought them the Fire. On this reading, *anna* (that) is in the accusative position, governed by the action of earning upon it." Qutrub said: "*Anna* is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: it has become necessary that theirs is the Fire." Whatever the i'rab (grammatical analysis), the meaning is that the Fire is rightfully theirs, necessary and established.

As for His saying ﴿and that they are *mufraṭūn*﴾: Nāfi' and Qutayba, on the authority of al-Kisā'ī, read *mufriṭūn* with a kasra on the rā', while the rest read *mufraṭūn* with a fatḥa on the rā'. Regarding Nāfi''s reading, al-Farrā' said: the meaning is that they were *mufriṭīn* ("excessive") against themselves in sins. It was also said: they went to excess in fabricating lies against God. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: it seems to derive from *afraṭa*, meaning he became one having *faraṭ* (precedence), like *ajraba* meaning he became one having *jarab* (scabies). The meaning is that they are those who have precedence toward the Fire, as if they had sent someone to prepare places for them therein.

As for the reading *mufraṭūn* with a fatḥa on the rā', there are two opinions:

The first opinion: the meaning is that they are *mutrakūn* (left behind) in the Fire. Al-Kisā'ī said: it is said, "I did not leave (*afraṭtu*) any one of the people," meaning, I did not leave any behind. Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs say, "I left (*afraṭtu*) people among them," meaning I left them behind and they were forgotten.

The second opinion: *mufraṭūn* means *mu'ajjalūn* (those hastened forward). Al-Wāḥidī, may God have mercy on him, said: this is the preferred view, and its basis is what Abū Zayd and others said: "*faraṭa al-rajulu aṣḥābahu yafrusuhum faraṭan wa furūṭan*," when he went ahead of them to the water to prepare the buckets and ropes; and "*afraṭa al-qawmu al-fārita wa farraṭūhu*" when they sent him ahead. So the meaning of His saying ﴿*mufraṭūn*﴾ on this interpretation is that they have been sent ahead to the Fire, and so they are a *faraṭ* (forerunner) for those who will enter after them.

Then God, exalted is He, explained that this kind of conduct which proceeds from the idolaters of Quraysh has previously proceeded from all the earlier nations regarding the earlier prophets, peace be upon them. He said: ﴿By God, We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾. This serves as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ regarding the grief he suffered because of the ignorance of his people.

The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of the Mujbirah (determinists) in several respects.

First: if the creator of their actions is God, Most High, then there is no benefit in the "making fair."

Second: since that adornment is by the creation of God, Most High, it is not permissible to blame Satan for it.

Third: the adornment is what calls a person to the act, and if the occurrence of the act in him is by the creation of God, Most High, then it is necessary, and so the adornment would not be a calling.

Fourth: on their view, the Creator of that deed is more worthy to be their patron than the one who calls to it.

Fifth: He, Most High, attributed the adornment to Satan, and if the one adorning were God, Most High, then attributing it to Satan would be a lie.

The answer: if the one who beautifies the ugly things in the eyes of the disbelievers is Satan, then if the one who beautifies those whisperings in the eyes of Satan is another satan, an infinite regress (*tasalsul*) follows. And if it is God, Most High, then that is what is sought.

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿So he is their patron today﴾, and in this there are two possibilities:

The first: what is meant is the disbelievers of Mecca, and by His saying ﴿so he is their patron today﴾ is meant: Satan, who takes charge of misguiding them and turning them away from you, just as he did with the disbelievers of the nations before you. On this interpretation, He has turned from reports about the earlier nations to reports about the disbelievers of Mecca.

The second: by "today" He intended the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: he is the patron of those who disbelieved, adorning their deeds for them on the Day of Resurrection. The name "the day" was applied to the Day of Resurrection because of the fame of that day.

[Page 51]

And what is intended by His saying ﴿so he is their patron today﴾ is that they will have no patron or helper on that day. That is because when they witness the punishment, and Satan too has been struck by it just as it has struck them, and they see that he has no way of escape from it just as they have none, they may be rebuked by being told, mockingly: "This is your patron today."

* * *

Then God, Most High, mentioned that alongside this severe threat, He established the proof and removed the excuse, saying: ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: the meaning is: We have not sent down the Qur'an to you except that you may, through the clarifications of this Qur'an, make clear to them the matters over which they differ. Those who differ are the people of the religions and the sects, and what they differ over is religion, such as monotheism and polytheism, determinism and free will, the affirmation and denial of the Return, and likewise rulings, such as their prohibiting things that are permitted, like the *baḥīrah* and the *sā'ibah* and others, and their permitting things that are forbidden, like carrion.

The second issue: the *lām* in His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾ indicates that the acts of God, Most High, are caused by purposes. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out...﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], and His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they may worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

The answer: since it has been established by reason that causation is impossible, it is necessary to turn it to interpretation (*ta'wīl*).

The third issue: the author of *al-Kashshāf* said: His saying ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ is coordinated with the position of His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾, except that they are in the accusative as objects of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), because they are the actions of Him who sent down the Book; and the *lām* entered upon His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾ because it is the act of the addressee, not the act of the one who sent it down. Only that which is an act of that same agent can be in the accusative as an object of purpose.

The fourth issue: al-Kalbī said: the description of the Qur'an as being "guidance and mercy for a people who believe" does not negate that it is so for everyone, just as His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] does not negate that it is guidance for all people, as He mentioned in His saying: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. He specified the believers in the mention only because they accepted it and benefited from it, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], because only this people benefited from his warning. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 61–64 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. And when their term comes, they will not remain behind it by an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be left neglected.﴾ ﴿By Allah, We had already sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. So he is their ally today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We did not send down upon you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had related the great disbelief of these people and their wretched speech, He explained that He gives these disbelievers respite and does not hasten punishment upon them, as a demonstration of grace, mercy and generosity. There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Those who object to the infallibility (*ʿismah*, the doctrine that prophets are protected from sin) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ in two ways:

The first: He said, ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾, attributing wrongdoing to all of mankind. Without doubt, wrongdoing is among the sins, so this requires that every human being commits sin and disobedience. The prophets, peace be upon them, are among mankind, so it is necessary that they too commit sin and disobedience.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾. This requires that everyone on the surface of the earth is committing wrongdoing and sin, so that the destruction of every wrongdoer would entail the destruction of all mankind.

But if we say that the prophets, peace be upon them, did not commit wrongdoing, then they need not be destroyed, and so the destruction of all the wrongdoers would not entail the destruction of all mankind, nor would no creature remain on the surface of the earth. Since this entailment is invalid, we know that all human beings are wrongdoers, whether they are prophets or not.

The answer: It has been established by evidence that not all people are wrongdoers, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We chose from among Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32]. That is: among the servants there is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost. If the moderate and the foremost were wrongdoers, that division would collapse. So we know that the moderate and the foremost are not wrongdoers. Thus it is established by this evidence that it is not permissible to say that all creation are wrongdoers.

Given this, we say: the people mentioned in His saying ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ are either all the sinners deserving punishment, or those previously mentioned, namely the polytheists and those who attributed daughters to Allah. On this interpretation the argument falls. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** Some people have argued from this verse that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition. They said: If harm were legislated, it would either be legislated in a way that constitutes a recompense for a crime committed by them, or not in this way. Both divisions are invalid, so it must be that harm is not legislated at all.

As for the demonstration of the invalidity of the first division, it is His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾.

The argument from it is in two ways:

The first: The word *law* (لَوْ) is used to indicate the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. So His saying, ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ implies that He did not take them to task for their wrongdoing, and that He left upon its back creatures.

The second: Since the verse indicates that the necessary consequence of Allah taking mankind to task for their wrongdoing is that He would not leave upon its back a single creature, and we observe that He, exalted is He, has left upon its back many creatures, it is certain that He does not take mankind to task for their wrongdoing. Thus it is established by this that harms cannot be legislated in a way that they fall as recompense for crimes.

As for the second division, namely that harm is legislated from the outset and not in a way that falls as recompense for a previous crime, this is invalid by consensus (*ijmaʿ*, the agreement of scholars). Thus it is established that the implication of this verse is the prohibition of harms absolutely. This is further reinforced by other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform﴾ [al-Araf: 56]; His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]; His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]; and His saying, peace be upon him: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm in Islam," and His saying: "Cursed is he who harms a Muslim." Thus it is established from the totality of these verses and reports that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition.

So we say: if an incident occurs that involves harm in every respect, and we find a specific text indicating that it is legislated, we judge by it, giving precedence to the specific over the general. Otherwise we judge that it is prohibited, based on this principle that we have established.

Some have said: This principle indicates that everything a person desires must be legislated for him, because preventing him from it is harm, and harm is not legislated according to this principle. And everything a person dislikes must be prohibited, because its existence is harm, and harm is not legislated. Thus it is established that this principle encompasses all the possible events until the Day of Resurrection.

Then we say: The analogy (*qiyas*, reasoning by extending a ruling from a known case to an unknown one) that is relied upon in establishing rulings is either in accordance with this principle or contrary to it. The first is invalid, because this principle makes it unnecessary. The second is invalid, because the text takes precedence over analogy. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: This verse indicates that wrongdoing and sins are not an act of Allah, the Exalted, but are acts of the servants, because He, exalted is He, attributed the wrongdoing of the servants to them, and not to Himself, saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾. Also, if it were a creation of Allah, the Exalted, then their being taken to task for it would be wrongdoing from Allah, the Exalted. And since Allah, the Exalted, prohibited the servants from wrongdoing in this verse, it is more fitting that He Himself be free from wrongdoing. They said: It also indicates that their deeds have an effect on the necessity of reward and punishment, since His saying, ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ — the *bāʾ* (ب, "for/because of") in it indicates causation, as in His saying: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 13].

Know that the discussion of these issues has been mentioned by us repeatedly, so we will not repeat it. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that people's engaging in wrongdoing necessitates the destruction of all living creatures, and that is not permissible, because the creature has committed no sin. How then is it permissible to destroy it because of the wrongdoing of people?

The answer to this is in two ways:

The first way: We do not concede that His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, encompasses all living creatures. Abu ʿAli al-Jubbaʾi answered this: The meaning is that if Allah took them to task for what they earned of disbelief and disobedience, He would hasten their destruction, and then they would have no offspring. Then it is known that there is no one except that among his forefathers there is someone who deserves punishment. And if they perished, their progeny would be extinguished, so it would follow that no human being would remain in the world. And if they were extinguished, it would necessarily follow that no living creature would remain either, since living creatures were created for the benefit and welfare of the servants. This is a subtle and good answer.

The second way: If the calamity befalls the wrongdoers, it also befalls the rest of mankind and the animals. For the wrongdoers that calamity is a punishment, and for others it is a trial. This event occurred in the time of Noah, peace be upon him.

The third way: If He were to seize them, rain would cease, and with its cessation vegetation would cease, so no creature would remain upon its back. It is reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say: "The wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by Allah! Rather, the bustard (*ḥubārā*) in its nest dies because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." And it is reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The dung beetle nearly perished in its burrow because of the sin of the son of Adam." These three answers are based on the assumption that the word *dābbah* (creature) encompasses all living creatures.

The second answer: The meaning of His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, is: He would not leave upon its back a single disbeliever. So the word *dābbah* refers to the disbeliever. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-Araf: 179]. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fifth issue:** The pronoun in His saying, ﴿upon it [ʿalayhā]﴾ refers to the earth, although it has not been previously mentioned. However, the mention of the creature indicates the earth, since the creature moves only upon it. It is very common to refer to the earth by a pronoun even when it has not been previously mentioned, because they say: "There is no one like so-and-so upon it" and "There is no one more noble than so-and-so upon it," meaning: upon the earth.

The answer: since it has been established by reason that causation is impossible, it is necessary to turn it to interpretation (*ta'wīl*).

The third issue: the author of *al-Kashshāf* said: His saying ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ is coordinated with the position of His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾, except that they are in the accusative as objects of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), because they are the actions of Him who sent down the Book; and the *lām* entered upon His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾ because it is the act of the addressee, not the act of the one who sent it down. Only that which is an act of that same agent can be in the accusative as an object of purpose.

The fourth issue: al-Kalbī said: the description of the Qur'an as being "guidance and mercy for a people who believe" does not negate that it is so for everyone, just as His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] does not negate that it is guidance for all people, as He mentioned in His saying: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. He specified the believers in the mention only because they accepted it and benefited from it, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], because only this people benefited from his warning. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 61–64 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. And when their term comes, they will not remain behind it by an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be left neglected.﴾ ﴿By Allah, We had already sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. So he is their ally today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We did not send down upon you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had related the great disbelief of these people and their wretched speech, He explained that He gives these disbelievers respite and does not hasten punishment upon them, as a demonstration of grace, mercy and generosity. There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** Those who object to the infallibility (*ʿismah*, the doctrine that prophets are protected from sin) of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾ in two ways:

The first: He said, ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾, attributing wrongdoing to all of mankind. Without doubt, wrongdoing is among the sins, so this requires that every human being commits sin and disobedience. The prophets, peace be upon them, are among mankind, so it is necessary that they too commit sin and disobedience.

The second: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾. This requires that everyone on the surface of the earth is committing wrongdoing and sin, so that the destruction of every wrongdoer would entail the destruction of all mankind.

But if we say that the prophets, peace be upon them, did not commit wrongdoing, then they need not be destroyed, and so the destruction of all the wrongdoers would not entail the destruction of all mankind, nor would no creature remain on the surface of the earth. Since this entailment is invalid, we know that all human beings are wrongdoers, whether they are prophets or not.

The answer: It has been established by evidence that not all people are wrongdoers, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those whom We chose from among Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32]. That is: among the servants there is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost. If the moderate and the foremost were wrongdoers, that division would collapse. So we know that the moderate and the foremost are not wrongdoers. Thus it is established by this evidence that it is not permissible to say that all creation are wrongdoers.

Given this, we say: the people mentioned in His saying ﴿if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾ are either all the sinners deserving punishment, or those previously mentioned, namely the polytheists and those who attributed daughters to Allah. On this interpretation the argument falls. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The second issue:** Some people have argued from this verse that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition. They said: If harm were legislated, it would either be legislated in a way that constitutes a recompense for a crime committed by them, or not in this way. Both divisions are invalid, so it must be that harm is not legislated at all.

As for the demonstration of the invalidity of the first division, it is His saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it a single creature﴾.

The argument from it is in two ways:

The first: The word *law* (لَوْ) is used to indicate the negation of one thing because of the negation of another. So His saying, ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ implies that He did not take them to task for their wrongdoing, and that He left upon its back creatures.

The second: Since the verse indicates that the necessary consequence of Allah taking mankind to task for their wrongdoing is that He would not leave upon its back a single creature, and we observe that He, exalted is He, has left upon its back many creatures, it is certain that He does not take mankind to task for their wrongdoing. Thus it is established by this that harms cannot be legislated in a way that they fall as recompense for crimes.

As for the second division, namely that harm is legislated from the outset and not in a way that falls as recompense for a previous crime, this is invalid by consensus (*ijmaʿ*, the agreement of scholars). Thus it is established that the implication of this verse is the prohibition of harms absolutely. This is further reinforced by other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform﴾ [al-Araf: 56]; His saying: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]; His saying: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]; and His saying, peace be upon him: "There shall be no harm nor reciprocating harm in Islam," and His saying: "Cursed is he who harms a Muslim." Thus it is established from the totality of these verses and reports that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition.

So we say: if an incident occurs that involves harm in every respect, and we find a specific text indicating that it is legislated, we judge by it, giving precedence to the specific over the general. Otherwise we judge that it is prohibited, based on this principle that we have established.

Some have said: This principle indicates that everything a person desires must be legislated for him, because preventing him from it is harm, and harm is not legislated according to this principle. And everything a person dislikes must be prohibited, because its existence is harm, and harm is not legislated. Thus it is established that this principle encompasses all the possible events until the Day of Resurrection.

Then we say: The analogy (*qiyas*, reasoning by extending a ruling from a known case to an unknown one) that is relied upon in establishing rulings is either in accordance with this principle or contrary to it. The first is invalid, because this principle makes it unnecessary. The second is invalid, because the text takes precedence over analogy. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: This verse indicates that wrongdoing and sins are not an act of Allah, the Exalted, but are acts of the servants, because He, exalted is He, attributed the wrongdoing of the servants to them, and not to Himself, saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing﴾. Also, if it were a creation of Allah, the Exalted, then their being taken to task for it would be wrongdoing from Allah, the Exalted. And since Allah, the Exalted, prohibited the servants from wrongdoing in this verse, it is more fitting that He Himself be free from wrongdoing. They said: It also indicates that their deeds have an effect on the necessity of reward and punishment, since His saying, ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾ — the *bāʾ* (ب, "for/because of") in it indicates causation, as in His saying: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 13].

Know that the discussion of these issues has been mentioned by us repeatedly, so we will not repeat it. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fourth issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that people's engaging in wrongdoing necessitates the destruction of all living creatures, and that is not permissible, because the creature has committed no sin. How then is it permissible to destroy it because of the wrongdoing of people?

The answer to this is in two ways:

The first way: We do not concede that His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, encompasses all living creatures. Abu ʿAli al-Jubbaʾi answered this: The meaning is that if Allah took them to task for what they earned of disbelief and disobedience, He would hasten their destruction, and then they would have no offspring. Then it is known that there is no one except that among his forefathers there is someone who deserves punishment. And if they perished, their progeny would be extinguished, so it would follow that no human being would remain in the world. And if they were extinguished, it would necessarily follow that no living creature would remain either, since living creatures were created for the benefit and welfare of the servants. This is a subtle and good answer.

The second way: If the calamity befalls the wrongdoers, it also befalls the rest of mankind and the animals. For the wrongdoers that calamity is a punishment, and for others it is a trial. This event occurred in the time of Noah, peace be upon him.

The third way: If He were to seize them, rain would cease, and with its cessation vegetation would cease, so no creature would remain upon its back. It is reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say: "The wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by Allah! Rather, the bustard (*ḥubārā*) in its nest dies because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer." And it is reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The dung beetle nearly perished in its burrow because of the sin of the son of Adam." These three answers are based on the assumption that the word *dābbah* (creature) encompasses all living creatures.

The second answer: The meaning of His saying, ﴿He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾, is: He would not leave upon its back a single disbeliever. So the word *dābbah* refers to the disbeliever. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-Araf: 179]. And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The fifth issue:** The pronoun in His saying, ﴿upon it [ʿalayhā]﴾ refers to the earth, although it has not been previously mentioned. However, the mention of the creature indicates the earth, since the creature moves only upon it. It is very common to refer to the earth by a pronoun even when it has not been previously mentioned, because they say: "There is no one like so-and-so upon it" and "There is no one more noble than so-and-so upon it," meaning: upon the earth.

\* \* \*

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But He defers them to a specified term﴾, so that they may reproduce. Regarding the interpretation of this term there are two views:

The first view: This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that it refers to the term of the Resurrection.

The second view: That it means the end of their lifespan.

The reasoning of the first view: most of the punishment reaches them on the Day of Resurrection.

The reasoning of the second view: The polytheists are taken to task with punishment when their lifespans end and they depart from the world.

The third category of the false statements which the disbelievers used to make, and which Allah, the Exalted, related about them, is His saying: ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike﴾.

Know that the meaning of His saying ﴿And they attribute [wa-yajʿalūna]﴾ is: the daughters, which they dislike for themselves. And the meaning of His saying ﴿they attribute﴾ is that they describe Allah with this and judge it for Him, like the saying: "I appointed Zayd over the people," meaning: I ruled with this ruling. We have mentioned the meaning of *jaʿl* (appointing/making) at His saying: ﴿Allah did not institute any *baḥīrah* or *sāʾibah*﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 103].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best﴾. Al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: The position of *anna* (أنَّ, "that") is in the accusative, because His saying ﴿that for them is the best﴾ is in apposition to *al-kadhib* (the lie), and the sentence is: "And their tongues describe that for them is the best."

Regarding the interpretation of "the best" (*al-ḥusnā*) here there are two views:

The first: What is meant by it is sons, meaning: they said: "For Allah are the daughters, and for us are the sons."

The second: That along with their assertion that daughters belong to Allah, the Exalted, they describe themselves as having gained the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, through this statement, and that they are upon the true religion and the good path.

The third: that they judged for themselves paradise and reward from Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: How can they judge this, when they were deniers of the Resurrection?

We say: Not all of them were deniers of the Resurrection. It has been said that among the Arabs there was a group who affirmed resurrection and the Day of Judgment, and for this reason they used to tie a precious camel at the grave of a dead person and leave it until it died, saying: "Indeed, that dead person, if..."

[Page 50]

...ḥushira fa-innahu yuḥsharu ma'ahu markūbuhu (he is gathered, and his mount is gathered with him). Also, on the assumption that they denied the Resurrection, they may have said: "If Muhammad is truthful in his claim of resurrection and gathering, then we shall obtain Paradise and reward through this true religion that we follow." Some people said: "It is preferable to take *al-ḥusnā* (the best reward) in this sense, as evidence by His saying after it: ﴿Undoubtedly, theirs is the Fire﴾. He thus rejected their claim and affirmed the Fire for them, which indicates that they had judged Paradise for themselves."

Al-Zajjāj said: "*Lā* (no) is a rejection of their statement, meaning: the matter is not as they describe. *Jarama* means: their act, that is, the earning of that statement, has brought them the Fire. On this reading, *anna* (that) is in the accusative position, governed by the action of earning upon it." Qutrub said: "*Anna* is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: it has become necessary that theirs is the Fire." Whatever the i'rab (grammatical analysis), the meaning is that the Fire is rightfully theirs, necessary and established.

As for His saying ﴿and that they are *mufraṭūn*﴾: Nāfi' and Qutayba, on the authority of al-Kisā'ī, read *mufriṭūn* with a kasra on the rā', while the rest read *mufraṭūn* with a fatḥa on the rā'. Regarding Nāfi''s reading, al-Farrā' said: the meaning is that they were *mufriṭīn* ("excessive") against themselves in sins. It was also said: they went to excess in fabricating lies against God. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: it seems to derive from *afraṭa*, meaning he became one having *faraṭ* (precedence), like *ajraba* meaning he became one having *jarab* (scabies). The meaning is that they are those who have precedence toward the Fire, as if they had sent someone to prepare places for them therein.

As for the reading *mufraṭūn* with a fatḥa on the rā', there are two opinions:

The first opinion: the meaning is that they are *mutrakūn* (left behind) in the Fire. Al-Kisā'ī said: it is said, "I did not leave (*afraṭtu*) any one of the people," meaning, I did not leave any behind. Al-Farrā' said: the Arabs say, "I left (*afraṭtu*) people among them," meaning I left them behind and they were forgotten.

The second opinion: *mufraṭūn* means *mu'ajjalūn* (those hastened forward). Al-Wāḥidī, may God have mercy on him, said: this is the preferred view, and its basis is what Abū Zayd and others said: "*faraṭa al-rajulu aṣḥābahu yafrusuhum faraṭan wa furūṭan*," when he went ahead of them to the water to prepare the buckets and ropes; and "*afraṭa al-qawmu al-fārita wa farraṭūhu*" when they sent him ahead. So the meaning of His saying ﴿*mufraṭūn*﴾ on this interpretation is that they have been sent ahead to the Fire, and so they are a *faraṭ* (forerunner) for those who will enter after them.

Then God, exalted is He, explained that this kind of conduct which proceeds from the idolaters of Quraysh has previously proceeded from all the earlier nations regarding the earlier prophets, peace be upon them. He said: ﴿By God, We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾. This serves as consolation to the Messenger ﷺ regarding the grief he suffered because of the ignorance of his people.

The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates the falsity of the view of the Mujbirah (determinists) in several respects.

First: if the creator of their actions is God, Most High, then there is no benefit in the "making fair."

Second: since that adornment is by the creation of God, Most High, it is not permissible to blame Satan for it.

Third: the adornment is what calls a person to the act, and if the occurrence of the act in him is by the creation of God, Most High, then it is necessary, and so the adornment would not be a calling.

Fourth: on their view, the Creator of that deed is more worthy to be their patron than the one who calls to it.

Fifth: He, Most High, attributed the adornment to Satan, and if the one adorning were God, Most High, then attributing it to Satan would be a lie.

The answer: if the one who beautifies the ugly things in the eyes of the disbelievers is Satan, then if the one who beautifies those whisperings in the eyes of Satan is another satan, an infinite regress (*tasalsul*) follows. And if it is God, Most High, then that is what is sought.

Then God, Most High, said: ﴿So he is their patron today﴾, and in this there are two possibilities:

The first: what is meant is the disbelievers of Mecca, and by His saying ﴿so he is their patron today﴾ is meant: Satan, who takes charge of misguiding them and turning them away from you, just as he did with the disbelievers of the nations before you. On this interpretation, He has turned from reports about the earlier nations to reports about the disbelievers of Mecca.

The second: by "today" He intended the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: he is the patron of those who disbelieved, adorning their deeds for them on the Day of Resurrection. The name "the day" was applied to the Day of Resurrection because of the fame of that day.

[Page 51]

And what is intended by His saying ﴿so he is their patron today﴾ is that they will have no patron or helper on that day. That is because when they witness the punishment, and Satan too has been struck by it just as it has struck them, and they see that he has no way of escape from it just as they have none, they may be rebuked by being told, mockingly: "This is your patron today."

* * *

Then God, Most High, mentioned that alongside this severe threat, He established the proof and removed the excuse, saying: ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: the meaning is: We have not sent down the Qur'an to you except that you may, through the clarifications of this Qur'an, make clear to them the matters over which they differ. Those who differ are the people of the religions and the sects, and what they differ over is religion, such as monotheism and polytheism, determinism and free will, the affirmation and denial of the Return, and likewise rulings, such as their prohibiting things that are permitted, like the *baḥīrah* and the *sā'ibah* and others, and their permitting things that are forbidden, like carrion.

The second issue: the *lām* in His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾ indicates that the acts of God, Most High, are caused by purposes. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out...﴾ [Ibrahim: 1], and His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they may worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

The answer: since it has been established by reason that causation is impossible, it is necessary to turn it to interpretation (*ta'wīl*).

The third issue: the author of *al-Kashshāf* said: His saying ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ is coordinated with the position of His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾, except that they are in the accusative as objects of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*), because they are the actions of Him who sent down the Book; and the *lām* entered upon His saying ﴿that you may make clear﴾ because it is the act of the addressee, not the act of the one who sent it down. Only that which is an act of that same agent can be in the accusative as an object of purpose.

The fourth issue: al-Kalbī said: the description of the Qur'an as being "guidance and mercy for a people who believe" does not negate that it is so for everyone, just as His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] does not negate that it is guidance for all people, as He mentioned in His saying: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. He specified the believers in the mention only because they accepted it and benefited from it, as in His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45], because only this people benefited from his warning. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 61–64 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature. But He defers them to a specified term. And when their term comes, they will not remain behind it by an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe the lie that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be left neglected.﴾ ﴿By Allah, We had already sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. So he is their ally today, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We did not send down upon you the Book except that you may make clear to them that over which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had related the great disbelief of these people and their wretched speech, He explained that He gives these disbelievers respite and does not hasten punishment upon them, as a demonstration of grace, mercy and generosity. There are several issues in this verse.
