As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None holds them up except Allah﴾, the meaning is: the body of the bird is a heavy body, and a heavy body cannot remain suspended in the air without a support beneath it or a tie above it; therefore the one who holds it up in that atmosphere must be Allah, exalted is He. Moreover, it is evident that its remaining suspended in the air is an action of His and occurs by His choice; so it is established that the creator of the action of the servant is Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: Allah, exalted is He, attributed this holding up to Himself only because He is the one who gave the instruments by which He enables the bird to perform those actions; and since He is the one who causes that, this attribution to Allah, exalted is He, is rightly valid.

The answer: This is abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence, and it is not permissible, especially since the rational proofs have shown that the actions of servants are created by Allah, exalted is He.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, and He specified these signs for the believers because they are the ones who benefit from them, although these signs are for all intelligent people, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a place of rest; and He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents that you find light [to carry] on the day of your travel and the day of your settling; and from their wool, their fur, and their hair [He has made] household goods and provision for a time.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the evidences of tawhid (Oneness of God), and of the categories of blessings and bounty, and of sakan (rest, dwelling) and maskan (dwelling-place). Al-Farra' recited:

"Winter has come and I have not yet prepared a sakan;
Woe to my palm, from the holes of the qaramis (tents of leather)."

And sakan is that in which you find rest and that in which you dwell. The author of al-Kashshaf said: sakan is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, and it is that to which one finds rest and to which one turns for refuge, from a house or a companion.

Know that the houses in which a person dwells are of two types:

The first type: houses built from wood, clay, and the tools by which houses can be roofed, and to this the saying of Him refers: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a place of rest﴾. This type of house cannot be moved; rather, a person moves to it.

The second type: domes, tents, and small tents (fasatit), and to these the saying of Him refers: ﴿and He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents that you find light [to carry] on the day of your travel and the day of your settling﴾. This type of house can be moved and transferred from place to place.

Know that what is meant is the anta' (leather mats/hides), and the Arabs did make houses from adam (tanned leather), which are the hides of livestock; that is, carrying them is light for you on your journeys. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr recited "yawma za'nikum" (ظَعَنِكُمْ) with a fatha on the ‘ayn, while the rest read it with a sukun on the ‘ayn. Al-Wahidi said: both are dialects, like sha'r and sha'ar, and nahr and nahar.

Know that al-zaʿn (ظعن) is the movement of the desert dwellers for pasture, or to reach water, or to seek grazing land; and it may be said of anyone setting out on a journey: ẓāʿin, and it is the opposite of khafid (one who stays). His saying: ﴿and the day of your settling﴾ means: it is not burdensome for you in either of the two states. His saying: ﴿and from their wool, their fur, and their hair﴾: the commentators and lexicographers said: ṣuwwāf (wool) is for sheep, awbār (fur) is for camels, and ash'ār (hair) is for goats. His saying: ﴿athāthan﴾: al-athath is the kinds of household goods, of furnishings and coverings. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular, just as matā' (goods) has no singular. He said: if you pluralize, saying āthithah for the few and uthuth for the many, it would not be far off. Abu Zayd said: its singular is athathah. Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿athāthan﴾, meant: cushions, rugs, garments, and clothing. Al-Khalil said: its root is from their saying: atha al-nabat and al-sha'r, when it became abundant. His saying: ﴿wa-matā'an﴾ means: that by which they enjoy themselves. His saying: ﴿ilā ḥīn﴾ means: until a time of trial; it was said: until the time of death; it was said: "ilā ḥīn" after a time; and it was said: until the Day of Resurrection.

Page 75

If it is said: He joined matā' (goods) to athāth (furnishings) by conjunction, and conjunction requires difference; what is the distinction between athāth and matā'?
We say: The closer view is that athāth is what a person clothes himself with and uses for covering and bedding, while matā' is what is spread out in homes and used for adornment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 81–83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you shades from what He has created, and has made for you refuges in the mountains, and has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence. Thus does He complete His favour upon you, that you may submit.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance.﴾ ﴿They recognise the favour of Allah, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾

Know that a person is either settled (muqim) or a traveller (musafir), and the traveller is either wealthy, able to take along tents and pavilions, or he is not able to do so. These are three categories.

As for the first category, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling place.﴾

As for the second category, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿And He has made for you, from the skins of livestock, houses.﴾

As for the third category, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you shades from what He has created.﴾ This is because the traveller who has no tent to shelter under must necessarily shelter under something else, such as walls and trees, and he may shelter under the clouds, as He said: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57].

Then He said: ﴿And He has made for you refuges in the mountains.﴾ The singular of al-Kinan is kinn, on the pattern of ahmal and himl (burdens and load), but what is meant is anything that shields something. It is said: istakanna and akanna, when one enters a kinn (shelter).

Know that the land of the Arabs is intensely hot, and their need for shade and for warding off the heat is great. For this reason, God Most High mentioned these meanings in the context of a great blessing. Also, temperate lands and temperate times are extremely rare, and what prevails is either the dominance of heat or the dominance of cold.

In every case, a person must have a dwelling to which he returns, so the bestowal of obtaining it is great. When God Most High mentioned the matter of dwelling, He mentioned after it the matter of clothing, saying: ﴿And He has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence.﴾ Al-sarabil: the shirts, singular sirbal. Al-Zajjaj said: whatever you wear is a sirbal, whether a shirt, a coat of mail, a cuirass, or other. What indicates the soundness of this view is that He divided the sarabil into two kinds:

One of them: what protects from heat and cold.

The second: what is used to guard against violence and wars, and that is the cuirass and other such things. This indicates that each of the two kinds is of the sarabil.

If it is said: why did He mention the heat and not the cold?

Page 76

They answered this from several aspects:

The first aspect: ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani said: those addressed by this speech are the Arabs, and their lands are hot, so their need for what wards off heat was greater than their need for what wards off cold, as He said: ﴿And from their wool, their fur and their hair﴾, and all other kinds of garments are more noble; but God Most High mentioned that first kind because their familiarity with it was greater and their habit of wearing it was more frequent. For this reason He said: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail﴾ [al-Nur: 43], because of their knowledge of that; and what He sends down of snow is greater, but they did not know it.

The second aspect in the answer: al-Mubarrad said: mentioning one of two opposites is an indication of the other.

I say: it is established in the rational sciences that knowledge of one of two opposites entails knowledge of the other opposite, for whenever heat comes to a person's mind, cold also comes to his mind; and likewise regarding light and darkness, black and white. Since awareness of one of them entails awareness of the other, mentioning one of them suffices in place of mentioning the other.

The third aspect: al-Zajjaj said: what protects from heat also protects from cold, so mentioning one of them suffices in place of mentioning the other.

If it is said: the opposite is more appropriate, because warding off heat is achieved by the sarabil which are shirts, without extra burden, whereas cold is not averted except with additional effort.

We say: since a single shirt serves to ward off heat, multiplying shirts benefits against cold, so what we have mentioned is sound. His saying: ﴿and garments that protect you from your violence﴾ means coats of iron mail; the meaning of ba's is severity, and here it means the severity of thrusting, striking and shooting.

Know that when God Most High enumerated the kinds of the blessings of this world, He said: ﴿Thus does He complete His favour upon you﴾, meaning: like His creating these things for you and bestowing them upon you, He completes for you the blessing of this world and the religion. ﴿That you may submit﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: that you, people of Makkah, may single out Allah for lordship and know that none other than Him can bestow these favours. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he read: "la-ʿallakum taslamun" with a fatha on the ta', and the meaning is: We gave you these garments so that you might be safe from the violence of war. It was also said: We gave you these blessings so that you would reflect upon them and believe, and thus be safe from the punishment of God.

Then God Most High said: ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance.﴾ That is: if they turn away, O Muhammad, and show aversion and prefer the pleasures of this world, the following of their fathers and hostility in disbelief, then they have brought that upon themselves; and upon you is nothing but the complete conveying of what you have done. Then He censured them by saying that they recognise the favour of Allah and then deny it, and this is the extreme of ingratitude for blessings.

If it is said: what is the meaning of "then" (thumma)?

We say: it indicates that their denial is something to be deemed strange after the attainment of knowledge, because the right of one who recognises a blessing is to acknowledge it, not to deny it. As for what is meant by this blessing, there are several views:

The first: al-Qadi said: what is meant by it is all that God Most High mentioned in the preceding verses of all kinds of blessings; and their denying it means that they did not single out God Most High with gratitude and worship, but rather thanked other than God for those blessings. And because they said: these blessings came about through the intercession of these idols.

The second: what is meant is that they knew that the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is true, then they denied it; and his prophethood is a great blessing, as God Most High said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

Page 77

The third: "they recognise the favour of Allah, then they deny it," that is, they do not employ it in seeking the pleasure of God Most High.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And most of them are disbelievers.﴾

If it is said: what is the meaning of His saying "and most of them are disbelievers," given that all of them were disbelievers?

We say: the answer has several aspects:

The first: He said "most of them" only because among them were those upon whom the proof had not been established, from among those who had not reached the age of responsibility, or who had deficient intellect and were feeble-minded; so by "most" He meant the adult sound ones.

The second: that by "disbeliever" is meant the obstinate denier, and in that case we say: He said "most of them" because among them were some who were not obstinate, but rather ignorant of the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and for whom it had not become clear that he was truly a prophet from Allah.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 84–85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness; then those who disbelieved will not be given leave [to speak], nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾ ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the state of these people, that they recognized the blessing of Allah and then denied it, and had also mentioned concerning them that most of them are disbelievers, He followed this with a warning, and mentioned the state of the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿And [remember] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾. This indicates that those witnesses will testify against them concerning that denial and that disbelief. By "these witnesses" are meant the prophets, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿How then will it be when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you as a witness against these?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41]. As for His saying: ﴿then those who disbelieved will not be given leave﴾, there are several aspects to it:

First: they will not be given leave to make excuses; this is based on His saying: ﴿nor will they be given leave, so they will not make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36].

Second: they will not be given leave to speak at length.

Third: they will not be given leave to return to the abode of this world and to moral obligation (al-taklif).

Fourth: they will not be given leave during the testimony of the witnesses; rather, all the people of the gathering will be silent so that the witnesses may testify.

Fifth: they will not be given leave to speak at length, so that it may become evident to them that they are despairing of the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

Then He said: ﴿nor will they be asked to make amends﴾. Al-isti'tab (asking to make amends) means seeking al-'itab (reproach that leads to reconciliation). A person seeks al-'itab from his opponent when he is certain that if he rebukes him, he will return to contentment. When he does not seek al-'itab from him, this indicates that he is firmly fixed in his anger and wrath.

Then, exalted is He, emphasized this warning, saying: ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them﴾. The meaning is that when the polytheists see the punishment and reach it, at that point the punishment will not be lightened for them. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning: they will not be delayed nor given respite, because repentance is not available there. Its verification is what the theologians (al-mutakallimun) say: that punishment must be pure, free of any admixture of benefit, and this is what is meant by His saying, "it will not be lightened for them." And the punishment must be perpetual, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 84–85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness; then those who disbelieved will not be given leave [to speak], nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾ ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 86–87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When those who associated partners with God see their partners, they will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You." But they will throw back at them the word: "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ ﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day, and what they used to invent will be lost to them.﴾

Know that this is also part of the threat against the polytheists. Regarding the "partners" there are two opinions.

The first opinion: God resurrects the idols that the polytheists used to worship. The purpose of their being brought back is that the polytheists witness them in the utmost humiliation and lowliness, and also that the idols will deny the polytheists. All of this necessarily increases grief and regret in their hearts. God described them as "partners" for two reasons:

First: the disbelievers used to call them "partners of God."

Second: the disbelievers assigned to them a share of their wealth.

The second opinion: the "partners" are the devils who called the disbelievers to disbelief. This is the view of al-Hasan. He adopted this view because God related about those partners that they said to those who associated partners with Him that they were liars. Idols are inanimate, so it is not valid that they make this statement. Therefore the "partners" must be the devils, so that this statement is valid from them. This is far-fetched, because God is capable of creating life in those idols and creating reason and speech within them, and then it would be valid for them to make this statement. Then God related about the polytheists that when they see those partners they say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You."

If it is said: What is the benefit to them in this statement?

We say: There are two answers to this.

First: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The polytheists' aim is to shift the blame onto these idols, thinking that this would save them from God's punishment or lessen their punishment. Thereupon those idols will deny them. Al-Qadi said: This is far-fetched, because the disbelievers will know with certain knowledge in the Hereafter that the punishment will descend upon them, and that there will be no help, no ransom, and no intercession.

The second opinion: the polytheists say this statement out of amazement at the presence of those idols although they have no fault, and acknowledging that they were mistaken in worshipping them. Then God related that the idols deny them, saying: ﴿But they will throw back at them the word: "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ The meaning: God creates life, reason and speech in those idols so that they say this statement. His saying ﴿Indeed, you are liars﴾ is a substitute for "the word," and the implied meaning is: "they throw back at them: indeed, you are liars."

If it is said: The polytheists did not say anything except that when they pointed to the idols they said: "These are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You," and they were truthful in all of that, so how did the idols say "Indeed, you are liars"?

We say: There are several answers to this. The most correct is to say: the meaning of their saying "These are our partners" is that these are the ones we used to claim were partners of God in divinity, so the idols denied them regarding the establishment of this partnership. It was also said: the meaning is "Indeed, you are liars in your saying that we deserve worship," and this is indicated by God's saying: ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them﴾ [Maryam: 82].

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾. Al-Kalbi said: the worshipper and the worshipped submit, and they acknowledge to God lordship and disavowal of partners and equals. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾. Regarding this there are two views. It was said: what Satan had adorned for them, namely that God has a partner, a consort and a son, has departed from them. It was also said: what they used to hope for, that their gods would intercede for them with God, has come to nothing.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 88:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment, because of what they used to corrupt.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the threat against those who disbelieve, He followed it with the threat against whoever adds to his own disbelief the barring of others from the way of Allah. Regarding His words ﴿and bar others from the way of Allah﴾ there are two views. It was said: its meaning is barring from the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). The more sound view is that it includes the whole of faith in Allah and His Messenger and the legislated laws, because the wording is general and there is no sense in restricting it. As for His words ﴿We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, the meaning is that they added to their own disbelief the barring of others from faith, so in reality they increased in disbelief upon disbelief, and therefore Allah, exalted is He, increases them in punishment upon punishment. Also, their followers only imitated them in disbelief, so it is necessary that they receive a punishment like the punishment of their followers, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-Ankabut: 13]. And according to His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever establishes an evil custom, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection."

Among the exegetes is one who mentioned the details of that increase. Ibn Abbas said: the intended meaning of that increase is five rivers of fire flowing from beneath the Throne, with which they are tormented: three by night and two by day. Some said: We increase them in punishment with serpents and scorpions like the Bactrian camels, so they seek refuge by fleeing from them into the Fire. Some of them mentioned: for each scorpion there are three hundred stings, in three hundred vessels of poison. It was also said: scorpions having fangs like tall palm trees.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿because of what they used to corrupt﴾, meaning: this increase in punishment occurred only as a consequence of that barring. This indicates that whoever calls another to disbelief and error, his punishment is magnified; likewise, whoever calls to the religion and certainty, his rank is magnified with Allah, exalted is He. And Allah knows best.

[Page 80]

**His saying, Exalted is He:** ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every community a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these. And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, and as guidance, mercy, and good tidings for the Muslims.﴾

Know that this is another type of warning that restrains the responsible from acts of disobedience. Know also that the *ummah* (community) refers to a generation and a group.

Having established this, we say: there are two opinions regarding the verse.

The first: the meaning is that every prophet is a witness over his own community.

The second: every gathering and generation that occurs in this world must have among them one who is a witness over them.

As for the witness over those who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), it is the Messenger himself, based on the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

It has also been established that after the time of the Messenger, there must be a witness in every age. From this it follows that no era of the eras is free of a witness over the people, and that witness must be incapable of error; otherwise he would require another witness, and this would continue without end, which is impossible. Thus it is established that in every age there must be groups whose statements constitute proof, and this necessitates that the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus) of the community is a proof.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the meaning of that witness is that God Exalted makes ten of a person's limbs speak, and they testify against him. They are the two ears, the two eyes, the two feet, the two hands, the skin, and the tongue. He said: the evidence for this is that He said in describing the witness that he is "from among themselves," and these limbs are undoubtedly from among themselves.

Al-Qadi answered him in several ways:

First: He, Exalted, said: ﴿a witness over them﴾, meaning over the community, so the witness must be other than them.

Second: He said: ﴿from every community﴾, so that witness must be from the community, and individual limbs cannot be described as being from the community. As for interpreting these witnesses as the prophets, it is far-fetched, because their being prophets sent to creation is a matter known by necessity, so there is no benefit in applying this verse to it.

* * *

Then God, Exalted, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾, and concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: the connection of this statement to what precedes it is that when He said: ﴿and We bring you as a witness against these﴾, He made clear that He had removed their excuse regarding what they were obligated to do, so they have no argument and no pretext.

The second issue: some people said: the Qur'an is an explanation of all things. This is because the sciences are either religious or non-religious. As for the non-religious sciences, they have no connection to this verse, because it is known by necessity that God, Exalted, only praised the Qur'an for containing the sciences of religion, and what is not among the sciences of religion is not to be given attention. As for the sciences of religion, they are either principles (*usul*) or branches (*furu'*). As for the science of principles, it is entirely present in the Qur'an. As for the science of branches, the default is the innocence of the obligation (*bara'at al-dhimmah*), except for what is mentioned in detail in this Book. This indicates that God, Exalted, imposes no obligation except what is mentioned in this Qur'an. Given this, analogical reasoning (*qiyas*) is invalid, and the Qur'an is sufficient in explaining all rulings.

As for the jurists, they said: the Qur'an is only an explanation of all things because it indicates that scholarly consensus (*ijma'*), a report transmitted by a single narrator (*khabar al-wahid*), and analogical reasoning (*qiyas*) are proofs. So when a ruling is established by one of these principles, that ruling is established by the Qur'an. This issue has already been discussed thoroughly in the commentary on Surah al-A'raf, and God knows best.

The third issue: al-Wahidi narrated with his chain of transmission from al-Zajjaj that he said: "*tibyanan*" is in the meaning of the noun *bayan* (clarification), and like *tibyan* is *tilqa'* (encounter). Tha'lab narrated from the Kufans, and al-Mubarrad from the Basrans, that they said: among verbal nouns of the form *tif'al*, only two words have come (*tibyanan* and *tilqa'an*). If you set these two words aside, the regular pattern holds: for every verbal noun you say *taf'al* with a fatha on the *ta'*, like *taysar*, *tadhkar*, and *takrar*, and you say for every noun *tif'al* with a kasra on the *ta'*, like *tiqsar* and *timthal*.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 90 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that you may be reminded.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had fully explained the promise and the threat, and the encouragement and the warning, He followed it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾. In this verse He gathered what relates to obligation, both obligatory and voluntary, and what relates to ethics and manners, both in general and in particular. There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue: on the virtues of this verse.** It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun al-Jumahi said: "I did not embrace Islam at first except out of shyness before Muhammad (ﷺ), and Islam had not yet settled in my heart. So I attended him one day, and while he was speaking to me, I saw his gaze lift toward the sky, then lower it to his right, then return to the same [state]. So I asked him, and he said: 'While I was speaking to you, suddenly Gabriel descended on my right and said: O Muhammad, indeed Allah commands justice and good conduct. Justice is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Good conduct is the performance of the obligations. Giving to relatives means maintaining ties of kinship. He forbids immorality, which is fornication, and bad conduct, which is what is not known in any law or sunnah, and oppression, which is domineering.'" ʿUthman said: "Faith then settled in my heart. So I went to Abu Talib and informed him, and he said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, follow my nephew and you will be guided. Whether he is truthful or lying, he only commands you to noble character.' When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw the softness of his uncle, he said: 'O uncle, do you command the people to follow me while you leave yourself [out]?' He strove hard with him, but he refused to embrace Islam. Then there was revealed His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]."

And it is related from Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him) that: "The most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and evil is this verse." And from Qatadah: "There is no good character that was practiced and esteemed in the Jahiliyyah except that Allah the Exalted commanded it in this verse, and there is no bad character except that Allah forbade it in this verse." Al-Qadi also related in his tafsir, from Ibn Majah, from ʿAli (peace be upon him), that he said: "Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to present himself to the tribes of the Arabs. So he went out, and I was with him, and Abu Bakr. We came upon a gathering who had dignity upon them. Abu Bakr said: 'Which people are you?' They said: 'From Shaybān ibn Thaʿlabah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to the two testimonies and to support him, for Quraysh had denied him. Then Maqrun ibn ʿAmr said: 'To what do you invite us, brother of Quraysh?' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾, the verse. Maqrun ibn ʿAmr said: 'By Allah, you have invited to noble character and excellent deeds. Indeed, a people who denied you and backed [others] against you have been turned away.'"

And from ʿIkrimah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse to al-Walid, and he asked him to repeat it, then said: 'Indeed it has sweetness, and indeed upon it is radiance.'" And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has prescribed excellence (ihsan) in everything. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and let him spare his animal [from suffering]." And Allah knows best.

**The second issue: on the interpretation of this verse.** People have said much concerning the interpretation of this verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said, in some narrations: "Justice is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and good conduct is the performance of the obligations." In another narration he said: "Justice is renouncing rivals, and good conduct is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and that you love for people what you love for yourself. So if he is a believer, you love that his faith increase; and if he is a disbeliever, you love that he become your brother in Islam." In a third narration he said: "Justice is Tawhid, and good conduct is sincerity (ikhlas) in it." Others said: "It means justice in actions and good conduct in words, so do not do anything except what is just, and do not say anything except what is good." His saying ﴿and giving to relatives﴾ means maintaining ties of kinship with wealth, and if one cannot, then with supplication. Abu Muslim related from his father that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the quickest of acts of obedience in reward is maintaining ties of kinship. Indeed, a household may be sinful, yet their wealth grows and their number increases when they maintain the ties of their kin."

His saying ﴿and forbids immorality﴾: it was said that it is fornication; it was said that it is stinginess; and it was said that it is all sins, whether small or great, and whether in speech or in action. As for ﴿bad conduct (munkar)﴾, it was said that it is disbelief in Allah the Exalted; and it was said that it is what is not known in any law or sunnah. As for ﴿oppression (baghy)﴾, it was said that it is arrogance and injustice; and it was said that it is that you transgress against your brother.

Know that there is a great number of commanded matters and also a great number of forbidden matters. The assignment of a specific word to a specific meaning is good only when there is a relation between that word and that meaning. If this relation does not exist, that interpretation is invalid. So when we interpret "justice" as one thing and "good conduct" as another, it is necessary to show that the word "justice" corresponds to that meaning, and the word "good conduct" corresponds to this meaning. Since we have not shown this, it is mere arbitrariness, and making some of those meanings an interpretation of some of those words is no more appropriate than the reverse. Thus it is established that these aspects we have mentioned are not strong in interpreting this verse.

I say: The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, commanded three things, namely justice, good conduct, and giving to relatives, and forbade three things, namely immorality, bad conduct, and oppression. Therefore justice, good conduct, and giving to relatives must be three distinct things, and immorality, bad conduct, and oppression must be three distinct things, because coordination requires distinction. So we say: As for justice, it is an expression for the intermediate matter between the two extremes of excess and deficiency, and this is a matter that must be observed in all things. And it is necessary to elaborate on this.

We say: The states for which obligation has been imposed are either beliefs (i'tiqadat) or actions of the limbs. As for beliefs, justice must be observed in all of them:

First: Ibn ʿAbbas said that what is meant by justice is the statement "there is no god but Allah." The detailed explanation is that denying a deity is pure nullification (ta'til), and affirming more than one deity is association and anthropomorphism (tashbih), and both are blameworthy. Justice is the affirmation of one God, and this is the statement "there is no god but Allah."

Second: The claim that God does not exist, and is not a thing, is pure nullification. The claim that He is a body and a substance composed of limbs and specific to a place is pure anthropomorphism. Justice is the affirmation of a God who exists and is established, on the condition that He is exalted above corporeality, substantiality, limbs, parts, and place.

Third: The claim that God is not described by attributes such as knowledge and power is pure nullification. The claim that His attributes are originated and changing is pure anthropomorphism. Justice is the affirmation that God is knowing, powerful, living, while acknowledging that His attributes are neither originated nor changing.

Fourth: The claim that the servant has no power or choice is pure compulsion (jabr). The claim that the servant is independent in his actions is pure predestination-as-human-autonomy (qadar), and both are blameworthy. Justice is to say that the servant performs the act, but through a power and a motive which Allah the Exalted creates in him.

Fifth: The claim that Allah the Exalted does not hold His servant accountable for any sins is a great leniency, and the claim that He eternally punishes in the Fire His servant who knows of one act of disobedience is a great severity. Justice is that He brings out of the Fire everyone who says and believes that there is no god but Allah. These are examples we have mentioned in observing the meaning of justice in beliefs.

As for observing justice in matters concerning actions of the limbs, we mention six examples of them:

First: Some who deny legal obligations say: it is not obligatory upon the servant to occupy himself with any act of obedience, nor is it obligatory upon him to abstain from any sin, and God has no obligation upon him at all. And some of the Hindus and the Manichaeans said: it is obligatory upon a person to abstain from all good things, to exert himself greatly in punishing his soul, and to avoid everything his nature inclines toward, to the extent that the Manichaeans castrate themselves, abstain from marriage, and abstain from eating good food. And the Hindus burn themselves and throw themselves from the peak of a mountain. These two ways are blameworthy, and the moderate middle is this law which Muhammad (ﷺ) brought to us.

Second: Strictness is very predominant in the religion of Moses (peace be upon him), and leniency is very predominant in the religion of Jesus (peace be upon him), and the just middle is the law of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It was said: the law of Moses (peace be upon him) required, for deliberate murder, the exaction of retaliation (qisas) without fail, while in the law of Jesus (peace be upon him) there is pardon. As for our law, if he wishes he may exact retaliation by way of equivalence, and if he wishes he may take blood money (diyya), and if he wishes he may pardon. Also, the law of Moses required great avoidance of a woman during her menstruation, while the law of Jesus permitted intercourse with a menstruating woman. The just [position] is what our law has ruled: that intercourse with her is forbidden, to avoid being polluted by that foul blood, but it is not obligatory to expel her from the house.

Third: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning distant from the two extremes of excess and deficiency in all matters. And He said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that a balance﴾ [al-Furqan: 67]. And He said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra: 29]. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) exceeded in acts of worship, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 1–2]. And when some people went to leniency, He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. What is intended by all of this is the observance of justice and the middle course.

Fourth: Our law commanded circumcision (khitan). The wisdom in it is that the head of the organ is a very sensitive part, and because of it the pleasure during intercourse is great. If the foreskin were left on that organ, the organ would remain in full strength and intense sensitivity, and so the pleasure would be greater. But when that foreskin is cut off and the organ remains bare, it encounters clothing and other bodies, so it hardens, its sensation weakens, and its feeling diminishes; thus pleasure in intercourse decreases, and the desire for it decreases. It is as if the law commanded circumcision in an effort to reduce that pleasure, so that a person's inclination toward satisfying sexual desire reaches a state of moderation, and the desire for it does not become dominant over nature. So castration and cutting off the organs, as the Manichaeans hold, is blameworthy, because it is excess; and leaving the foreskin is an exaggeration in strengthening that pleasure. The just middle is performing circumcision.

Thus it becomes clear from these examples that justice must be observed in all states. Among the well-known sayings is their saying: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand." Its meaning is: if the quantities of the elements were not balanced and equal, but some of them were greater than the others in quantity and in quality, the dominant would overpower the subdued and the subdued would weaken, and all natures would transform into the nature of the dominant body. And if the distance of the sun from the earth were less than it is now, heat in this world would become intense and everything in this world would burn; and if its distance were greater than it is now, cold and frost would overcome this world. The same applies to the quantities of the movements of the stars and the degrees of their speed and slowness: if any one of them were greater than it is now or less than it is now, the interests of this world would be disrupted. Thus, by this cause we have mentioned, the truth of their saying becomes evident: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand." This is a brief indication to explain the reality of justice.

[p. 82]

Now as for ihsan (excellence), know that going beyond justice (adl) may be ihsan, and it may be wrongdoing. An example: justice in acts of obedience is the performance of obligatory duties. As for going beyond the obligatory duties, these too are acts of obedience, and that falls under the category of ihsan. In sum, striving to the utmost in performing acts of obedience, both in quantity and in quality, is ihsan. The proof for this is: "When Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about ihsan, he said: 'Ihsan is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you.'"

صفحة ٨٤

If they say: Why was this meaning called ihsan?

We say: It is as if, by striving to the utmost in obedience, one does good (yuhsinu) to oneself and brings goodness and a good deed to oneself. The summary is that justice is an expression for the required measure of good deeds, while ihsan is an expression for the increase in those acts of obedience in quantity and in quality, in accordance with the motives and deterrents, and in accordance with being absorbed in contemplating the stations of servanthood and lordship. This is ihsan.

Know that ihsan, according to the explanation we have mentioned, includes glorifying the command of Allah the Exalted and showing compassion to the creatures of Allah. It is evident that compassion towards the creatures of Allah has many kinds, and the most noble and most exalted of them is maintaining family ties (silat al-rahim). Therefore, glorified is He, He singled it out for mention when He said: ﴿and giving to the near of kin﴾. This is the detailed discussion of these three things which Allah the Exalted commanded.

As for the three things from which Allah forbade, namely indecency (fahsha'), the reprehensible (munkar) and transgression (baghy), we say: Allah the Exalted placed in the human soul four powers: the appetitive, bestial power (al-shahwaniyya al-bahimiyya), the irascible, predatory power (al-ghadabiyya al-sab'iyya), the imaginative, satanic power (al-wahmiyya al-shaytaniyya), and the intellective, angelic power (al-'aqliyya al-malakiyya). This fourth power, I mean the intellective, angelic power, does not require a person to discipline and refine it, because it is from the substances of the angels and from the products of the holy, lofty spirits. Rather, what needs discipline and refinement are the first three powers. As for the appetitive power, it only inclines towards attaining bestial pleasures, and this type is specifically called fuhsh (indecency). Do you not see that Allah the Exalted called fornication a fahisha, when He said: ﴿Indeed it was an indecency and a hateful thing, and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra' 17:32]. So His saying: ﴿and forbids indecency﴾ means the prohibition of attaining bestial pleasures that go beyond what the Shari'ah permits. As for the irascible, predatory power, it is always striving to inflict evil, harm and injury upon the rest of people, and there is no doubt that people reject that state, so the munkar is an expression for the excess occurring in the effects of the irascible power. As for the imaginative, satanic power, it is always striving to dominate over people, to be haughty, to display leadership and superiority, and that is what is meant by baghy, for baghy means nothing but overbearing towards people and being arrogant over them. Thus it becomes clear from what we have mentioned that these three terms correspond to the states of these three powers. Among the wonders in this regard is that the wise said: the lowliest of these three powers is the appetitive, the middle one is the irascible, and the highest is the imaginative. Allah the Exalted observed this order, beginning with fahsha', which is the result of the appetitive power, then with munkar, which is the result of the irascible power, then with baghy, which is the result of the imaginative power. This is what my intellect and my reflection have reached in explaining these terms. If it is correct, then it is from the Most Merciful, and if it is in error, then it is from me and from Satan, and Allah and His Messenger are free of it. Praise be to Allah for having granted us this kind of favour and excellence; indeed He is the King, the Judge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 91–92 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He admonishes you so that you may remember.﴾ By His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He admonishes you﴾ is meant His commanding you with those three things and forbidding you from those three things. ﴿So that you may remember﴾. On this there are issues.

The first issue: when He, exalted is He, said in the first verse, ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ (al-Nahl 89), He followed it with this verse, which contains the command to these three things and the prohibition of those three things. This is a reminder that what is meant by the Qur'an being an explanation of all things is these six obligations. In reality this is so, because the essence of the soul is of the company of the angels and one of the results of the high, holy spirits. However, it entered this world empty and bare of attachments. Those three things that God commanded are what raise it through divine knowledge and righteous deeds. And those knowledges and deeds are what raise it to the world of the unseen, the pavilions of holiness, and the neighbourhood of the angels brought near, in the presence of the Lord of the worlds. Those three things that God forbade are what block it from those felicities and prevent it from attaining those goods. So when God, exalted is He, commanded those three and forbade those three, He drew attention to everything that travellers from the world of this life to the threshold of the Day of Resurrection need.

The second issue: al-Ka'bi said: the verse indicates that God does not create injustice and immorality. This is so for several reasons.

First: how would He forbid them from what He creates in them, and how would He forbid what He wants to bring about in them? If the matter were as they say, it would be as if He had said: God commands you to do the opposite of what He created in you, and forbids you from acts He created in you. It is known by the immediate judgment of reason that this is false.

Second: when He commanded justice, good conduct, and giving to close relatives, and forbade indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression, then if He commanded these three and then did not Himself do them, He would fall under His saying: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people and forget yourselves?﴾ (al-Baqarah 44), and under His saying: ﴿O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? It is greatly hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do﴾ (al-Saff 2–3).

Third: His saying ﴿so that you may remember﴾ does not mean hope and wishing, for that is impossible for God. So its meaning must be that He admonishes you in order that you may remember His obedience. That indicates that He wills faith from all.

Fourth: if He had stated explicitly, "God commands justice, good conduct, and giving to close relatives, but He prevents it, blocks it, and does not enable the servant to do it," and then said, "He forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression, but He brings all three into existence in the servant, whether he wills or not, and wills them from him, and prevents him from abandoning them or guarding against them," then everyone would judge that speech to be incoherent and its composition and structure corrupt. That indicates that He, glorified is He, is exalted above doing ugly deeds.

Know that this kind of argument is common, and its answer has already passed. The reliable approach in repelling these disputes is to rely on the question of the caller and the question of knowledge. And God knows best.

The third issue: the theologians of the People of the Sunnah and the Mu'tazilites agreed that remembering things is an act of God and not an act of the servant. The proof is that remembrance is the seeking of what is to be remembered. The state of seeking either involves awareness of it or does not. If there is awareness of it, then that remembrance is already present, and what is already present is not sought to be brought about. If there is no awareness of it, how can one seek it specifically? For directing the seeking at it specifically, at a time when it is not itself specifically present, is inconceivable.

Having established this, we say: His saying ﴿so that you may remember﴾ means that the aim of this admonition is that they proceed to bring about that remembrance. If remembrance is not an act of theirs, how could He demand that they bring it about? This is what our companions use as an argument that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so that you may remember﴾ does not indicate that He wills that from them. And God knows best.

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you make a covenant, and do not break oaths after making them firm, and you have indeed made God your surety over you. Indeed God knows what you do.﴾ ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her yarn after it was strong, into fragments, taking your oaths as a deception among yourselves, because one community is more numerous than another. God only tests you thereby; and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ.﴾

* * *

[p. 86]

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant of God when you make a covenant, and do not break oaths after making them firm, and you have indeed made God your surety over you. Indeed God knows what you do.﴾ ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her yarn after it was strong, into fragments, taking your oaths as a deception among yourselves, because one community is more numerous than another. God only tests you thereby; and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, gathered all the commanded and forbidden matters in the first verse in summary, He mentioned in this verse some of those categories. He began, exalted is He, with the command to fulfil the covenant. In the verse there are issues.

The first issue: they mentioned several interpretations of His saying ﴿the covenant of God﴾:

The first: the author of al-Kashshaf said: the covenant of God is the pledge of allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) upon Islam, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are pledging allegiance only to God; the hand of God is over their hands﴾ (al-Fath 10). That is, ﴿do not break the oaths of the pledge after their confirmation﴾, that is, after their confirmation by the name of God.

The second: that what is meant by it is every covenant that a person binds himself to by his own choice. Ibn 'Abbas said: a promise is a covenant. Maymun ibn Mihran said: whoever you make a covenant with, fulfil his covenant, whether he is a Muslim or a disbeliever, for the covenant is only for God, exalted is He.

The third: al-Asamm said: what is meant by it is jihad and what God has enjoined regarding rights in wealth.

The fourth: the covenant of God is the oath by God. The speaker of this said: fulfilling an oath is obligatory only when there is no benefit in its opposite, because he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever swears to an oath and sees something else better than it, let him do what is better and then make expiation."

The fifth: al-Qadi said: the covenant encompasses every matter whose fulfilment is obligatory. It is known that the proofs of reason and revelation are more emphatic in the obligation to fulfil what they indicate is obligatory than an oath is. For this reason, change and disagreement are not valid regarding these two proofs, whereas that is valid regarding an oath, and sometimes its opposite of fulfilment is recommended in it.

One may say: He, exalted is He, said ﴿fulfil the covenant of God when you make a covenant﴾. So this must be restricted to the covenants a person binds himself to by his own choice, because His saying ﴿when you make a covenant﴾ indicates this meaning. In that case, the meaning al-Qadi mentioned has no weight. Also, He said at the end of the verse ﴿you have indeed made God your surety over you﴾. This indicates that the verse is addressed to those who believed in God and His Messenger. Also, this covenant must not be taken to mean the oath, because if we took it that way, His subsequent saying ﴿and do not break oaths after making them firm﴾ would be a repetition, since fulfilling the covenant and forbidding its breaking are close in meaning. The command to do an act necessarily implies the prohibition of abandoning it, unless it is said that fulfilling the covenant is general and so includes the oath. Then He, exalted is He, singled out the oath for mention, to draw attention to its being the most important kind of covenant to observe. At this point we say: it is better to take this covenant to mean what a person binds himself to by his own choice, and this includes the pledge of allegiance upon belief in God and His Messenger, and includes the covenant of jihad, and the covenant of fulfilling commitments made by vows and by things he confirmed by oath and swearing.

Regarding His saying ﴿and do not break oaths after making them firm﴾ there are discussions:

The first discussion: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "wakkadtu" and "akkadtu," both are good dialects, and the original is the waw, and the hamza is a substitute for it.

The second discussion: the companions of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, said: the oath of nonsense (laghw) is the oath of deliberate false swearing (ghamus). The proof is that He, exalted is He, said ﴿do not break oaths after making them firm﴾, so in this verse He forbade the breaking of oaths. Therefore every oath must be capable of being kept or broken. The oath of deliberate false swearing is not capable of being kept or broken, so it must not be counted among oaths.

Al-Wahidi used this verse to argue that the oath of nonsense is the saying of the Arabs: "No, by God" and "Yes, by God." He said: God only said ﴿after making them firm﴾ to distinguish oaths confirmed by resolve and by binding oneself from the nonsense of oaths.

The third discussion: His saying ﴿do not break oaths after making them firm﴾ is general, and it has been subjected to restriction. For we have shown that the report indicates that whenever there is benefit in breaking oaths, breaking them is permitted.

Then He said: ﴿and you have indeed made God your surety over you﴾. This is the waw of circumstance, meaning: do not break them while you have made God a surety over you for fulfilling them. This is because whoever swears by God, exalted is He, has as it were made God a surety for fulfilment by means of that oath.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed God knows what you do﴾. In this there is encouragement and warning. The meaning is: He will reward you for what you do; if it is good, then good, and if it is evil, then evil. Then He, exalted is He, reinforced the obligation to fulfil and the prohibition of breaking, and said: ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her yarn after it was strong, into fragments﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: there are two opinions about the one being likened to:

The first opinion: she was a woman from Quraysh called Rayita, and it is said Rayta, and it is said she was nicknamed Ja'ra'. She was foolish, and she and her female slaves spun yarn. When they had spun and twisted it, she ordered them, and they unravelled what they had spun.

The second opinion: what is meant by the example is the description, not the specific identification. This is because the purpose of parables is to turn the one under obligation away from something when it is ugly, and to call him to it when it is good, and this is accomplished without specific identification.

The second issue: His saying ﴿after strength﴾ means: after the strength of the yarn through its twisting and spinning.

The third issue: His saying ﴿into fragments (ankathan)﴾. Al-Azhari said: its singular is nikth, which is yarn of wool or hair that is twisted and woven. When she has finished the weaving and then cut it, she unravels its twisted threads and scatters those threads, mixes them with wool, and then spins them again. Nakth is the verbal noun, and from it one says: "Fulan broke his covenant (nakatha 'ahdahu)" when he breaks it after making it firm, just as wool thread is unravelled after being twisted.

The fourth issue: regarding the grammatical status of His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ there are several views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: ankathan is in the accusative because it has the meaning of a verbal noun, since the meaning of "nakathat" is "naqadat" (she broke), and the meaning of "naqadat" is "nakathat." This is an error on his part, because ankath is the plural of nikth, which is a noun and not a verbal noun, so how can His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ have the meaning of a verbal noun?

The second: al-Wahidi said: ankathan is a second object, as you say: "He broke it into pieces (aqta'an)," and "He divided it into parts (ajza'an)," meaning he made it into pieces and parts. Likewise here, His saying "she unravelled her yarn into fragments" means she made her yarn into fragments.

The third: His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial accusative.

The fifth issue: Ibn Qutayba said: this verse is connected to what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: "And fulfil the covenant of God when you make a covenant, and do not break oaths after making them firm. For if you do that, you will be like the woman who spun yarn and made it firm, and when it became strong she unravelled it and made it into fragments."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves﴾. Al-Wahidi said: al-dakhal and al-daghal are deceit and treachery. Al-Zajjaj said: everything into which a defect has entered is said to be "madkhul" (defective), and there is "dakhal" in it. Others said: al-dakhal is that which is introduced into a thing in a corrupt manner.

Then He said: ﴿that one community should be more numerous than another﴾. Arba (more numerous) means more, from "raba al-shay'u yarbu" when a thing increases; and this increase may be in number, in strength, or in nobility. Mujahid said: They used to make alliances with the allies, then they would find someone who was more powerful and more noble than them, so they would break the alliance of the first and ally themselves with those who were more powerful. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade them from that.

His saying ﴿"an takuna"﴾ (that...be) means: that you take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves on account of a community being more numerous than another in number, strength and nobility. Thus His saying ﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves﴾ is an interrogative in the form of denunciation, and the meaning is: Do you take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves because one community is greater in strength and multitude than another community?

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only tests you thereby﴾, i.e., by what He commands you and forbids you; the mention of commanding and forbidding has already preceded. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection He will surely make clear to you that over which you used to differ﴾, so that the righteous is distinguished from the falsifier by the degrees of reward and punishment that become manifest. And Allah knows best.
