The third discussion: His saying ﴿do not break oaths after making them firm﴾ is general, and it has been subjected to restriction. For we have shown that the report indicates that whenever there is benefit in breaking oaths, breaking them is permitted.

Then He said: ﴿and you have indeed made God your surety over you﴾. This is the waw of circumstance, meaning: do not break them while you have made God a surety over you for fulfilling them. This is because whoever swears by God, exalted is He, has as it were made God a surety for fulfilment by means of that oath.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed God knows what you do﴾. In this there is encouragement and warning. The meaning is: He will reward you for what you do; if it is good, then good, and if it is evil, then evil. Then He, exalted is He, reinforced the obligation to fulfil and the prohibition of breaking, and said: ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her yarn after it was strong, into fragments﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: there are two opinions about the one being likened to:

The first opinion: she was a woman from Quraysh called Rayita, and it is said Rayta, and it is said she was nicknamed Ja'ra'. She was foolish, and she and her female slaves spun yarn. When they had spun and twisted it, she ordered them, and they unravelled what they had spun.

The second opinion: what is meant by the example is the description, not the specific identification. This is because the purpose of parables is to turn the one under obligation away from something when it is ugly, and to call him to it when it is good, and this is accomplished without specific identification.

The second issue: His saying ﴿after strength﴾ means: after the strength of the yarn through its twisting and spinning.

The third issue: His saying ﴿into fragments (ankathan)﴾. Al-Azhari said: its singular is nikth, which is yarn of wool or hair that is twisted and woven. When she has finished the weaving and then cut it, she unravels its twisted threads and scatters those threads, mixes them with wool, and then spins them again. Nakth is the verbal noun, and from it one says: "Fulan broke his covenant (nakatha 'ahdahu)" when he breaks it after making it firm, just as wool thread is unravelled after being twisted.

The fourth issue: regarding the grammatical status of His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ there are several views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: ankathan is in the accusative because it has the meaning of a verbal noun, since the meaning of "nakathat" is "naqadat" (she broke), and the meaning of "naqadat" is "nakathat." This is an error on his part, because ankath is the plural of nikth, which is a noun and not a verbal noun, so how can His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ have the meaning of a verbal noun?

The second: al-Wahidi said: ankathan is a second object, as you say: "He broke it into pieces (aqta'an)," and "He divided it into parts (ajza'an)," meaning he made it into pieces and parts. Likewise here, His saying "she unravelled her yarn into fragments" means she made her yarn into fragments.

The third: His saying ﴿ankathan﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial accusative.

The fifth issue: Ibn Qutayba said: this verse is connected to what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: "And fulfil the covenant of God when you make a covenant, and do not break oaths after making them firm. For if you do that, you will be like the woman who spun yarn and made it firm, and when it became strong she unravelled it and made it into fragments."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves﴾. Al-Wahidi said: al-dakhal and al-daghal are deceit and treachery. Al-Zajjaj said: everything into which a defect has entered is said to be "madkhul" (defective), and there is "dakhal" in it. Others said: al-dakhal is that which is introduced into a thing in a corrupt manner.

Then He said: ﴿that one community should be more numerous than another﴾. Arba (more numerous) means more, from "raba al-shay'u yarbu" when a thing increases; and this increase may be in number, in strength, or in nobility. Mujahid said: They used to make alliances with the allies, then they would find someone who was more powerful and more noble than them, so they would break the alliance of the first and ally themselves with those who were more powerful. So Allah, exalted is He, forbade them from that.

His saying ﴿"an takuna"﴾ (that...be) means: that you take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves on account of a community being more numerous than another in number, strength and nobility. Thus His saying ﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves﴾ is an interrogative in the form of denunciation, and the meaning is: Do you take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves because one community is greater in strength and multitude than another community?

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah only tests you thereby﴾, i.e., by what He commands you and forbids you; the mention of commanding and forbidding has already preceded. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection He will surely make clear to you that over which you used to differ﴾, so that the righteous is distinguished from the falsifier by the degrees of reward and punishment that become manifest. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but He sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had obligated the people to fulfil the covenant and prohibited breaking it, He followed this with an explanation that He is able to bring them together upon this fulfilment and upon all the other aspects of faith. But He, glorified is He, by the judgment of divinity, sends astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. As for the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school), they interpreted this as *ilja'* (compulsion), meaning: if He had willed to compel them to faith or to disbelief, He would have been able to do so. However, that would nullify the obligation (*taklif*). Therefore He did not compel them to it, but left the matter to their choice in these obligations. As for the statement of our companions on this, it is evident. This debate has been repeated many times.

Al-Wahidi narrated that Uzayr (Ezra) said: "O Lord, You created the creation, and You send astray whom You will and guide whom You will." He said: "O Uzayr, turn away from this." He repeated it a second time, and He said: "Turn away from this." He repeated it a third time, and He said: "Turn away from this, or I will erase your name from prophethood."

The Mu'tazila said: Among what indicates that the intended meaning of this will is the will of compulsion is that He said after it: ﴿and you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾ For if the deeds of the servants were by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, then questioning them about them would be pointless. The answer to this has been given many times before. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 94–97:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And do not make your oaths a means of deception among yourselves, lest a foot slip after being firmly planted and you taste evil for having averted [others] from the way of Allah, and for you is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah is lasting. And We will surely give those who were patient their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, warned in the first verse against breaking covenants and oaths in general, He warned in this verse, saying: ﴿And do not make your oaths a means of deception among yourselves.﴾ The intent here is not a warning against breaking oaths in general, for otherwise it would entail a repetition devoid of benefit in one place. Rather, the intent is a prohibition to those people addressed by this address against breaking particular oaths that they had entered into. For this reason the exegetes said: the intent of this verse is the prohibition of those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against breaking his covenant, because this threat, namely His saying ﴿lest a foot slip after being firmly planted﴾, does not befit the breaking of a covenant that precedes it, but befits only the breaking of the covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding faith in him and his laws.

As for His saying ﴿lest a foot slip after being firmly planted﴾, it is a parable mentioned for everyone who falls into affliction after well-being, and into tribulation after blessing, for whoever breaks the covenant of Islam has fallen from the lofty ranks and has fallen into such misguidance. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you taste evil﴾, i.e., punishment, ﴿for having averted [others]﴾, i.e., for your averting ﴿from the way of Allah, and for you is a great punishment﴾, i.e., that evil which you taste is a great evil and severe retribution. Then He emphasized this warning, saying: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾, meaning the goods of this world, even if they are many. However, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew. That is, even if you find in breaking the covenant of Islam some good from the good things of this world, do not turn to it, because what Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for remaining upon Islam is better, more excellent and more perfect than what you find in this world by breaking the covenant of Islam, if you know the disparity between the good things of this world and the good things of the Hereafter.

Then he mentioned the decisive proof that what is with Allah is better than what they find of the good things of this world, saying: ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah is lasting.﴾ And in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: sense perception bears witness that the good things of this world are cut off, and reason shows that the good things of the Hereafter are lasting, and the lasting is better than the cut off. The proof of this is that this cut-off thing either is said to have been a lofty, noble good, or a base, lowly good. If we say it was a lofty, noble good, then knowledge that it will come to an end makes it troubled while it is attained; and as for the time of that cessation, grief and sorrow become great, and the fact that that lofty, noble blessing is like this troubles it and diminishes its rank, and desire for it wanes. And if we say that that cut-off blessing was of the base, lowly goods, then we understand from the outward sense that that lasting good must be better than that cut-off good. Thus it is established by this that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah is lasting﴾ is a decisive proof that the good things of the Hereafter are more excellent than the good things of this world.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿but what is with Allah is lasting﴾ indicates that the bliss of the people of Paradise is lasting and does not cease. Jahm ibn Safwan said that it ceases, and the verse is a proof against him.

Know that when the believer believes in Allah, he has committed himself to the laws of Islam and faith, and then two matters become obligatory upon him:

One of them: that he be patient in that commitment, that he not turn back from it, and that he not break it after it has been established.

The second: that he perform everything that is among the laws of Islam and its requirements.

Having known this, we say: He, exalted is He, encouraged the believers toward the first division, which is patience in what they have committed to, saying: ﴿And We will surely give those who were patient﴾, i.e., in what they committed to of the laws of Islam, ﴿their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., He will reward them

صفحة ٩٠
according to their best deeds. This is because the believer may perform permissible acts, recommended acts, and obligatory acts, and there is no doubt that he is rewarded for performing recommended and obligatory acts, not for performing permissible acts; therefore He said: ﴿And We will surely give those who were patient their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, encouraged the believers toward the second division, which is performing everything that is among the laws of Islam, saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ In the verse there are questions:

The first question: the word "man" (مَن) in His saying ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ conveys generality, so what is the benefit of mentioning male and female?

The answer: this verse is for the promise of good things, and emphasizing the promise is among the greatest indications of generosity and mercy; it affirms emphasis and removes the illusion of restriction.

The second question: does this verse indicate that faith is distinct from righteous deeds?

The answer: Yes, because He, exalted is He, made faith a condition for righteous deeds to entail reward, and the condition of a thing is distinct from that thing.

The third question: the apparent sense of the verse requires that righteous deeds produce effect only with the condition of faith. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7] indicates that righteous deeds produce effect, whether accompanied by faith or by its absence.

The answer: the production of a good life by righteous deeds is conditioned upon faith; but their producing an effect other than this good life, namely the lightening of punishment, does not depend on faith.

The fourth question: does this good life occur in this world, or in the grave, or in the Hereafter?

The answer: there are three opinions concerning it.

The first opinion: al-Qadi said: the closer view is that it occurs in this world, by the evidence that He, exalted is He, followed it with His saying: ﴿And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ And there is no doubt that the intended meaning of that is what will occur in the Hereafter.

One may say: it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of the good life is what occurs in the Hereafter; then, along with that, Allah promised them that He would reward them according to their best deeds, and there is no impossibility in this.

If it is said: assuming this good life occurs in this world, what is it? The answer: they mentioned several views concerning it. It was said: it is lawful, good provision; it was said: worship of Allah together with eating what is lawful; it was said: contentment; it was said: provision for each day by its day. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his supplication: "Make me content with what You have provided me."

And from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to supplicate: "O Allah, make the provision of the family of Muhammad sufficient (kafaf)."

Al-Wahidi said: the saying of whoever says that it is contentment is a good and preferred view, because no one's life is pleasant in this world except the life of the contented person; as for the greedy, he is always in toil and hardship.

Page 91

Know that the life of the believer in this world is more pleasant than the life of the disbeliever, for several reasons:

The first: when he knows that his provision came about through the arrangement of Allah, exalted is He, and knows that He is benevolent, generous, who does only what is right, he is content with everything He has decreed and destined, and he knows that his welfare lies in that. As for the ignorant, he does not know these principles, so he is always in grief and misery.

The second: the believer always keeps in his mind the various kinds of calamities and trials, and estimates their occurrence; and upon their occurrence he is content with them, because contentment with the decree of Allah, exalted is He, is obligatory; so when they occur he does not regard them as great. Unlike the ignorant, who is heedless of those knowledges, so when calamities occur their effect on his heart is great.

The third: the heart of the believer is expanded by the light of knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and when the heart is filled with these knowledges it has no room for the sorrows caused by the circumstances of this world. As for the heart of the ignorant, it is empty of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, so it inevitably becomes filled with the sorrows caused by the calamities of this world.

The fourth: the believer knows that the good things of corporeal life are base, so his joy at finding them does not greatly increase, nor his grief at losing them. As for the ignorant, he knows no other happiness that differs from it, so inevitably his joy at finding them and his grief at losing them become great.

The fifth: the believer knows that the good things of this world are necessarily subject to change and swift to fluctuate, and were it not for their change and transformation they would not reach him from another.

And know that whatever is necessarily subject to change, when it reaches a person its reality does not transform and its quiddity does not change; so when it reaches him it is also necessarily subject to change. At that point the intelligent person does not seal his heart upon it, nor give it any weight in his heart. Unlike the ignorant, who is heedless of these knowledges, so he seals his heart upon them and embraces them like a lover embracing his beloved; so when they are lost and vanish, his heart burns and the affliction becomes great for him. These are sufficient aspects to show that the life of the knowing believer is more pleasant than the life of the disbeliever. All of this applies when we interpret the good life as being in this world.

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Suddi: this good life occurs in the grave.

The third opinion, which is the view of al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: this good life does not occur except in the Hereafter. The evidence for it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O man, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. He made clear that this labor continues until one reaches his Lord, and that is what we have said. As for the demonstration that the good life is in Paradise: it is a life without death, wealth without poverty, health without sickness, sovereignty without cessation, and happiness without misery. Thus it is established that the good life is nothing other than that life. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾, and its explanation has already preceded. And Allah knows best.

For this reason the exegetes said: the intent of this verse is the prohibition of those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against breaking his covenant, because this threat, namely His saying ﴿lest a foot slip after being firmly planted﴾, does not befit the breaking of a covenant that precedes it, but befits only the breaking of the covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding faith in him and his laws.

As for His saying ﴿lest a foot slip after being firmly planted﴾, it is a parable mentioned for everyone who falls into affliction after well-being, and into tribulation after blessing, for whoever breaks the covenant of Islam has fallen from the lofty ranks and has fallen into such misguidance. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you taste evil﴾, i.e., punishment, ﴿for having averted [others]﴾, i.e., for your averting ﴿from the way of Allah, and for you is a great punishment﴾, i.e., that evil which you taste is a great evil and severe retribution. Then He emphasized this warning, saying: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾, meaning the goods of this world, even if they are many. However, what is with Allah is better for you, if you only knew. That is, even if you find in breaking the covenant of Islam some good from the good things of this world, do not turn to it, because what Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for remaining upon Islam is better, more excellent and more perfect than what you find in this world by breaking the covenant of Islam, if you know the disparity between the good things of this world and the good things of the Hereafter.

Then he mentioned the decisive proof that what is with Allah is better than what they find of the good things of this world, saying: ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah is lasting.﴾ And in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: sense perception bears witness that the good things of this world are cut off, and reason shows that the good things of the Hereafter are lasting, and the lasting is better than the cut off. The proof of this is that this cut-off thing either is said to have been a lofty, noble good, or a base, lowly good. If we say it was a lofty, noble good, then knowledge that it will come to an end makes it troubled while it is attained; and as for the time of that cessation, grief and sorrow become great, and the fact that that lofty, noble blessing is like this troubles it and diminishes its rank, and desire for it wanes. And if we say that that cut-off blessing was of the base, lowly goods, then we understand from the outward sense that that lasting good must be better than that cut-off good. Thus it is established by this that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah is lasting﴾ is a decisive proof that the good things of the Hereafter are more excellent than the good things of this world.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿but what is with Allah is lasting﴾ indicates that the bliss of the people of Paradise is lasting and does not cease. Jahm ibn Safwan said that it ceases, and the verse is a proof against him.

Know that when the believer believes in Allah, he has committed himself to the laws of Islam and faith, and then two matters become obligatory upon him:

One of them: that he be patient in that commitment, that he not turn back from it, and that he not break it after it has been established.

The second: that he perform everything that is among the laws of Islam and its requirements.

Having known this, we say: He, exalted is He, encouraged the believers toward the first division, which is patience in what they have committed to, saying: ﴿And We will surely give those who were patient﴾, i.e., in what they committed to of the laws of Islam, ﴿their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., He will reward them

صفحة ٩٠
according to their best deeds. This is because the believer may perform permissible acts, recommended acts, and obligatory acts, and there is no doubt that he is rewarded for performing recommended and obligatory acts, not for performing permissible acts; therefore He said: ﴿And We will surely give those who were patient their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, encouraged the believers toward the second division, which is performing everything that is among the laws of Islam, saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ In the verse there are questions:

The first question: the word "man" (مَن) in His saying ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ conveys generality, so what is the benefit of mentioning male and female?

The answer: this verse is for the promise of good things, and emphasizing the promise is among the greatest indications of generosity and mercy; it affirms emphasis and removes the illusion of restriction.

The second question: does this verse indicate that faith is distinct from righteous deeds?

The answer: Yes, because He, exalted is He, made faith a condition for righteous deeds to entail reward, and the condition of a thing is distinct from that thing.

The third question: the apparent sense of the verse requires that righteous deeds produce effect only with the condition of faith. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7] indicates that righteous deeds produce effect, whether accompanied by faith or by its absence.

The answer: the production of a good life by righteous deeds is conditioned upon faith; but their producing an effect other than this good life, namely the lightening of punishment, does not depend on faith.

The fourth question: does this good life occur in this world, or in the grave, or in the Hereafter?

The answer: there are three opinions concerning it.

The first opinion: al-Qadi said: the closer view is that it occurs in this world, by the evidence that He, exalted is He, followed it with His saying: ﴿And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ And there is no doubt that the intended meaning of that is what will occur in the Hereafter.

One may say: it is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of the good life is what occurs in the Hereafter; then, along with that, Allah promised them that He would reward them according to their best deeds, and there is no impossibility in this.

If it is said: assuming this good life occurs in this world, what is it? The answer: they mentioned several views concerning it. It was said: it is lawful, good provision; it was said: worship of Allah together with eating what is lawful; it was said: contentment; it was said: provision for each day by its day. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his supplication: "Make me content with what You have provided me."

And from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to supplicate: "O Allah, make the provision of the family of Muhammad sufficient (kafaf)."

Al-Wahidi said: the saying of whoever says that it is contentment is a good and preferred view, because no one's life is pleasant in this world except the life of the contented person; as for the greedy, he is always in toil and hardship.

Page 91

Know that the life of the believer in this world is more pleasant than the life of the disbeliever, for several reasons:

The first: when he knows that his provision came about through the arrangement of Allah, exalted is He, and knows that He is benevolent, generous, who does only what is right, he is content with everything He has decreed and destined, and he knows that his welfare lies in that. As for the ignorant, he does not know these principles, so he is always in grief and misery.

The second: the believer always keeps in his mind the various kinds of calamities and trials, and estimates their occurrence; and upon their occurrence he is content with them, because contentment with the decree of Allah, exalted is He, is obligatory; so when they occur he does not regard them as great. Unlike the ignorant, who is heedless of those knowledges, so when calamities occur their effect on his heart is great.

The third: the heart of the believer is expanded by the light of knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, and when the heart is filled with these knowledges it has no room for the sorrows caused by the circumstances of this world. As for the heart of the ignorant, it is empty of the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, so it inevitably becomes filled with the sorrows caused by the calamities of this world.

The fourth: the believer knows that the good things of corporeal life are base, so his joy at finding them does not greatly increase, nor his grief at losing them. As for the ignorant, he knows no other happiness that differs from it, so inevitably his joy at finding them and his grief at losing them become great.

The fifth: the believer knows that the good things of this world are necessarily subject to change and swift to fluctuate, and were it not for their change and transformation they would not reach him from another.

And know that whatever is necessarily subject to change, when it reaches a person its reality does not transform and its quiddity does not change; so when it reaches him it is also necessarily subject to change. At that point the intelligent person does not seal his heart upon it, nor give it any weight in his heart. Unlike the ignorant, who is heedless of these knowledges, so he seals his heart upon them and embraces them like a lover embracing his beloved; so when they are lost and vanish, his heart burns and the affliction becomes great for him. These are sufficient aspects to show that the life of the knowing believer is more pleasant than the life of the disbeliever. All of this applies when we interpret the good life as being in this world.

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Suddi: this good life occurs in the grave.

The third opinion, which is the view of al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: this good life does not occur except in the Hereafter. The evidence for it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O man, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 6]. He made clear that this labor continues until one reaches his Lord, and that is what we have said. As for the demonstration that the good life is in Paradise: it is a life without death, wealth without poverty, health without sickness, sovereignty without cessation, and happiness without misery. Thus it is established that the good life is nothing other than that life. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾, and its explanation has already preceded. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 98–100:

God's words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾

Know that when He said before this verse, ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾, He guided them to the action by which their deeds are kept free from whisperings. So He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ There are several issues in this verse:

[Page 92]

The first issue: Satan works to cast whisperings into the heart, even against the prophets, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke [or recited], Satan threw [something] into his wish.﴾ [al-Hajj: 52].

Seeking refuge in God (al-isti'adhah) prevents Satan from casting whisperings, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember [Him], and at once they are seeing clearly.﴾ [al-A'raf: 201]. For this reason God commanded His Messenger to seek refuge at the time of recitation, so that the recitation remains protected from whisperings.

The second issue: His words ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ are addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, but the intended meaning is everyone. Since the Messenger needed to seek refuge at the time of recitation, others are more in need of it.

The third issue: The "fa" (then) in His words ﴿so seek refuge in God﴾ indicates sequence. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that seeking refuge is after reciting the Qur'an, and a group of the Companions and the Successors held this view. al-Wahidi said: This is the opinion of Abu Hurayrah, Malik, and Dawud. They said: The benefit of this is that when one recites the Qur'an, he earns a great reward; if he does not seek refuge, a whispering falls into his heart, and that whispering nullifies the reward of the recitation. But if he seeks refuge after the recitation, the whisperings are repelled and the reward remains protected from being nullified.

As for the majority of the scholars among the Companions and the Successors, they agreed that seeking refuge precedes the recitation. They said: The meaning of the verse is: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, then seek refuge; it does not mean seek refuge after the recitation. Similar to this is: when you eat, say "In the name of God"; and when you travel, prepare yourself. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], meaning: when you intend to stand up for prayer, wash. Also, since it is established that Satan cast whisperings during the Messenger's recitation, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke [or recited], Satan threw [something] into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], it is clear that God commanded the Messenger to seek refuge at the time of recitation only to repel those whisperings. This purpose is achieved only when seeking refuge is placed before the recitation.

The fourth issue: The view of Ata' is that seeking refuge is obligatory at the time of reciting the Qur'an, whether the recitation is in prayer or outside it. The rest of the jurists agreed that this is not the case, because there is no disagreement among them that if one does not seek refuge before reciting in prayer, his prayer is valid. The same applies to recitation outside prayer, but the status of recitation in prayer is more emphatic.

The fifth issue: As for the meaning of "Satan" in this verse, it is said to be Iblis, but the closer view is that it is a generic term, because all the rebellious devils have a share in whispering.

Know that when He commanded His Messenger to seek refuge from Satan, and that might give the impression that Satan has power to act upon people's bodies, God removed this illusion and explained that he has absolutely no power except over whispering. So He said: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ It appears from this that seeking refuge is beneficial only when a person's heart is aware of his own weakness, and that he cannot guard himself against Satan's whispering except by God's protection. For this reason the researchers said: There is no power to turn away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no strength for obedience to God except by God's grant of success. The entrusting that results from this understanding is what is meant by His words: ﴿and rely upon their Lord﴾.

Then He said: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: they obey him; it is said: "tawallaytuhu" means "I obeyed him," and "tawallaytu 'anhu" means "I turned away from him." ﴿And those who associate others with Him﴾: concerning the pronoun in His words "bihi" (with Him/with him), to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: it refers back to their Lord.

[Page 93]

The second: it refers back to Satan, and the meaning is "because of him." This is like when you say to a man who has spoken a word leading to disbelief: "You disbelieved because of this word," meaning on account of it. Likewise His words: ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾, meaning: on account of him and on account of his leading them to associate partners with God, they became polytheists.

So He said: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ It appears from this that seeking refuge is beneficial only when a person's heart is aware of his own weakness, and that he cannot guard himself against Satan's whispering except by God's protection. For this reason the researchers said: There is no power to turn away from disobedience to God except by God's protection, and no strength for obedience to God except by God's grant of success. The entrusting that results from this understanding is what is meant by His words: ﴿and rely upon their Lord﴾.

Then He said: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: they obey him; it is said: "tawallaytuhu" means "I obeyed him," and "tawallaytu 'anhu" means "I turned away from him." ﴿And those who associate others with Him﴾: concerning the pronoun in His words "bihi" (with Him/with him), to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: it refers back to their Lord.

[Page 93]

The second: it refers back to Satan, and the meaning is "because of him." This is like when you say to a man who has spoken a word leading to disbelief: "You disbelieved because of this word," meaning on account of it. Likewise His words: ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾, meaning: on account of him and on account of his leading them to associate partners with God, they became polytheists.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 98–100:

God's words: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him.﴾

Know that when He said before this verse, ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾, He guided them to the action by which their deeds are kept free from whisperings. So He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ There are several issues in this verse:

[Page 92]

The first issue: Satan works to cast whisperings into the heart, even against the prophets, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke [or recited], Satan threw [something] into his wish.﴾ [al-Hajj: 52].

Seeking refuge in God (al-isti'adhah) prevents Satan from casting whisperings, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember [Him], and at once they are seeing clearly.﴾ [al-A'raf: 201]. For this reason God commanded His Messenger to seek refuge at the time of recitation, so that the recitation remains protected from whisperings.

The second issue: His words ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ are addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, but the intended meaning is everyone. Since the Messenger needed to seek refuge at the time of recitation, others are more in need of it.

The third issue: The "fa" (then) in His words ﴿so seek refuge in God﴾ indicates sequence. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that seeking refuge is after reciting the Qur'an, and a group of the Companions and the Successors held this view. al-Wahidi said: This is the opinion of Abu Hurayrah, Malik, and Dawud. They said: The benefit of this is that when one recites the Qur'an, he earns a great reward; if he does not seek refuge, a whispering falls into his heart, and that whispering nullifies the reward of the recitation. But if he seeks refuge after the recitation, the whisperings are repelled and the reward remains protected from being nullified.

As for the majority of the scholars among the Companions and the Successors, they agreed that seeking refuge precedes the recitation. They said: The meaning of the verse is: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, then seek refuge; it does not mean seek refuge after the recitation. Similar to this is: when you eat, say "In the name of God"; and when you travel, prepare yourself. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿When you stand up for prayer, wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], meaning: when you intend to stand up for prayer, wash. Also, since it is established that Satan cast whisperings during the Messenger's recitation, as evidenced by God's words: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke [or recited], Satan threw [something] into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], it is clear that God commanded the Messenger to seek refuge at the time of recitation only to repel those whisperings. This purpose is achieved only when seeking refuge is placed before the recitation.

The fourth issue: The view of Ata' is that seeking refuge is obligatory at the time of reciting the Qur'an, whether the recitation is in prayer or outside it. The rest of the jurists agreed that this is not the case, because there is no disagreement among them that if one does not seek refuge before reciting in prayer, his prayer is valid. The same applies to recitation outside prayer, but the status of recitation in prayer is more emphatic.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 101–102:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are but a fabricator." Rather, most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, began with this subject in relating the doubts of those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Whenever a verse containing severity was revealed, and then a verse gentler than it was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh would say, "By Allah, Muhammad only mocks his companions: today he orders a matter, and tomorrow he forbids it. He says these things only from his own self." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed His saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾. The meaning of substitution (tabdil) is the removal of a thing while placing another in its stead. The substitution of a verse is its removal by another verse other than it, and this is its abrogation (naskh) by a different verse. His saying: ﴿and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ is an interjection that entered into the speech, and the meaning is: Allah knows best what He sends down of the abrogating and the abrogated, and of the strictness and the leniency, that is, He knows all of that in what serves the interests of the servants. This is a rebuke to the disbelievers for their saying: ﴿You are but a fabricator﴾. That is: if He is the One who knows best what He sends down, then what is wrong with them that they attribute Muhammad (ﷺ) to fabrication because of the substitution and abrogation? His saying: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾. That is: they do not know the reality of the Qur'an and the benefit of abrogation and substitution, and that this is for the interests of the servants, just as a physician orders the patient a certain draught, then after a period forbids him from it and orders him the opposite of that draught. His saying: ﴿Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord"﴾ explains the Holy Spirit, which was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. The author of al-Kashshaf said: The Holy Spirit is Jibril (peace be upon him). It is idafa (construct) to al-Quds, which is purity, as one says: Hatim al-Jud and Zayd al-Khayr, and the intended meaning is: the purified spirit, and Hatim the generous and Zayd the good. Al-Muqaddas means: purified from water. And "min" in His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to the Qur'an, that is: Jibril brought down the Qur'an from your Lord, to make firm those who believe; that is, to test them with abrogation, so that when they say about it, "It is the truth from our Lord," they are judged to have firm footing in the religion and sound certainty that Allah is Wise, so He does not do except what is wisdom and correctness. ﴿And guidance and good tidings﴾ are two objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu) conjoined with the position (mahall) of "li-yuthabbita," and the implied meaning is: as a making firm for them, and guidance and good news. Within this is an allusion to the attainment of the opposites of these attributes by others.

The second issue: We have mentioned that the view of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani is that abrogation does not occur in this Shariah. He said: The intended meaning here is, "When We substitute one verse in place of another," in the earlier books; such as when He changed the qibla from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah, the polytheists said, "You are a fabricator in this substitution." As for the rest of the exegetes, they said: abrogation does occur in this Shariah, and the discussion of it in full detail is in the other surahs.

The third issue: al-Shafiʿi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The Qur'an is not abrogated by the Sunnah. He argued for its soundness by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾. This requires that a verse does not become abrogated except by another verse. This is weak, because this indicates that He, exalted is He, substitutes a verse with another verse, and there is no indication in it that He does not substitute a verse except with a verse. Also, Jibril (peace be upon him) may descend with the Sunnah just as he descends with a verse. Also, the Sunnah may itself establish a verse. Also, this is a report of the speech of the disbelievers, so how is it valid to rely on it? And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 103–105:

[The Exalted] said: ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent lies, and it is they who are the liars.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to relate another of the doubts raised by those who denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). They used to say: Muhammad only mentions these stories and these words because he takes them from another person and learns them from him.

Scholars differed about this human being from whom the polytheists claimed the Prophet (ﷺ) learned. It was said: he is a slave of the Banu ʿAmir ibn Lu'ayy, called Yaʿish, who used to read the scriptures. It was said: he is ʿAddas, the slave of ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah. It was said: he is a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, a possessor of books, whose name was Jabr. Quraysh used to say: "The slave of the Banu al-Hadrami teaches Khadijah, and Khadijah teaches Muhammad." It was also said: there was in Mecca a Christian whose tongue was non-Arabic, named Balʿam, also called Abu Maysarah, who spoke Greek (al-Rumiyyah). It was said: he is Salman al-Farisi. In sum, there is no benefit in enumerating these names. The essential point is that the people accused him of learning these words from someone else, then displaying them as his own, while claiming that he knew them through revelation, which is a lie on his part.

Then [the Exalted] answered them, saying: ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic speech.﴾

The meaning of ilhad (inclination, deviation) linguistically is "leaning." It is said: laḥada and alḥada, when one deviates from the right course, and from this the one who deviates from the truth is called mulhid (a deviator). Hamzah and al-Kisai read yalhadūna with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', while the rest read yulhidūna with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Al-Wahidi said: the better reading is with the damma on the ya', because it is the dialect of the Qur'an, and the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with injustice﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. Ilhad may also mean "inclining," and from this one says: alḥadtu lahu laḥdan when you dig a niche in the side of a grave, inclining away from the straight; a grave is then called maḥdūd or malḥūd. From this comes the word mulḥid, because he inclined his creed away from all religions, not inclining it from one religion to another. The word ilhad in this verse has been explained according to both meanings. Al-Farra' said: "they incline," from mayl (inclination). Al-Zajjaj said: "they incline," from imalah (causing to incline), meaning: the tongue of those to whom they incline the speech is foreign.

As for His saying ﴿aʿjamī﴾ (foreign), Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili said: the root ʿ-j-m was established in Arabic speech to express concealment, obscurity, and the opposite of clarity and explanation. From it comes the expression rajulun aʿjam and imra'atun ʿajmāʾ, when they cannot express themselves clearly. ʿAjam al-dhanab (the stump of the tail) is so named because it is hidden and concealed. Al-ʿAjmāʾ is the animal, because it does not make clear what is in its mind. They also called the two prayers of Dhuhr and ʿAsr ʿajmāwayn, because the recitation in them is made silently and not aloud. As for the saying ʿajamtu al-kitab (I made the book unclear), it means "I removed its obscurity." The form afʿala can also indicate removal, as in their saying ashkaytu fulānan (I removed the complaint of so-and-so), when you remove what he complains of. This is the original meaning of this word. Then the Arabs call everyone who does not know their language or speak their tongue aʿjam and aʿjamī. Al-Farra' and Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the aʿjam is one who has an impediment in his speech even if he is an Arab, while aʿjamī and ʿajamī are one whose origin is from the ʿAjam (non-Arabs). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the aʿjam is one who does not speak clearly, whether he is of the Arabs or of the non-Arabs. Do you not see that they called Ziyad "al-Aʿjam," because there was an impediment in his speech even though he was an Arab? As for the meaning of ʿarabī (Arab) and its derivation, we have mentioned it at His saying: ﴿The Bedouins are stronger in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97]. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said regarding this verse: it is said ʿaruba lisānuhu ʿarābatan wa ʿurūbatan (his tongue became eloquent in Arabic). This is the explanation of the words of the verse.

As for establishing the way of the answer: know that it becomes clear when we say that the Qur'an was miraculous only because of the eloquence in its wording, which returns to the expression itself. It is as if it were said: suppose he learns the meanings from that foreigner. Still, the Qur'an was miraculous only because of the eloquence in its words. So even if you were truthful that Muhammad (ﷺ) learns those meanings from that man, this does not harm the purpose, since the Qur'an was miraculous for its eloquence, and what you mention does not affect that purpose.

When Allah the Exalted mentioned this answer, He followed it with a threat and a warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them.﴾ As for the explanation of our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) of this verse, it is clear. Al-Qadi said: the strongest thing said about it is that He will not guide them to the path of Paradise. Therefore He said after it: ﴿and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ The meaning is that since they abandoned faith in Allah, Allah will not guide them to Paradise, but will drive them to the Fire. Then He, the Exalted, showed that they were liars in that statement, saying: ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent lies, and it is they who are the liars.﴾ There are issues in this:

The first issue: the purpose of this is that the Exalted showed in the preceding verse that what they said, even if it were true, would not harm the purpose. Then He showed in this verse that what they said was not true, and that they lied in it. The evidence that they were liars in that statement consists of several points:

The first: they do not believe in the signs of Allah, and they are disbelievers. When this is the case, they are enemies of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the words of enemies are a kind of raving, and there is no testimony from one accused.

The second: the matter of learning cannot be accomplished in one sitting, nor is it completed in secret. Rather, learning is only completed when the teacher goes to the student over long periods and widely separated times. If this were the case, it would have become known among people that Muhammad (peace be upon him) learns sciences from so-and-so and so-and-so.

The third: the sciences present in the Qur'an are many, and learning them cannot be achieved unless the teacher is at the peak of virtue and verification. If there had existed among them a person who reached this level in teaching and verification, he would have been pointed to with fingers for verification and precision in the world. So how is it possible to acquire these lofty sciences and precious discourses from so-and-so and so-and-so?

Know that the attack on the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with such weak words indicates that the proof for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was manifest and dazzling, for the opponents were unable to attack it, and out of utter inability they turned to these weak words.

The second issue: in this verse there is a strong indication that lying is among the greatest of major sins and the most vile of abominations. The evidence for this is that the word innamā (only) indicates restriction, and the meaning is: lying and fabrication are undertaken only by one who does not believe in the signs of Allah the Exalted, and only by one who is a disbeliever, and this is a threat in the extreme.

[Page 96]

If it is said: His saying ﴿do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ is a verb (fiʿl), while His saying ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾ is a nominal sentence (ism), and conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is ugly. What is the reason for its occurrence here?

We say: the verb may be indicative of continuity or of non-continuity. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Then it seemed good to them, after they had seen the signs, to imprison him for a time﴾ [Yusuf: 35]. He mentioned it in the form of the verb, to indicate that this imprisonment would not last. Pharaoh said to Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 29]. He mentioned it in the form of the noun, to indicate permanence. Our companions said: Allah said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ [Taha: 121]. It is not permissible to say that Adam was disobedient and erring in a continuous sense, because the verbal form does not indicate continuity, while the nominal form does.

Having understood this introduction, we say: His saying ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent lies﴾ mentions this as a warning that whoever engages in lying has, as it were, entered into disbelief. Then He said: ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾, as a warning that the attribute of lying is firmly established in them, lasting and constant. This is like when you say to someone: "You lied, and you are a liar." Your saying "and you are a liar" adds an emphasis to the attribute of lying, and its meaning is: lying is your habit.

The third issue: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the liar and fabricator is the one who does not believe in the signs of Allah, and this is the case, because there is no meaning of disbelief except denying divinity and the prophethood of the prophets, and this denial includes lying and fabrication. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Does a believer ever lie?" He said: "No." Then he recited this verse. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying ﴿aʿjamī﴾ (foreign), Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili said: the root ʿ-j-m was established in Arabic speech to express concealment, obscurity, and the opposite of clarity and explanation. From it comes the expression rajulun aʿjam and imra'atun ʿajmāʾ, when they cannot express themselves clearly. ʿAjam al-dhanab (the stump of the tail) is so named because it is hidden and concealed. Al-ʿAjmāʾ is the animal, because it does not make clear what is in its mind. They also called the two prayers of Dhuhr and ʿAsr ʿajmāwayn, because the recitation in them is made silently and not aloud. As for the saying ʿajamtu al-kitab (I made the book unclear), it means "I removed its obscurity." The form afʿala can also indicate removal, as in their saying ashkaytu fulānan (I removed the complaint of so-and-so), when you remove what he complains of. This is the original meaning of this word. Then the Arabs call everyone who does not know their language or speak their tongue aʿjam and aʿjamī. Al-Farra' and Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the aʿjam is one who has an impediment in his speech even if he is an Arab, while aʿjamī and ʿajamī are one whose origin is from the ʿAjam (non-Arabs). Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: the aʿjam is one who does not speak clearly, whether he is of the Arabs or of the non-Arabs. Do you not see that they called Ziyad "al-Aʿjam," because there was an impediment in his speech even though he was an Arab? As for the meaning of ʿarabī (Arab) and its derivation, we have mentioned it at His saying: ﴿The Bedouins are stronger in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97]. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said regarding this verse: it is said ʿaruba lisānuhu ʿarābatan wa ʿurūbatan (his tongue became eloquent in Arabic). This is the explanation of the words of the verse.

As for establishing the way of the answer: know that it becomes clear when we say that the Qur'an was miraculous only because of the eloquence in its wording, which returns to the expression itself. It is as if it were said: suppose he learns the meanings from that foreigner. Still, the Qur'an was miraculous only because of the eloquence in its words. So even if you were truthful that Muhammad (ﷺ) learns those meanings from that man, this does not harm the purpose, since the Qur'an was miraculous for its eloquence, and what you mention does not affect that purpose.

When Allah the Exalted mentioned this answer, He followed it with a threat and a warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them.﴾ As for the explanation of our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) of this verse, it is clear. Al-Qadi said: the strongest thing said about it is that He will not guide them to the path of Paradise. Therefore He said after it: ﴿and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ The meaning is that since they abandoned faith in Allah, Allah will not guide them to Paradise, but will drive them to the Fire. Then He, the Exalted, showed that they were liars in that statement, saying: ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent lies, and it is they who are the liars.﴾ There are issues in this:

The first issue: the purpose of this is that the Exalted showed in the preceding verse that what they said, even if it were true, would not harm the purpose. Then He showed in this verse that what they said was not true, and that they lied in it. The evidence that they were liars in that statement consists of several points:

The first: they do not believe in the signs of Allah, and they are disbelievers. When this is the case, they are enemies of the Messenger (ﷺ), and the words of enemies are a kind of raving, and there is no testimony from one accused.

The second: the matter of learning cannot be accomplished in one sitting, nor is it completed in secret. Rather, learning is only completed when the teacher goes to the student over long periods and widely separated times. If this were the case, it would have become known among people that Muhammad (peace be upon him) learns sciences from so-and-so and so-and-so.

The third: the sciences present in the Qur'an are many, and learning them cannot be achieved unless the teacher is at the peak of virtue and verification. If there had existed among them a person who reached this level in teaching and verification, he would have been pointed to with fingers for verification and precision in the world. So how is it possible to acquire these lofty sciences and precious discourses from so-and-so and so-and-so?

Know that the attack on the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with such weak words indicates that the proof for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was manifest and dazzling, for the opponents were unable to attack it, and out of utter inability they turned to these weak words.

The second issue: in this verse there is a strong indication that lying is among the greatest of major sins and the most vile of abominations. The evidence for this is that the word innamā (only) indicates restriction, and the meaning is: lying and fabrication are undertaken only by one who does not believe in the signs of Allah the Exalted, and only by one who is a disbeliever, and this is a threat in the extreme.

[Page 96]

If it is said: His saying ﴿do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ is a verb (fiʿl), while His saying ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾ is a nominal sentence (ism), and conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is ugly. What is the reason for its occurrence here?

We say: the verb may be indicative of continuity or of non-continuity. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Then it seemed good to them, after they had seen the signs, to imprison him for a time﴾ [Yusuf: 35]. He mentioned it in the form of the verb, to indicate that this imprisonment would not last. Pharaoh said to Moses (peace be upon him): ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 29]. He mentioned it in the form of the noun, to indicate permanence. Our companions said: Allah said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ [Taha: 121]. It is not permissible to say that Adam was disobedient and erring in a continuous sense, because the verbal form does not indicate continuity, while the nominal form does.

Having understood this introduction, we say: His saying ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent lies﴾ mentions this as a warning that whoever engages in lying has, as it were, entered into disbelief. Then He said: ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾, as a warning that the attribute of lying is firmly established in them, lasting and constant. This is like when you say to someone: "You lied, and you are a liar." Your saying "and you are a liar" adds an emphasis to the attribute of lying, and its meaning is: lying is your habit.

The third issue: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the liar and fabricator is the one who does not believe in the signs of Allah, and this is the case, because there is no meaning of disbelief except denying divinity and the prophethood of the prophets, and this denial includes lying and fabrication. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Does a believer ever lie?" He said: "No." Then he recited this verse. And Allah knows best.

It was said: he is a slave of the Banu ʿAmir ibn Lu'ayy, called Yaʿish, who used to read the scriptures. It was said: he is ʿAddas, the slave of ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah. It was said: he is a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, a possessor of books, whose name was Jabr. Quraysh used to say: "The slave of the Banu al-Hadrami teaches Khadijah, and Khadijah teaches Muhammad." It was also said: there was in Mecca a Christian whose tongue was non-Arabic, named Balʿam, also called Abu Maysarah, who spoke Greek (al-Rumiyyah). It was said: he is Salman al-Farisi. In sum, there is no benefit in enumerating these names. The essential point is that the people accused him of learning these words from someone else, then displaying them as his own, while claiming that he knew them through revelation, which is a lie on his part.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 106–110 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith—but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing and sight Allah has sealed, and they are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾

Know that when Allah magnified the threat against the disbelievers, He mentioned in this verse a detailed explanation of who disbelieves with his tongue but not his heart, and who disbelieves with both his tongue and his heart together. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is not mentioned. For this reason the exegetes differed and offered several opinions:

The first: that ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ is a *badal* (substitute or apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾. The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve in Allah after their belief fabricate lies," and He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he is not included in the ruling of fabrication. On this reading, His saying ﴿and those are the liars﴾ is a *i'tiraD* (parenthetical interjection) that falls between the substitute and what it substitutes.

The second: it is also permissible that it be a *badal* from the predicate, which is "the liars." The meaning is: "And those are the ones who disbelieved in Allah after their belief."

The third: it is permissible that it be in the accusative of dispraise (*nasb 'ala al-dhamm*). The meaning is: "And those are the liars; I mean, those who disbelieved in Allah after their belief." This is the best of the opinions in my view and the furthest from strained interpretation.

The fourth: that His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a conditional *mubtada'* (*shart*), and its response is omitted, because the response of the condition mentioned after it indicates its response. It is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, upon them is wrath from Allah, except one who is compelled"; then ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah﴾.

* * *

**The second issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." It is narrated that some people of Makkah were tested and apostatized from Islam after entering it. Among them were those who were compelled and uttered the word of disbelief with their tongues, while in their hearts they were steadfast in faith. Among them were Ammar, his parents Yasir and Sumayyah, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and Salim. They were tortured. As for Sumayyah, it is said that she was tied between two camels and pierced in her private parts with a spear, and they said: "You embraced Islam only for the sake of men." She was killed, and Yasir was killed; they were the first two killed in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue under compulsion. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, Ammar has disbelieved." He said: "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from the crown of his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and saying: "What is the matter with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said." Among them was Jabr, the client of al-Hadrami, whose master compelled him, so he disbelieved; then his master embraced Islam, and he embraced Islam too, and their Islam was good, and they migrated.

* * *

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿except one who is compelled﴾ is not an exception (*istithna'*) in the strict sense, because the one who is compelled is not a disbeliever, so it is not correct to make it an exception from the disbelievers. Rather, since what appeared from him after belief is like what appears from a disbeliever willingly, this exception is valid because of this resemblance (*mushakalah*).

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Here it is necessary to explain the compulsion that makes it permissible to utter the word of disbelief: it is that the one compelling him inflicts a punishment he cannot bear, such as threatening him with death, or severe beating and strong torment. Mujahid said: "The first seven to openly profess Islam were: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar and Sumayyah. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), Abu Talib protected him. As for Abu Bakr, his people protected him. The others were seized, dressed in iron armor, and then made to sit in the sun, so that they suffered greatly from the heat of the iron and the sun. Abu Jahl came to them, reviling and rebuking them and insulting Sumayyah; then he thrust the spear into her private parts. The others said: 'They did not harm them except Bilal, for they began torturing him, and he kept saying: One, One, until they grew weary. Then they bound him and put a rope of palm fiber around his neck, and handed him over to their children, who dragged him about until they grew tired of him and left him.'" Ammar said: "All of us spoke what they wanted except Bilal, whose soul became contemptible to him, so they left him." Khabbab said: "They lit a fire for me, and nothing extinguished it except the fat of my back."

* * *

**The fifth issue:** They agreed that when uttering the word of disbelief, he must cleanse his heart of approval of it, and restrict himself to allusions (*ta'ridat*), such as saying: "Muhammad is a liar," meaning among the disbelievers, or meaning by it another Muhammad, or uttering it in the form of a question meaning denial. Here there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** If the one compelling him preoccupies him from bringing this intention to mind, or because his fear is so great that the remembrance of this intention has left his heart, he is blameworthy, but Allah's pardon is hoped for.

**The second discussion:** If the compeller constricts the matter upon him, explains to him all the categories of allusions, and demands that he state explicitly that he did not intend any of them but only that meaning, then here it becomes necessary either to commit a lie or to expose himself to being killed. Some people said: lying is permitted for him here. Others said: it is not permitted for him, and this is what al-Qadi chose. He said: "Lying is ugly only because it is a lie, so it must be ugly in every state. If it were permissible to depart from what is ugly to preserve some benefits, it would not prevent Allah from doing a lie to preserve some benefits. In that case, no reliance could be placed on Allah's promise or His threat, because of the possibility that He did that lie to preserve some benefit that none knows but Allah the Exalted."

* * *

**The sixth issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter the word of disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not say: "You did wrongly," but rather magnified him for it. This shows that it is not obligatory to utter the word of disbelief.

The second: what is related that Musaylimah the Liar seized two men. He said to one of them: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "He is the Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "You too." So he released him. Then he said to the other: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "I am deaf." He repeated this to him three times, and each time he gave the same answer, so he killed him. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "As for the first, he took the concession of Allah. As for the second, he declared the truth openly, so good tidings to him." The argument from this report is in two respects:

The first: he called uttering the word of disbelief a concession (*rukhsah*).

The second: he magnified the state of the one who refrained from it until he was killed.

The third: giving up the soul in establishing the truth is more difficult, so it must be more rewarded, because of his saying (peace be upon him): "The most excellent acts of worship are the most arduous," that is, the most difficult.

The fourth: the one who refrained from the word of disbelief purified his heart and tongue from disbelief. As for the one who uttered it, even if his heart is pure of it, his tongue has outwardly been stained with that wicked word. So the state of the first must be more excellent. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Know that compulsion has degrees.

The first degree: the compelled act becomes obligatory, such as when he is compelled to drink wine, eat pork, or eat carrion. If he is compelled to do it at the point of a sword, then here eating is obligatory, because preserving the soul from perishing is obligatory, and there is no way to it in this case except by this eating. There is no harm to any living being in this eating, nor any disrespect to the right of Allah the Exalted, so it must be obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿and do not throw yourselves into destruction﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195].

The second degree: that act becomes permissible but not obligatory. An example is when he is compelled to utter the word of disbelief. Here it is permissible for him, but not obligatory, as we have established.

The third degree: it is neither obligatory nor permissible, but forbidden. This is like when a person compels another to kill a third person, or to cut off one of his limbs. Here the act remains under its original prohibition. Does retaliation (*qisas*) fall from the compelled person or not? Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in one of his two opinions: retaliation is required. The evidence for this is two-fold:

The first: he killed him intentionally and aggressively, so retaliation is required of him, based on His saying: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 178].

The second: we are agreed that if the compelled person intends to kill him, it is lawful for him to repel him from himself even by killing. So if the mere expectation of his advancing to kill makes his blood forfeit, then when killing actually proceeds from him, his blood becoming forfeit is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The eighth issue:** Among acts are those that accept compulsion, such as killing and uttering the word of disbelief, and among them are those that do not accept compulsion. It has been said that this is fornication (*zina*), because compulsion produces intense fear, and that prevents the organ from erection. So whenever fornication occurs, it is known that it happened by choice and not by way of compulsion.

* * *

**The ninth issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the divorce of one who is compelled does not take effect. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it takes effect. Al-Shafi'i's proof is His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 256]. The meaning cannot be the negation of its essence, because its essence exists, so it must be understood as the negation of its effects. The meaning is: it has no effect and no consideration is given to it. Also His saying (peace be upon him): "My Ummah is pardoned for error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do." Also His saying (peace be upon him): "There is no divorce in *ighlaq*," that is, in compulsion. If they say: he divorced her, then it falls under His saying: ﴿And if he divorces her, then she is not lawful to him﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 230]. The answer is: since the proofs conflict, what was the case must remain as it was, which is our position. And Allah knows best.

**The tenth issue:** His saying ﴿while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ indicates that the locus of faith is the heart. What has the heart as its locus is either belief (*i'tiqad*) or the speech of the soul (*kalam al-nafs*). So faith must be an expression either of knowledge (*ma'rifah*) or of assent through the speech of the soul. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, opens it and widens it to accept disbelief.
