Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 106–110 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith—but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing and sight Allah has sealed, and they are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾

Know that when Allah magnified the threat against the disbelievers, He mentioned in this verse a detailed explanation of who disbelieves with his tongue but not his heart, and who disbelieves with both his tongue and his heart together. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is not mentioned. For this reason the exegetes differed and offered several opinions:

The first: that ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ is a *badal* (substitute or apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾. The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve in Allah after their belief fabricate lies," and He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he is not included in the ruling of fabrication. On this reading, His saying ﴿and those are the liars﴾ is a *i'tiraD* (parenthetical interjection) that falls between the substitute and what it substitutes.

The second: it is also permissible that it be a *badal* from the predicate, which is "the liars." The meaning is: "And those are the ones who disbelieved in Allah after their belief."

The third: it is permissible that it be in the accusative of dispraise (*nasb 'ala al-dhamm*). The meaning is: "And those are the liars; I mean, those who disbelieved in Allah after their belief." This is the best of the opinions in my view and the furthest from strained interpretation.

The fourth: that His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a conditional *mubtada'* (*shart*), and its response is omitted, because the response of the condition mentioned after it indicates its response. It is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, upon them is wrath from Allah, except one who is compelled"; then ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah﴾.

* * *

**The second issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." It is narrated that some people of Makkah were tested and apostatized from Islam after entering it. Among them were those who were compelled and uttered the word of disbelief with their tongues, while in their hearts they were steadfast in faith. Among them were Ammar, his parents Yasir and Sumayyah, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and Salim. They were tortured. As for Sumayyah, it is said that she was tied between two camels and pierced in her private parts with a spear, and they said: "You embraced Islam only for the sake of men." She was killed, and Yasir was killed; they were the first two killed in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue under compulsion. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, Ammar has disbelieved." He said: "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from the crown of his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and saying: "What is the matter with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said." Among them was Jabr, the client of al-Hadrami, whose master compelled him, so he disbelieved; then his master embraced Islam, and he embraced Islam too, and their Islam was good, and they migrated.

* * *

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿except one who is compelled﴾ is not an exception (*istithna'*) in the strict sense, because the one who is compelled is not a disbeliever, so it is not correct to make it an exception from the disbelievers. Rather, since what appeared from him after belief is like what appears from a disbeliever willingly, this exception is valid because of this resemblance (*mushakalah*).

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Here it is necessary to explain the compulsion that makes it permissible to utter the word of disbelief: it is that the one compelling him inflicts a punishment he cannot bear, such as threatening him with death, or severe beating and strong torment. Mujahid said: "The first seven to openly profess Islam were: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar and Sumayyah. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), Abu Talib protected him. As for Abu Bakr, his people protected him. The others were seized, dressed in iron armor, and then made to sit in the sun, so that they suffered greatly from the heat of the iron and the sun. Abu Jahl came to them, reviling and rebuking them and insulting Sumayyah; then he thrust the spear into her private parts. The others said: 'They did not harm them except Bilal, for they began torturing him, and he kept saying: One, One, until they grew weary. Then they bound him and put a rope of palm fiber around his neck, and handed him over to their children, who dragged him about until they grew tired of him and left him.'" Ammar said: "All of us spoke what they wanted except Bilal, whose soul became contemptible to him, so they left him." Khabbab said: "They lit a fire for me, and nothing extinguished it except the fat of my back."

* * *

**The fifth issue:** They agreed that when uttering the word of disbelief, he must cleanse his heart of approval of it, and restrict himself to allusions (*ta'ridat*), such as saying: "Muhammad is a liar," meaning among the disbelievers, or meaning by it another Muhammad, or uttering it in the form of a question meaning denial. Here there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** If the one compelling him preoccupies him from bringing this intention to mind, or because his fear is so great that the remembrance of this intention has left his heart, he is blameworthy, but Allah's pardon is hoped for.

**The second discussion:** If the compeller constricts the matter upon him, explains to him all the categories of allusions, and demands that he state explicitly that he did not intend any of them but only that meaning, then here it becomes necessary either to commit a lie or to expose himself to being killed. Some people said: lying is permitted for him here. Others said: it is not permitted for him, and this is what al-Qadi chose. He said: "Lying is ugly only because it is a lie, so it must be ugly in every state. If it were permissible to depart from what is ugly to preserve some benefits, it would not prevent Allah from doing a lie to preserve some benefits. In that case, no reliance could be placed on Allah's promise or His threat, because of the possibility that He did that lie to preserve some benefit that none knows but Allah the Exalted."

* * *

**The sixth issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter the word of disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not say: "You did wrongly," but rather magnified him for it. This shows that it is not obligatory to utter the word of disbelief.

The second: what is related that Musaylimah the Liar seized two men. He said to one of them: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "He is the Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "You too." So he released him. Then he said to the other: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "I am deaf." He repeated this to him three times, and each time he gave the same answer, so he killed him. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "As for the first, he took the concession of Allah. As for the second, he declared the truth openly, so good tidings to him." The argument from this report is in two respects:

The first: he called uttering the word of disbelief a concession (*rukhsah*).

The second: he magnified the state of the one who refrained from it until he was killed.

The third: giving up the soul in establishing the truth is more difficult, so it must be more rewarded, because of his saying (peace be upon him): "The most excellent acts of worship are the most arduous," that is, the most difficult.

The fourth: the one who refrained from the word of disbelief purified his heart and tongue from disbelief. As for the one who uttered it, even if his heart is pure of it, his tongue has outwardly been stained with that wicked word. So the state of the first must be more excellent. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Know that compulsion has degrees.

The first degree: the compelled act becomes obligatory, such as when he is compelled to drink wine, eat pork, or eat carrion. If he is compelled to do it at the point of a sword, then here eating is obligatory, because preserving the soul from perishing is obligatory, and there is no way to it in this case except by this eating. There is no harm to any living being in this eating, nor any disrespect to the right of Allah the Exalted, so it must be obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿and do not throw yourselves into destruction﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195].

The second degree: that act becomes permissible but not obligatory. An example is when he is compelled to utter the word of disbelief. Here it is permissible for him, but not obligatory, as we have established.

The third degree: it is neither obligatory nor permissible, but forbidden. This is like when a person compels another to kill a third person, or to cut off one of his limbs. Here the act remains under its original prohibition. Does retaliation (*qisas*) fall from the compelled person or not? Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in one of his two opinions: retaliation is required. The evidence for this is two-fold:

The first: he killed him intentionally and aggressively, so retaliation is required of him, based on His saying: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 178].

The second: we are agreed that if the compelled person intends to kill him, it is lawful for him to repel him from himself even by killing. So if the mere expectation of his advancing to kill makes his blood forfeit, then when killing actually proceeds from him, his blood becoming forfeit is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The eighth issue:** Among acts are those that accept compulsion, such as killing and uttering the word of disbelief, and among them are those that do not accept compulsion. It has been said that this is fornication (*zina*), because compulsion produces intense fear, and that prevents the organ from erection. So whenever fornication occurs, it is known that it happened by choice and not by way of compulsion.

* * *

**The ninth issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the divorce of one who is compelled does not take effect. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it takes effect. Al-Shafi'i's proof is His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 256]. The meaning cannot be the negation of its essence, because its essence exists, so it must be understood as the negation of its effects. The meaning is: it has no effect and no consideration is given to it. Also His saying (peace be upon him): "My Ummah is pardoned for error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do." Also His saying (peace be upon him): "There is no divorce in *ighlaq*," that is, in compulsion. If they say: he divorced her, then it falls under His saying: ﴿And if he divorces her, then she is not lawful to him﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 230]. The answer is: since the proofs conflict, what was the case must remain as it was, which is our position. And Allah knows best.

**The tenth issue:** His saying ﴿while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ indicates that the locus of faith is the heart. What has the heart as its locus is either belief (*i'tiqad*) or the speech of the soul (*kalam al-nafs*). So faith must be an expression either of knowledge (*ma'rifah*) or of assent through the speech of the soul. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, opens it and widens it to accept disbelief. The word ﴿breast (*sadran*)﴾ is in the accusative as the object of ﴿opens (*sharaha*)﴾. The implied construction is: "but whoever opens his breast to disbelief." He omitted the pronoun because it would not be ambiguous with the breast of another, since no human can open the breast of another. So it is an indefinite noun used to mean a definite one.

Then He said: ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah﴾. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted has decreed punishment upon them. Then He described that punishment, saying: ﴿and for them is a great punishment.﴾

* * *

* * *

The first: that ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ is a *badal* (substitute or apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾. The second: it is also permissible that it be a *badal* from the predicate, which is "the liars." The meaning is: "And those are the ones who disbelieved in Allah after their belief."

Then He said: ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah﴾. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted has decreed punishment upon them. Then He described that punishment, saying: ﴿and for them is a great punishment.﴾

ثم قال تعالى: ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهُمُ اسْتَحَبُّوا الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا عَلى الآخِرَةِ﴾ أي: رجّحوا الدنيا على الآخرة. والمعنى: أنّ ذلك الارتداد وذلك الإقدام على الكفر كان لأجل أنه تعالى ما هداهم إلى الإيمان، وما عصمهم عن الكفر. قال القاضي: المراد أنّ الله لا يهديهم إلى الجنة. فيُقال له: هذا ضعيف، لأنّ قوله: ﴿وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ معطوف على قوله: ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهُمُ اسْتَحَبُّوا الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا عَلى الآخِرَةِ﴾، فوجب أن يكون قوله: ﴿وأنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ علةً وسببًا موجبًا لإقدامهم على ذلك الارتداد، وعدم الهداية يوم القيامة إلى الجنة ليس سببًا لذلك الارتداد، ولا علةً له، بل مسبَّبًا عنه ومعلولًا له، فبطل هذا التأويل. ثم أكّد بيان أنه تعالى صرفهم عن الإيمان فقال: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ طَبَعَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وسَمْعِهِمْ وأبْصارِهِمْ﴾. قال القاضي: الطبع ليس يمنع من الإيمان، ويدل عليه وجوه:

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verses 106–110 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith—but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing and sight Allah has sealed, and they are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾

Know that when Allah magnified the threat against the disbelievers, He mentioned in this verse a detailed explanation of who disbelieves with his tongue but not his heart, and who disbelieves with both his tongue and his heart together. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is not mentioned. For this reason the exegetes differed and offered several opinions:

The first: that ﴿whoever disbelieves﴾ is a *badal* (substitute or apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾. The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve in Allah after their belief fabricate lies," and He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he is not included in the ruling of fabrication. On this reading, His saying ﴿and those are the liars﴾ is a *i'tiraD* (parenthetical interjection) that falls between the substitute and what it substitutes.

The second: it is also permissible that it be a *badal* from the predicate, which is "the liars." The meaning is: "And those are the ones who disbelieved in Allah after their belief."

The third: it is permissible that it be in the accusative of dispraise (*nasb 'ala al-dhamm*). The meaning is: "And those are the liars; I mean, those who disbelieved in Allah after their belief." This is the best of the opinions in my view and the furthest from strained interpretation.

The fourth: that His saying ﴿whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾ is a conditional *mubtada'* (*shart*), and its response is omitted, because the response of the condition mentioned after it indicates its response. It is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, upon them is wrath from Allah, except one who is compelled"; then ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah﴾.

* * *

**The second issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." It is narrated that some people of Makkah were tested and apostatized from Islam after entering it. Among them were those who were compelled and uttered the word of disbelief with their tongues, while in their hearts they were steadfast in faith. Among them were Ammar, his parents Yasir and Sumayyah, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and Salim. They were tortured. As for Sumayyah, it is said that she was tied between two camels and pierced in her private parts with a spear, and they said: "You embraced Islam only for the sake of men." She was killed, and Yasir was killed; they were the first two killed in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue under compulsion. It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, Ammar has disbelieved." He said: "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from the crown of his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and saying: "What is the matter with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said." Among them was Jabr, the client of al-Hadrami, whose master compelled him, so he disbelieved; then his master embraced Islam, and he embraced Islam too, and their Islam was good, and they migrated.

* * *

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿except one who is compelled﴾ is not an exception (*istithna'*) in the strict sense, because the one who is compelled is not a disbeliever, so it is not correct to make it an exception from the disbelievers. Rather, since what appeared from him after belief is like what appears from a disbeliever willingly, this exception is valid because of this resemblance (*mushakalah*).

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Here it is necessary to explain the compulsion that makes it permissible to utter the word of disbelief: it is that the one compelling him inflicts a punishment he cannot bear, such as threatening him with death, or severe beating and strong torment. Mujahid said: "The first seven to openly profess Islam were: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, Khabbab, Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar and Sumayyah. As for the Messenger (peace be upon him), Abu Talib protected him. As for Abu Bakr, his people protected him. The others were seized, dressed in iron armor, and then made to sit in the sun, so that they suffered greatly from the heat of the iron and the sun. Abu Jahl came to them, reviling and rebuking them and insulting Sumayyah; then he thrust the spear into her private parts. The others said: 'They did not harm them except Bilal, for they began torturing him, and he kept saying: One, One, until they grew weary. Then they bound him and put a rope of palm fiber around his neck, and handed him over to their children, who dragged him about until they grew tired of him and left him.'" Ammar said: "All of us spoke what they wanted except Bilal, whose soul became contemptible to him, so they left him." Khabbab said: "They lit a fire for me, and nothing extinguished it except the fat of my back."

* * *

**The fifth issue:** They agreed that when uttering the word of disbelief, he must cleanse his heart of approval of it, and restrict himself to allusions (*ta'ridat*), such as saying: "Muhammad is a liar," meaning among the disbelievers, or meaning by it another Muhammad, or uttering it in the form of a question meaning denial. Here there are two discussions:

**The first discussion:** If the one compelling him preoccupies him from bringing this intention to mind, or because his fear is so great that the remembrance of this intention has left his heart, he is blameworthy, but Allah's pardon is hoped for.

**The second discussion:** If the compeller constricts the matter upon him, explains to him all the categories of allusions, and demands that he state explicitly that he did not intend any of them but only that meaning, then here it becomes necessary either to commit a lie or to expose himself to being killed. Some people said: lying is permitted for him here. Others said: it is not permitted for him, and this is what al-Qadi chose. He said: "Lying is ugly only because it is a lie, so it must be ugly in every state. If it were permissible to depart from what is ugly to preserve some benefits, it would not prevent Allah from doing a lie to preserve some benefits. In that case, no reliance could be placed on Allah's promise or His threat, because of the possibility that He did that lie to preserve some benefit that none knows but Allah the Exalted."

* * *

**The sixth issue:** They agreed that it is not obligatory for him to utter the word of disbelief. Several proofs indicate this:

The first: we have related that Bilal endured that torture and used to say: "One, One." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not say: "You did wrongly," but rather magnified him for it. This shows that it is not obligatory to utter the word of disbelief.

The second: what is related that Musaylimah the Liar seized two men. He said to one of them: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "He is the Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "You too." So he released him. Then he said to the other: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "I am deaf." He repeated this to him three times, and each time he gave the same answer, so he killed him. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "As for the first, he took the concession of Allah. As for the second, he declared the truth openly, so good tidings to him." The argument from this report is in two respects:

The first: he called uttering the word of disbelief a concession (*rukhsah*).

The second: he magnified the state of the one who refrained from it until he was killed.

The third: giving up the soul in establishing the truth is more difficult, so it must be more rewarded, because of his saying (peace be upon him): "The most excellent acts of worship are the most arduous," that is, the most difficult.

The fourth: the one who refrained from the word of disbelief purified his heart and tongue from disbelief. As for the one who uttered it, even if his heart is pure of it, his tongue has outwardly been stained with that wicked word. So the state of the first must be more excellent. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Know that compulsion has degrees.

The first degree: the compelled act becomes obligatory, such as when he is compelled to drink wine, eat pork, or eat carrion. If he is compelled to do it at the point of a sword, then here eating is obligatory, because preserving the soul from perishing is obligatory, and there is no way to it in this case except by this eating. There is no harm to any living being in this eating, nor any disrespect to the right of Allah the Exalted, so it must be obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿and do not throw yourselves into destruction﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195].

The second degree: that act becomes permissible but not obligatory. An example is when he is compelled to utter the word of disbelief. Here it is permissible for him, but not obligatory, as we have established.

The third degree: it is neither obligatory nor permissible, but forbidden. This is like when a person compels another to kill a third person, or to cut off one of his limbs. Here the act remains under its original prohibition. Does retaliation (*qisas*) fall from the compelled person or not? Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said in one of his two opinions: retaliation is required. The evidence for this is two-fold:

The first: he killed him intentionally and aggressively, so retaliation is required of him, based on His saying: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 178].

The second: we are agreed that if the compelled person intends to kill him, it is lawful for him to repel him from himself even by killing. So if the mere expectation of his advancing to kill makes his blood forfeit, then when killing actually proceeds from him, his blood becoming forfeit is more fitting. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The eighth issue:** Among acts are those that accept compulsion, such as killing and uttering the word of disbelief, and among them are those that do not accept compulsion. It has been said that this is fornication (*zina*), because compulsion produces intense fear, and that prevents the organ from erection. So whenever fornication occurs, it is known that it happened by choice and not by way of compulsion.

* * *

**The ninth issue:** Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the divorce of one who is compelled does not take effect. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it takes effect. Al-Shafi'i's proof is His saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 256]. The meaning cannot be the negation of its essence, because its essence exists, so it must be understood as the negation of its effects. The meaning is: it has no effect and no consideration is given to it. Also His saying (peace be upon him): "My Ummah is pardoned for error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do." Also His saying (peace be upon him): "There is no divorce in *ighlaq*," that is, in compulsion. If they say: he divorced her, then it falls under His saying: ﴿And if he divorces her, then she is not lawful to him﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 230]. The answer is: since the proofs conflict, what was the case must remain as it was, which is our position. And Allah knows best.

**The tenth issue:** His saying ﴿while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ indicates that the locus of faith is the heart. What has the heart as its locus is either belief (*i'tiqad*) or the speech of the soul (*kalam al-nafs*). So faith must be an expression either of knowledge (*ma'rifah*) or of assent through the speech of the soul. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, opens it and widens it to accept disbelief. The word ﴿breast (*sadran*)﴾ is in the accusative as the object of ﴿opens (*sharaha*)﴾. The implied construction is: "but whoever opens his breast to disbelief." He omitted the pronoun because it would not be ambiguous with the breast of another, since no human can open the breast of another. So it is an indefinite noun used to mean a definite one.

Then He said: ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah﴾. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted has decreed punishment upon them. Then He described that punishment, saying: ﴿and for them is a great punishment.﴾

* * *

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then strove and endured — indeed your Lord, after that, is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ ﴿on the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself, and every soul will be paid in full what it has done, and they will not be wronged﴾.

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: When He, may He be exalted, mentioned in the preceding verse the state of one who disbelieves in Allah after his faith, and the state of one who is compelled to disbelief, mentioning by reason of fear the utterance of disbelief, and the state of one who did not utter it, He mentioned after that the state of one who emigrated after being tried, saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried﴾.

Second issue: Ibn ʿAmir recited "fatanū" with a fatha on the fa', attributing the verb to the agent, while the rest recited it with a damma on the fa', in the passive form (fiʿl mā lam yusamma fāʿiluh, the passive voice). As for the reading of the first, there are several points:

The first: that the intended meaning is that the leaders of the polytheists, who were those who harmed the poor Muslims, if they repented, emigrated and endured, then Allah accepts their repentance.

The second: that fatana and aftana have the same meaning, just as it is said that māna and amana have the same meaning.

The third: that those weak ones, when they uttered the word of disbelief by way of taqiyya (dissimulation),

Page 101
it is as if they had tried themselves (fatanū anfusahum), and this was made a trial only because the concession to utter the word of disbelief had not yet been revealed at that time. As for the reading with the passive verb, it is evident: those who were tried are the oppressed whom the powerful polytheists compelled to apostasy and to turning back from faith. So He, may He be exalted, made clear that if they emigrated, strove and endured, Allah, may He be exalted, will forgive them their uttering the word of disbelief.

Third issue: His saying: ﴿after they had been tried﴾ may mean that they were tormented; it may mean that they were made to fear torment; and it may mean that those Muslims apostatized. Al-Hasan said: These who emigrated from among the believers were in Mecca; a trial befell them and they apostatized, and doubted the Messenger ﷺ. Then they embraced Islam again and emigrated, and this verse was revealed concerning them. It was also said: It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, who apostatized; then on the day of the Conquest the Prophet ﷺ ordered his killing, but ʿUthman sought protection for him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted him protection; then he embraced Islam and his Islam was good. This report is only valid if we consider this sura to be Medinan, or consider this verse from it to be Medinan. It may also be that the intended meaning is that those weak tormented ones uttered the word of disbelief by way of taqiyya. So His saying ﴿after they had been tried﴾ admits each of these four possibilities, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates a specific one.

Having known this, we say: If this verse was revealed concerning one who manifested disbelief, then the meaning is that this is something for which there is no sin, and his state, if he emigrates, strives and endures, is like the state of one who was not compelled. If it was revealed concerning one who apostatized, then the meaning is that repentance and the performance of what is obligatory upon him removes that punishment, and he attains forgiveness and mercy. The pronoun in His saying ﴿after that﴾ returns to the deeds mentioned before, namely emigration, striving and endurance.

As for His saying: ﴿on the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

First discussion: Al-Zajjaj said: "Yawma" (on the day) is in the accusative in two ways:

One of them: that the meaning is: ﴿Indeed your Lord, after that, is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ ﴿on the Day when﴾, meaning: He gives mercy and forgiveness on that Day, on which man's need for mercy and forgiveness is greatest.

The second: that the estimate is: "And remind them, or mention the day of such and such," because the sense of the Qur'an is magnificence, warning and reminder.

Second discussion: Someone may say: a soul does not have another soul; so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿every soul will come pleading for itself﴾?

The answer: "nafs" may be used to mean the body of a living being, and may be used to mean the essence and reality of a thing. So the first "nafs" is the corpse and body, and the second is its very self and essence. It is as if it were said: on the day when every person comes pleading for his own self, not concerned with the affair of another. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿For every one of them on that Day there will be an affair that will occupy him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 37]. It is related from some of them: Hell will exhale a breath such that no angel brought near and no prophet sent will remain but he will fall upon his knees saying: "O Lord, myself, myself," until even Abraham the Friend (ʿalayhi al-salam) will do so. The meaning of "pleading for it" is making excuse for it, like their saying: ﴿They led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], and their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-Anʿam: 23].

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and every soul will be paid in full what it has done﴾. There is an ellipsis in it; the meaning is: every soul will be paid the recompense of what it has done, without diminution or reduction. As for His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, al-Wahidi said: its meaning is that they will not be deprived (of their deeds). Al-Qadi said: this verse is among the strongest that indicate what we hold concerning the threat (waʿid), because it indicates that He, may He be exalted, delivers to each one his right without any reduction; and if He, may He be exalted, removed the punishment of the sinner by means of intercession, that would not be correct.

The answer: There is no dispute that the apparent sense of the general expressions supports your view, but our position is that adhering to the apparent sense of general expressions does not yield certainty. Moreover, the apparent sense of the threat is opposed by the apparent sense of the promise. Then we explained in the sura of al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], that the side of promise outweighs the side of threat in many respects. And Allah knows best.

The Almighty said: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town that was secure and at rest, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, yet it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues (masāʾil, sing. masʾalah, "questions"):

The first issue: Know that when Allah threatened the disbelievers with a severe warning of the Hereafter, He also threatened them with the calamities of this world, namely falling into hunger and fear, as He mentions in this verse.

The second issue: A parable (mathal) may be coined with a thing described by a specific attribute, whether that thing exists or does not exist. It may also be coined with a specific existing thing. So this town by which Allah coined this parable may be a hypothetical thing, or it may be a specific town. On the second assumption, that town may be Makkah or another. Most of the exegetes (mufassirūn) hold that it is Makkah, but the closer view is that it is other than Makkah, because it is given as a parable for Makkah, and the parable of Makkah must be other than Makkah.

The third issue: Allah mentioned attributes for this town:

The first attribute: that it was secure (āminah), meaning possessing security, such that its people were not raided, as He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 67]. The matter in Makkah was like this, because the Arabs used to raid one another, but as for the people of Makkah, they were the people of Allah's sanctuary, and the Arabs used to revere them and single them out with honour and esteem.

Know that it is permissible to describe the town with security, even though that security belongs to its people, because it is the place of security and its container. Times and places are described by what inhabits them, as one says: "pleasant," "hot," and "cold."

The second attribute: His saying ﴿at rest (muṭmaʾinnah)﴾. Al-Wāḥidī said: its meaning is that it is settled and still, so its people do not need to move away from it out of fear or hardship. I say: if what is meant by its being at rest is that its people do not need to move away from it because of fear, then this is the meaning of its being secure. And if what is meant is that they do not need to move away from it because of hardship, then this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿its provision comes to it abundantly from every place﴾. On both interpretations there is repetition.

The answer: the wise have said:

Three things have no end: security, health, and sufficiency.

His saying ﴿secure﴾ points to security, and His saying ﴿at rest﴾ points to health, because when the air of that land suited their temperaments, they were at ease with it and settled in it. His saying ﴿its provision comes to it abundantly from every place﴾ points to sufficiency. The exegetes said: the reason for His saying ﴿from every place﴾ is the answer to the supplication of Ibrāhīm (ʿalayhi al-salām), which is His saying: ﴿So make hearts from among people incline toward them and provide them with fruits﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 37].

Then, when Allah described the town with these three attributes, He said: ﴿so it denied the favours of Allah.﴾ The word al-anʿum (favours) is the plural ofniʿmah (favour), like ashadd and shiddah. I say here there is a question: al-anʿum is a plural of paucity (jamʿ qillah), so the meaning would be that the people of that town denied a few kinds of favours, and so Allah punished them. The fitting expression would have been: they denied great favours of Allah and so deserved punishment. What is the reason for mentioning the plural of paucity?

The answer: The intent is to alert to the higher by means of the lower, that is: since denying a few favours necessitated punishment, denying many favours is more deserving of necessitating punishment. This is like the people of Makkah, for they were in security, tranquillity, and abundance, then Allah bestowed upon them the great favour, namely Muḥammad (ﷺ), but they denied him and went to extremes in harming him, so Allah surely imposed affliction upon them. The exegetes said: Allah punished them with hunger for seven years, until they ate carrion, bones, ʿilhiz, and qadd (dried hide). As for fear, the Prophet (ﷺ) used to send expeditions (sarāyā) against them, and they would raid them.

It is reported that Ibn al-Rāwandī said to Ibn al-Aʿrābī the man of letters: "Can clothing be tasted?" Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: "No garment and no clothing, O you man-ape (nisnās). Suppose you doubt that Muḥammad was a prophet, were he not an Arab?" Ibn al-Rāwandī's intent was to criticise this verse, namely that clothing is not tasted but worn, so it should have been said: "Then Allah clothed them with the garment of hunger," or "Then Allah made them taste the taste of hunger." I say his response comes from several aspects:

The first aspect: the states that occur to them through hunger are of two kinds:

One is that what is tasted is food, so when they lost the food, they became as though they were tasting hunger.

The second is that this hunger was intense and complete, so it became as though it surrounded them from all directions, and so it resembled a garment. The conclusion is that in that hunger there is a state resembling something tasted and a state resembling something worn. So Allah considered both considerations, and said: ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear.﴾

The second aspect: the meaning is that Allah made them know (ʿarrafahā) the garment of hunger and fear, but Allah expressed the making-known by the word "tasting" (idhāqah). The root of dhawq is with the mouth, then it may be borrowed and placed in the position of acquaintance, which is testing (ikhtibār). You say: "Examine so-and-so and taste what he has." The poet said:

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it,
and its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.

The garment of hunger and fear is what appeared upon them of emaciation, pallor of complexion, wasting of body, change of condition, and dimness of circumstance. Just as you say, "I came to know the bad effect of fear and hunger upon so-and-so," so too it is permissible to say, "I tasted the garment of hunger and fear upon so-and-so."

The third aspect: the word "garment" (libās) may be taken to mean contact (mamāssah), so the meaning becomes: "Then Allah made them taste the touch of hunger and fear."

Then Allah said: ﴿for what they used to do.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbās said: he means: for their deed toward the Prophet (ﷺ) when they denied him, expelled him from Makkah, and resolved to kill him. Al-Farrāʾ said: He did not say "for what she did," and similar to it in the Qur'an is abundant, among it His saying: ﴿So Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were resting at midday﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 4]. He did not say "while she was resting." The reality of the statement is that Allah described the town as being at rest, its provision coming to it abundantly, yet it denied the favours of Allah. All these attributes, although by the wording they are applied to the town, the real intended referent is its people. Therefore, at the end of the verse, He said: ﴿for what they used to do.﴾ And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 16, verses 113–114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And certainly there came to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the blessing of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the parable, He mentioned what was exemplified, saying: ﴿And certainly there came to them﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿a Messenger from among themselves﴾, meaning from themselves, whom they know by his lineage and descent, ﴿but they denied him, so the punishment seized them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "It means the hunger that was in Makkah." It has also been said: "It means the killing on the Day of Badr." I say: Ibn ʿAbbas's view is more preferable, because He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the blessing of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ That is, that hunger was only because of your disbelief, so abandon disbelief until you may eat. For this reason He said: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "So eat, O company of Muslims, of what Allah has provided for you," meaning from the spoils of war (*ghanaʾim*). Al-Kalbi said: "The leaders of Makkah spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when they were in distress, and they said: 'You have been hostile to the men, so what about the women and the children?' The supply of food had been cut off from them by the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he permitted the carrying of food to them, and food was carried to them. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good.﴾"

The statement that stands is what Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, after this verse: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah⦆ and so on. That is, when you believed and abandoned disbelief, eat the lawful and good, which is the spoils of war, and leave off the wicked things, which are carrion and blood.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that this verse, to its end, is mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah, where it has been explained, and there is no benefit in repetition. I say: He, exalted is He, restricted the prohibited things to these four items in this surah, because the word ʾinnamā (only, indicating restriction) conveys restriction. He also restricted them to these four in Surah al-An'am, in His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

Page 105
These two surahs are Meccan. He also restricted them to these four in Surah al-Baqarah, because this verse with this wording occurs in Surah al-Baqarah. He also restricted them in Surah al-Ma'idah, for He, exalted is He, said at the beginning of that surah: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Thus He permitted everything except what is recited to them. They agreed that what is meant by His saying ﴿to you﴾ is His saying in that surah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾. So He mentioned those four, which are mentioned in those three surahs. Then He said: ﴿and the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered; and what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. These things fall within carrion, and then He said: ﴿and what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], which is one of the categories falling under His saying: ﴿and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾.

Thus it is established that these four surahs indicate the restriction of the prohibited things to these four: two are Meccan and two are Medinan, for Surah al-Baqarah is Medinan, and Surah al-Ma'idah is among the last things Allah, exalted is He, revealed at Medina. Whoever denies the restriction of prohibition to these four, except what consensus and decisive proofs have excluded, is in danger of being brought to account, because these surahs show that restricting the prohibited things to these four was an established ruling at the beginning and end of the Meccan period and at the beginning and end of the Medinan period, and that He, exalted is He, repeated this explanation in these four surahs to cut off excuses and remove doubt. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 16, verses 116–117:

**His saying, may He be exalted:** ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as falsehood, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to fabricate against Allah a lie. Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah a lie will not succeed.﴾ ﴿A brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

**On the verse, there are several issues:**

**The first issue:** Know that when Allah, may He be exalted, restricted the prohibited things to those four, He emphasized that restriction and refuted the practice of the disbelievers, who sometimes added to these four and sometimes subtracted from them. They used to prohibit the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and which was left unridden), the *sa'iba* (a camel released to roam freely), the *wasila* (a she-goat that gave birth to females in succession, or similar practices), and the *ham* (a stallion camel freed after a set number of uses). They would also say: "What is in the bellies of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives." Thus they added to the prohibited things. They also added to the permitted things, because they made lawful carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what was dedicated to other than Allah, may He be exalted. So Allah, may He be exalted, made clear that the prohibited things are these four, and made clear that the things about which they say, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," are a lie and a fabrication against Allah. Then He mentioned the severe warning against this lie.

I say: When He, may He be exalted, clarified this restriction in these four surahs, and then mentioned in this verse that adding to them or subtracting from them is a lie and a fabrication against Allah, and something that warrants a severe warning, we know that there is nothing to add to this restriction. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Regarding the accusative case of *al-kadhib* (the lie) in His saying: ﴿what your tongues describe as the lie﴾, there are two views:

**The first:** Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: *ma* (ما) is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyya*), and the sense is: "Do not say, for the sake of your tongues' describing the lie, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful.'" Its parallel is that one would say: "Do not say: for such-and-such, such-and-such."

If they say: Reading the verse this way leads to repetition, since His saying ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ is the same thing.

The answer: His saying ﴿what your tongues describe as the lie﴾ does not contain a clarification that it is a lie against Allah, the Exalted. So He repeated His saying ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ in order to include this additional clarification. Similar instances in the Qur'an are numerous, namely that He, may He be exalted, mentions a statement and then repeats it exactly, with an added benefit.

**The second:** That *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), and the sense is: "Do not say about that which your tongues describe as a lie, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful.'" The word *fihi* (فيه, "in it/about it") is omitted because it is understood.

**The third issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿what your tongues describe as the lie﴾ is from eloquent and refined speech, as if the reality and essence of the lie were unknown, and their lying speech reveals the reality of the lie and clarifies its essence. This is an exaggeration in describing their speech as a lie. A parallel to it is the saying of Abu al-'Ala al-Ma'arri:

*"The lightning of al-Ma'arra passed after a lull, and it spent the night at Rama describing exhaustion."*

The meaning is that this lightning passed describing exhaustion; similarly here. And Allah knows best.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah a lie﴾. The meaning is that they used to attribute that prohibition and permission to Allah, may He be exalted, and say: "He commanded us with this." I think this *lam* (لام) is not the *lam* of purpose (*lam al-gharad*), because that fabrication was not their aim; rather it is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqiba*), like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that it would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

Al-Wahidi said: His saying ﴿so that you fabricate against Allah a lie﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for His saying ﴿what your tongues describe as the lie﴾, because their describing the lie is a fabrication against Allah, may He be exalted. So He explained their describing the lie as fabrication against Allah, may He be exalted. Then He threatened the fabricators, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah a lie will not succeed.﴾

Then He clarified that what they enjoy of the pleasures of this world will leave them soon, so He said: ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: their enjoyment is a brief enjoyment. Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed, the enjoyment of this whole world is a brief enjoyment. Then they will be returned to a painful punishment, which is His saying: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited what We have related to you before. And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Know that when Exalted is He explained what is lawful and what is unlawful for the people of Islam, He followed it with an explanation of the prohibitions specific to the Jews, saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited what We have related to you before﴾, and this is what was mentioned earlier in Surat al-An'am.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ Its explanation is what is mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 160].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed your Lord – for those who did evil in ignorance, then repented after that and reformed – indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Page 107
Know that the purpose is to show that fabricating lies against Allah and opposing the command of Allah does not prevent them from repentance and from obtaining forgiveness and mercy. The word "evil" (al-su') covers everything that is not fitting, namely disbelief (kufr) and sins (ma'asi), and everyone who does evil does it out of ignorance (jahala). As for disbelief: no one is pleased with it while knowing it to be disbelief, for he does not choose or approve of a creed unless he believes that creed to be true and right. As for sin: as long as desire does not come to dominate the intellect and knowledge, that sin does not proceed from him. Thus it is established that everyone who does evil only undertakes it because of ignorance. Then He said, may He be exalted: We have certainly emphasized the threat against those disbelievers who make things lawful and unlawful according to desire and who fabricate lies against Allah, may He be exalted. Then, after that, We say: indeed your Lord, with regard to those who did evil because of ignorance, then repented after that – that is, after that evil deed; it is also said: after that ignorance – and then, after repentance from those evil deeds, they reformed, that is, they believed and obeyed Allah.

Then He repeated His saying: ﴿indeed your Lord, after that﴾ as an emphasis. Then He said: ﴿is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He is indeed Forgiving and Merciful toward that evil which proceeded from them because of ignorance. The gist of the discussion is that a person, even if he has persisted in disbelief and sins for an age, an extremely long time, when he repents from it, believes, and performs righteous deeds, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful; He accepts his repentance and delivers him from punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 16, verses 120–123:

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah), devoutly obedient to God, a hanif (one who inclines wholly to the religion of Islam), and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Grateful for His bounties. He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾ ﴿We gave him good in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, refuted in this surah the doctrines of the polytheists regarding several matters, among them their claim that God has partners and equals, and their criticism of the prophecy of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, and their saying: "If God had sent a messenger, that messenger would have been from the angels." Among them also was their claim to make lawful things that God had forbidden and to forbid things that God had made lawful. When He had thoroughly refuted their doctrines in these statements, and since Abraham, peace be upon him, was the leader of the monotheists and the exemplar of the fundamentalists (usul, i.e., the foundations of religion), and he was the one who called people to monotheism, the abandonment of polytheism, and the sacred law (shara'i'), and since the polytheists took pride in him, acknowledged the excellence of his way, and affirmed the obligation of following him, God, exalted is He, therefore mentioned him at the end of this surah and related his method regarding monotheism, so that this would lead these polytheists to acknowledge monotheism and to turn back from polytheism.

Know that God, exalted is He, described Abraham, peace be upon him, with several attributes:

**The first attribute:** that he was an ummah. There are several interpretations of this:

The first: that he alone was a nation among the nations, because of his perfection in the qualities of goodness, as in the saying:

*"It is not far-fetched for God to gather the whole world into one [man]."*

Page 108

The second: Mujahid said: he was a believer alone, while all the people were disbelievers; for this reason he alone was an ummah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say concerning Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl: "God will raise him up as an ummah alone."

The third: that ummah is in the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul (object), like ruhlah and bughyah. Thus the ummah is the one who is followed as a leader. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader (imam) for the people.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 124]

The fourth: that he, peace be upon him, was the cause for which his community was distinguished from others by monotheism and the true religion. Since he operated as the cause for the emergence of that community, God named him by the term ummah, applying the name of the effect to the cause. It is related from Shahr ibn Hawshab that there was never a land without fourteen (such persons) through whom God repels harm from the people of the earth, except in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he was alone.

**The second attribute:** that he was qanit (devoutly obedient) to God. The qanit is one who fulfills what God has commanded him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: its meaning is that he was obedient to God.

**The third attribute:** that he was hanif. The hanif is one who inclines toward the religion of Islam with an inclination that never leaves him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: he was the first to undergo circumcision, to perform the rites of the Hajj, and to sacrifice animals. These are the characteristics of the hanifiyyah.

**The fourth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾ Its meaning is that he was a monotheist in his youth and in his old age. What confirms this is that most of the concern of Abraham, peace be upon him, was in establishing the science of the fundamentals (usul al-'ilm). He established the proof for the existence of the Creator (al-Sani') before the king of his time, namely His saying: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 258] Then he refuted the worship of idols and stars by His saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ [Al-An'am: 76] Then he smashed those idols, until the matter reached the point where they threw him into the fire. Then he asked God to show him how the dead are brought to life, so that he might attain greater tranquility. Whoever understands the science of the Qur'an knows that Abraham, peace be upon him, was immersed in the sea of monotheism.

**The fifth attribute:** His saying: ﴿grateful for His bounties.﴾ It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, would not eat his midday meal except with a guest. One day he found no guest, so he delayed his meal. Then he saw a group of angels in the form of humans, and he invited them to the meal. They revealed that they had the illness of leprosy (judham). He said: "Now it is obligatory upon me to eat with you. Were it not for your honor before God, exalted is He, He would not have afflicted you with this affliction!"

If it is said: the word "bounties" (an'um) is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah), while the bounties of God upon Abraham, peace be upon him, were numerous. Why then did He say: ﴿grateful for His bounties⌋?

We say: The meaning is that he was grateful for all the bounties of God, if they were few, so how much more so for the numerous ones!

**The sixth attribute:** His saying: ﴿He chose him﴾, that is, He selected him for prophethood. Al-ijtiba' is to take a thing in its entirety. It is an ifti'al form from jabaytu, and its root meaning is the gathering of water in a basin; al-jabiyah is the basin.

**The seventh attribute:** His saying: ﴿and guided him to a straight path,﴾ that is, in calling to God, encouraging adherence to the true religion, and warning against the false religion. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it.﴾ [Al-An'am: 153]

**The eighth attribute:** His saying: ﴿We gave him good in this world.﴾ Qatadah said: God made him beloved to all creation, so all the adherents of religions acknowledge him. As for Muslims, Jews, and Christians, this is clear. As for the disbelievers of Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs, they have no pride except in him. The fuller explanation is that God answered his supplication in His saying: ﴿and make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 84]

Others said: it is the saying of one of us who prays: "As You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham." It was also said: it means truthfulness, fidelity, and worship.

Page 109

**The ninth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.﴾

If it is said: why did He say: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous,﴾ and not say: "and indeed in the Hereafter he is in the highest ranks of the righteous"?

We say: Because God related of him that he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 83] So He said here: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous,﴾ as an indication that God answered his supplication. Moreover, being among the righteous does not preclude that he is in the highest ranks of the righteous, for God has explained this in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people; We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ [Al-An'am: 83]

Know that when God, exalted is He, described Abraham, peace be upon him, with these lofty and noble attributes, He said: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif.﴾ Concerning this there are several discussions:

**The first discussion:** Some people said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was upon the shari'ah of Abraham, peace be upon him, and he had no sacred law that was unique to him; rather, the purpose of his mission, peace be upon him, was to revive the shari'ah of Abraham, peace be upon him. They relied upon this verse to establish their position. This view is weak, because God described Abraham, peace be upon him, in this verse as one who was not among the polytheists; so when He said: ﴿follow the religion of Abraham,﴾ that is what was meant.

If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) negated polytheism and affirmed monotheism on the basis of decisive proofs, and if that is the case he was not a follower of anyone; therefore it is impossible to interpret His saying: ﴿that you follow﴾ in this sense; it must therefore be interpreted as referring to the laws in which following is valid.

We say: It is possible that what is meant is the command to follow him in the manner of calling to monotheism, namely that one should call to it with gentleness and ease, presenting proofs repeatedly in many varieties, according to the customary method found in the Qur'an.

**The second discussion:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The word "then" (thumma) in His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you﴾ indicates the magnification of the rank of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the exaltation of his station, and the announcement that the most noble honor granted to the friend of God (Abraham), and the most exalted blessing he was given, was that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would follow his religion. For this word indicates that this description is far removed in rank from the other praises with which God praised him.

If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) negated polytheism and affirmed monotheism on the basis of decisive proofs, and if that is the case he was not a follower of anyone; therefore it is impossible to interpret His saying: ﴿that you follow﴾ in this sense; it must therefore be interpreted as referring to the laws in which following is valid.

We say: It is possible that what is meant is the command to follow him in the manner of calling to monotheism, namely that one should call to it with gentleness and ease, presenting proofs repeatedly in many varieties, according to the customary method found in the Qur'an.

**The second discussion:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The word "then" (thumma) in His saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you﴾ indicates the magnification of the rank of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the exaltation of his station, and the announcement that the most noble honor granted to the friend of God (Abraham), and the most exalted blessing he was given, was that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would follow his religion. For this word indicates that this description is far removed in rank from the other praises with which God praised him.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 16, verses 120–123:

**His saying, exalted is He:** ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah), devoutly obedient to God, a hanif (one who inclines wholly to the religion of Islam), and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Grateful for His bounties. He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾ ﴿We gave him good in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, refuted in this surah the doctrines of the polytheists regarding several matters, among them their claim that God has partners and equals, and their criticism of the prophecy of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, and their saying: "If God had sent a messenger, that messenger would have been from the angels." Among them also was their claim to make lawful things that God had forbidden and to forbid things that God had made lawful. When He had thoroughly refuted their doctrines in these statements, and since Abraham, peace be upon him, was the leader of the monotheists and the exemplar of the fundamentalists (usul, i.e., the foundations of religion), and he was the one who called people to monotheism, the abandonment of polytheism, and the sacred law (shara'i'), and since the polytheists took pride in him, acknowledged the excellence of his way, and affirmed the obligation of following him, God, exalted is He, therefore mentioned him at the end of this surah and related his method regarding monotheism, so that this would lead these polytheists to acknowledge monotheism and to turn back from polytheism.

Know that God, exalted is He, described Abraham, peace be upon him, with several attributes:

**The first attribute:** that he was an ummah. There are several interpretations of this:

The first: that he alone was a nation among the nations, because of his perfection in the qualities of goodness, as in the saying:

*"It is not far-fetched for God to gather the whole world into one [man]."*

Page 108

The second: Mujahid said: he was a believer alone, while all the people were disbelievers; for this reason he alone was an ummah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say concerning Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl: "God will raise him up as an ummah alone."

The third: that ummah is in the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul (object), like ruhlah and bughyah. Thus the ummah is the one who is followed as a leader. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader (imam) for the people.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 124]

The fourth: that he, peace be upon him, was the cause for which his community was distinguished from others by monotheism and the true religion. Since he operated as the cause for the emergence of that community, God named him by the term ummah, applying the name of the effect to the cause. It is related from Shahr ibn Hawshab that there was never a land without fourteen (such persons) through whom God repels harm from the people of the earth, except in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he was alone.

**The second attribute:** that he was qanit (devoutly obedient) to God. The qanit is one who fulfills what God has commanded him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: its meaning is that he was obedient to God.

**The third attribute:** that he was hanif. The hanif is one who inclines toward the religion of Islam with an inclination that never leaves him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: he was the first to undergo circumcision, to perform the rites of the Hajj, and to sacrifice animals. These are the characteristics of the hanifiyyah.

**The fourth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and he was not one of the polytheists.﴾ Its meaning is that he was a monotheist in his youth and in his old age. What confirms this is that most of the concern of Abraham, peace be upon him, was in establishing the science of the fundamentals (usul al-'ilm). He established the proof for the existence of the Creator (al-Sani') before the king of his time, namely His saying: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 258] Then he refuted the worship of idols and stars by His saying: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ [Al-An'am: 76] Then he smashed those idols, until the matter reached the point where they threw him into the fire. Then he asked God to show him how the dead are brought to life, so that he might attain greater tranquility. Whoever understands the science of the Qur'an knows that Abraham, peace be upon him, was immersed in the sea of monotheism.

**The fifth attribute:** His saying: ﴿grateful for His bounties.﴾ It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, would not eat his midday meal except with a guest. One day he found no guest, so he delayed his meal. Then he saw a group of angels in the form of humans, and he invited them to the meal. They revealed that they had the illness of leprosy (judham). He said: "Now it is obligatory upon me to eat with you. Were it not for your honor before God, exalted is He, He would not have afflicted you with this affliction!"

If it is said: the word "bounties" (an'um) is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah), while the bounties of God upon Abraham, peace be upon him, were numerous. Why then did He say: ﴿grateful for His bounties⌋?

We say: The meaning is that he was grateful for all the bounties of God, if they were few, so how much more so for the numerous ones!

**The sixth attribute:** His saying: ﴿He chose him﴾, that is, He selected him for prophethood. Al-ijtiba' is to take a thing in its entirety. It is an ifti'al form from jabaytu, and its root meaning is the gathering of water in a basin; al-jabiyah is the basin.

**The seventh attribute:** His saying: ﴿and guided him to a straight path,﴾ that is, in calling to God, encouraging adherence to the true religion, and warning against the false religion. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is My straight path, so follow it.﴾ [Al-An'am: 153]

**The eighth attribute:** His saying: ﴿We gave him good in this world.﴾ Qatadah said: God made him beloved to all creation, so all the adherents of religions acknowledge him. As for Muslims, Jews, and Christians, this is clear. As for the disbelievers of Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs, they have no pride except in him. The fuller explanation is that God answered his supplication in His saying: ﴿and make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 84]

Others said: it is the saying of one of us who prays: "As You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham." It was also said: it means truthfulness, fidelity, and worship.

Page 109

**The ninth attribute:** His saying: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous.﴾

If it is said: why did He say: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous,﴾ and not say: "and indeed in the Hereafter he is in the highest ranks of the righteous"?

We say: Because God related of him that he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 83] So He said here: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous,﴾ as an indication that God answered his supplication. Moreover, being among the righteous does not preclude that he is in the highest ranks of the righteous, for God has explained this in another verse, namely His saying: ﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people; We raise by degrees whom We will.﴾ [Al-An'am: 83]
