Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it. And indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾

Know that when the Exalted commanded Muhammad ﷺ to follow Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and Muhammad (peace be upon him) had chosen Friday, this following is achieved only if we say that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had, in his law, chosen Friday. At this point, a questioner may ask: why did the Jews choose Saturday?

God the Exalted answered him with His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it.﴾ Regarding the verse there are two views.

The first view: al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said: Musa commanded them concerning Friday, and said: "Devote yourselves to Allah one day in every seven days, which is Friday; do not do any of your works on it." But they refused to accept this and said: "We want only the day on which He finished the creation," which is Saturday. So God the Exalted made the Sabbath theirs and made it strict upon them concerning it. Then 'Isa (peace be upon him) also came to them with Friday, and the Christians said: "We do not want their festival to come after our festival," and they adopted Sunday.

Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed Allah prescribed Friday upon those who were before us, and they differed concerning it, but Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Having understood this, we say: His saying, ﴿concerning it﴾, means: concerning their prophet Musa, since he commanded them concerning Friday, but they chose Saturday. Thus their differing about Saturday was a differing against their prophet concerning that day, i.e., on account of it. The meaning of His saying ﴿they differed concerning it﴾ is not that the Jews differed about it, some of them saying for Saturday and some not saying so, because the Jews agreed upon that. So it is not possible to interpret His saying ﴿they differed concerning it﴾ in this way; rather, the correct view is what we have already presented.

If someone says: Is there in reason an aspect that indicates that Friday is more excellent than Saturday? This is because the people of the religions agree that God created the world in six days, and began creation and bringing into being on Sunday, and it was completed on Friday, so Saturday became the day of rest. The Jews said: "We agree with our Lord in ceasing works," so they designated Saturday for this meaning. The Christians said: "The beginning of creation and bringing into being is Sunday, so we will make this day our festival." These two aspects are intelligible. So what is the aspect in making Friday a festival for us?

We say: Friday is the day of perfection and completion, and the attainment of completion and perfection necessitates complete joy and great delight. So making Friday the day of festival is more fitting from this aspect. And Allah knows best.

The second view concerning their differing about Saturday: they permitted hunting on it at times and forbade it at other times, whereas it was obligatory upon them to agree on its prohibition with one word.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾ The meaning: He, may He be exalted, will judge on the Day of Resurrection, rewarding the righteous and punishing the wrongdoers.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 16, verse 125:**

God Most High says: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom (*hikmah*) and good admonition (*mawʿizah hasanah*), and argue with them in the best manner. Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾

[p. 111]

Know that when God Most High commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow Ibrahim (peace be upon him), He explained the thing in which he was to follow him, so He said: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾.

Know also that God Most High commanded His Messenger to invite people by one of these three methods: wisdom, good admonition, and disputation in the best manner. God Most High mentioned this disputation in another verse, saying: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 46]. Since God Most High mentioned these three methods and joined some of them to others, it follows that they must be distinct and different methods. I have not seen in the exegetes any concise and precise discussion of this.

Know that calling to a doctrine or a position must necessarily be based on proof (*hujjah*) and clear evidence (*bayyinah*). The purpose of mentioning the proof is either to establish that doctrine and that belief in the hearts of the listeners, or the purpose is to bind the opponent and silence him.

As for the first category: it is again divided into two, because the proof is either a true proof that is certain, definitive, free from the possibility of its contradictory, or it is not so, but rather a proof that yields apparent probability and complete persuasion. Through this division it becomes clear that the proofs are confined to these three categories:

The first: the definitive proof that yields certain beliefs. This is what is called *hikmah* (wisdom), and this is the most noble of ranks and the highest of stations. It is the one of which God said in describing it: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269].

The second: the probable indications and persuasive proofs, and this is the good admonition (*mawʿizah hasanah*).

The third: the proofs whose purpose in mentioning them is to bind opponents and silence them, and this is disputation (*jidal*). This disputation is of two kinds:

The first kind: that it be an argument composed of premises accepted as known among the majority, or of premises accepted by that speaker. This disputation is the disputation conducted in the best manner.

The second kind: that the argument be composed of false and corrupt premises, yet its speaker tries to pass them off upon the listeners through foolishness, clamor, false tricks, and corrupt methods. This kind does not befit people of virtue; what befits them is the first kind, and that is what is meant by God's words: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that the proofs and arguments are confined to these three categories mentioned in this verse.

Having understood this, we say: the people of knowledge are three groups. The perfect seekers of true knowledge and certain sciences; dialogue with these cannot take place except through definitive, certain proofs, and this is wisdom.

The second kind: those whose natures are dominated by contentiousness and quarrelsomeness, not by the seeking of true knowledge and certain sciences. The dialogue befitting these is disputation that yields silencing and binding.

These two kinds are the two extremes: the first is the extreme of perfection, and the second is the extreme of deficiency.

As for the third kind: it is the middle, and these are the people who have not reached in perfection the level of the verifying sages, nor in deficiency and baseness the level of the clamorous quarrelsome ones. Rather they are people who have remained upon the original nature and innate soundness, and have not reached the degree of readiness to grasp certain proofs and wise knowledge. Dialogue with these cannot take place except through good admonition, and the least of it is disputation. The highest ranks of creation are the verifying sages, and the middle of them is the general mass of people, who are the people of soundness, and among them is the majority and the dominance; and the lowest ranks are those who are disposed to the nature of contention and quarrel. Thus God's words: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ mean: invite the strong, perfect ones to the true religion with wisdom, which is the definitive, certain demonstrations, and invite the common people with good admonition, which is the persuasive probable certain indications. And speak with the clamorous ones through disputation in the best and most perfect manner.

Among the subtleties of this verse is that He said: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾, restricting the invitation to the mention of these two kinds; because if the invitation is by definitive proofs, it is wisdom, and if it is by probable proofs, it is good admonition. As for disputation, it is not of the category of invitation; rather its aim is another purpose different from invitation, namely binding and silencing. For this reason He did not say: "Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom, good admonition, and the best disputation," but rather He separated disputation from the category of invitation, as an alert that invitation is not achieved by it, and that its purpose is something else. And God knows best.

Know that these discussions indicate that God Most High included in this verse these lofty and noble secrets, although most of creation was heedless of them. Thus it becomes clear that this noble Book does not lead to what is in it of secrets except those who are among the elite of people of insight.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best those who are guided﴾. The meaning is: you are charged with calling to God Most High by these three methods, but as for the attainment of guidance, it does not depend on you. He knows best the astray, and He knows best the guided. What I hold in this matter is that the essences of human souls differ in their quiddity: some are souls that are luminous and pure, little attached to corporeal things, and much drawn to the world of spiritual things; and some are dark and turbid, strongly attached to corporeal things, and utterly unmindful of spiritual things. Since these dispositions are necessary consequences of their essences, it is therefore impossible for them to be transformed or to cease. For this reason God Most High said, in effect: Occupy yourself with the invitation, and do not hope for the attainment of guidance for all, for He is the One who knows the misguidance of the misguided, ignorant souls and the illumination of the luminous, pure souls. For every soul there is a particular innate nature and a particular quiddity, as He said: ﴿The nature of God upon which He created people; there is no altering of the creation of God﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. And God knows best.

[Page 113]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were made to suffer. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient.﴾ ﴿Be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah. And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress at what they plot.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good.﴾

Concerning the verse there are issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: There are three opinions regarding this verse.

[Page 114]

The first opinion, which is held by the majority: "When the Prophet ﷺ saw Hamzah, and they had mutilated him, he said: 'By Allah, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place.' Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended with the final verses of Surat al-Nahl, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained and held back from what he had intended."

This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the narration of Ata', and of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Sha'bi. Based on this, they said: the whole of Surat al-Nahl is Meccan except these three verses.

The second opinion: that this was before the command to take up the sword and fight, when the Muslims had been commanded to fight only against those who fought them and not to initiate combat. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190]. In this verse, Allah commanded that they punish with the like of the harm inflicted on them, and not exceed it.

The third opinion: that the purpose of this verse is to forbid the wronged person from taking more than his due from the wrongdoer. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Sirin. Ibn Sirin said: If a man takes something from you, take from him the like of it.

I say: To apply this verse to a particular incident that has no connection with what precedes it would cause disorder in the arrangement of Allah's speech, and that would open the way to criticism of it, and that is extremely far-fetched. Rather, the most correct view in my opinion is to say: The meaning is that He, Exalted is He, commanded Muhammad ﷺ to invite people to the true religion by one of three methods: wisdom, good admonition, and disputation in the best manner. Then that invitation entails calling them to abandon the religion of their fathers and forefathers, to turn away from it, and to judge it as disbelief and error. This disturbs hearts and alarms breasts, and it moves most of the listeners to intend harm to that caller: at times by killing, at times by striking, and at times by insulting. Then when that righteous man witnesses such folly and hears such clamor, his nature will inevitably move him to discipline those fools, at times by killing and at times by striking. At this point, He commanded those who are in the right in this situation to observe justice and fairness and to refrain from excess. This is the correct interpretation to which the verse must be applied.

If it is said: Do you then reject what is reported, that "he, peace be upon him, gave up his resolve to mutilate and expiated for his oath," on account of this verse?

We say: There is no need to reject that report, for we say: that incident falls within the general scope of this verse, so it is possible to invoke the general sense of this verse concerning that incident. What is disputed is only that it is not permissible to restrict this verse to that single incident, because that would cause disorder in the arrangement of Allah's speech.

The second issue: Know that He, Exalted is He, commanded the observance of justice and fairness in this verse, and arranged this in four stages.

The first stage: His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were made to suffer.﴾ That is, if you desire to exact retribution (qisas), then be content with an equal measure and do not exceed it, for exacting more is injustice, and injustice is forbidden by Allah's justice and mercy. In His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were made to suffer,﴾ there is an indication that the better course for him is not to act. It is as when you say to the sick person: "If you eat fruit, then eat apples." What is meant is that the better course for you is not to eat it. So Allah, Exalted is He, has mentioned by way of indication and allusion that the better course is to leave it.

The second stage: the movement from allusion to explicit statement, which is His saying: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient.﴾ This is an explicit statement that the better course is to abandon that retaliation, because mercy is better than harshness, and forgiveness is better than inflicting pain.

[Page 114]

The third stage: the coming of a command in definite terms to abandon it, which is His saying: ﴿Be patient.﴾ Because in the second stage He mentioned that abandoning it is better and preferable, in this third stage He explicitly commanded patience. And since patience in this situation is difficult and hard, He mentioned after it what indicates its ease, saying: ﴿And your patience is not but by Allah,﴾ that is, by His enabling and His help. This is the general, fundamental cause that yields patience and the attainment of all kinds of acts of obedience. And when He mentioned this general, fundamental cause, He mentioned after it the particular, proximate cause, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress at what they plot.﴾ This is because a person's resort to retaliation, and to inflicting harm on others, occurs only at the surge of anger, and intense anger arises only from one of two things:

The first: the loss of a benefit that was present in the past, and to this the words ﴿do not grieve over them﴾ refer. It has been said: its meaning is: do not grieve over the slain of Uhud. Its meaning is: do not grieve because of the loss of those friends. Its outcome returns to the loss of benefit.

The second cause: the intense anger caused by the expectation of harm in the future, and to this the words ﴿and do not be in distress at what they plot﴾ refer. Whoever comprehends these subtleties will know that no speech can be more inclusive of beauty and precision than this speech.

It is as when you say to the sick person: "If you eat fruit, then eat apples." What is meant is that the better course for you is not to eat it. So Allah, Exalted is He, has mentioned by way of indication and allusion that the better course is to leave it.

The second stage: the movement from allusion to explicit statement, which is His saying: ﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient.﴾ This is an explicit statement that the better course is to abandon that retaliation, because mercy is better than harshness, and forgiveness is better than inflicting pain.

[Page 114]

The third stage: the coming of a command in definite terms to abandon it, which is His saying: ﴿Be patient.﴾ Because in the second stage He mentioned that abandoning it is better and preferable, in this third stage He explicitly commanded patience. And since patience in this situation is difficult and hard, He mentioned after it what indicates its ease, saying: ﴿And your patience is not but by Allah,﴾ that is, by His enabling and His help. This is the general, fundamental cause that yields patience and the attainment of all kinds of acts of obedience. And when He mentioned this general, fundamental cause, He mentioned after it the particular, proximate cause, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress at what they plot.﴾ This is because a person's resort to retaliation, and to inflicting harm on others, occurs only at the surge of anger, and intense anger arises only from one of two things:

The first: the loss of a benefit that was present in the past, and to this the words ﴿do not grieve over them﴾ refer. It has been said: its meaning is: do not grieve over the slain of Uhud. Its meaning is: do not grieve because of the loss of those friends. Its outcome returns to the loss of benefit.

The second cause: the intense anger caused by the expectation of harm in the future, and to this the words ﴿and do not be in distress at what they plot﴾ refer. Whoever comprehends these subtleties will know that no speech can be more inclusive of beauty and precision than this speech.

Remaining discussions on the wording of the verse:

First issue: Ibn Kathir recited "وَلَا تَكُ فِي ضِيقٍ" (wa-la taku fi ḍīqin) with a kasra on the ḍād, and likewise in Surah an-Naml. The rest of the readers recited it with a fatḥa on the ḍād in both places. As for the basis of the well-known reading, there are several points. Abu 'Ubayda said: ḍīq with a kasra refers to scarcity of livelihood and dwellings, while what is in the heart is ḍayq. Abu 'Amr said: ḍīq with a kasra means hardship (shiddah), while ḍayq with a fatḥa means grief (ghamm). Al-Qutaybi said: ḍayq is a lightened form of ḍayyiq, like hayn and hayyin, and layn and layyin. By this route we say that Ibn Kathir's reading is sound.

Second issue: it has been read as "وَلَا تَكُنْ فِي ضَيْقٍ" (wa-la takun fi ḍayqin).

Third issue: this is from the language of inversion (al-maqlub), because ḍayq is an attribute, and an attribute exists in the thing described, while the thing described does not exist in the attribute. So the meaning is: let there be no constriction in you. However, the benefit of His saying "وَلَا تَكُ فِي ضَيْقٍ" is that when constriction becomes great and strong, it becomes like a thing encompassing a person from all sides, and becomes like a garment enveloping him. Thus the benefit of mentioning this expression is this meaning, and God knows best.

The fourth rank: His saying, "إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا وَالَّذِينَ هُم مُّحْسِنُونَ" (Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good). This runs in the manner of a warning, because in the first rank He encouraged abandoning retaliation by way of allusion; in the second rank He moved from allusion to explicit statement, which is His saying, "وَلَئِن صَبَرْتُمْ لَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لِّلصَّابِرِينَ" (But if you are patient, it is better for the patient); in the third rank He commanded patience categorically; and in this fourth rank it is as if He mentioned the threat regarding the act of retaliation, saying, "إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا" (those who refrain from exceeding the measure in exacting retribution) "وَالَّذِينَ هُم مُّحْسِنُونَ" (those who are doers of good in abandoning the very principle of retaliation). So if you wish that I be with you, then be among the God-fearing and among the good-doers.

Whoever reflects on this order will know that enjoining good and forbidding evil must be carried out gently and kindly, rank by rank. When Allah said to His Messenger, "ادْعُ إِلَىٰ سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِالْحِكْمَةِ وَالْمَوْعِظَةِ الْحَسَنَةِ" (Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition), He mentioned these four ranks, as a reminder that calling to God with wisdom and good admonition must take place in this manner. And upon standing on these subtleties, the intelligent person knows that this noble Book is a sea without shore.

Third matter: His saying, "إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا" refers to His being with them through mercy, favour and rank. His saying, "الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا" indicates veneration of the command of Allah, the Exalted, and His saying, "وَالَّذِينَ هُم مُّحْسِنُونَ" indicates compassion toward the creatures of Allah. This shows that the perfection of happiness for a human being lies in these two matters: namely, venerating the command of Allah, the Exalted, and compassion toward the creatures of Allah. Some shaykhs expressed this, saying: The perfection of the path is truthfulness with the Truth and good conduct with creation. The sages said: The perfection of a human being is to know the Truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. It is reported of Hirim ibn Hayyan that when he was near death he was told, "Make a bequest," and he said: "A bequest is only of wealth, and I have no wealth; but I bequeath to you the final verses of Surat an-Nahl."

Fourth matter: Some said that His statement, exalted is He, "وَإِنْ عَاقَبْتُمْ فَعَاقِبُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا عُوقِبْتُم بِهِ وَلَئِن صَبَرْتُمْ لَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لِّلصَّابِرِينَ" (And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted; but if you are patient, it is better for the patient), is abrogated by the verse of the sword. This is extremely far-fetched, because the purpose of this verse is to teach good manners in the manner of calling to Allah, the Exalted, and abandoning transgression and seeking more; these matters have no connection with the verse of the sword. Most commentators are preoccupied with multiplying claims of abrogation, and I see no benefit in it. And Allah knows best what is correct.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed on Tuesday night, after the late night prayer, at a moderate time. He, may Allah have mercy on him, also said: The Truth is precious, the path is distant, the vehicle is weak, nearness is distance, union is separation, realities are guarded, meanings are hidden in the deepest unseen, secrets beyond might are stored away, and in the hand of creation there is only talk and rumour, and perfection belongs only to Allah, Lord of majesty and honour. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family and companions, and peace.
